Exhibitions › Approaches

Approaches

The theoretical framings, concepts and methods used in the 54 books and articles this site is built from, grouped into 13 families, with suggestions for carrying each over to a new case study. 452 concepts are recorded, each with the author's definition, a quotation, and a page reference.

How this was made: each text's introduction, conclusion and theoretical passages were read by machine and its concepts recorded with line references; every quotation was checked by script to occur in the text. The thematic essays were then written from those records. Nothing here was checked by a person, and the readers did not read every chapter of every book. Definitions report how each author uses a term in that text, which may differ from the theorist's own usage. "Carrying it over" and "Possible use elsewhere" are suggestions for research, not findings. References lead to the text's entry on the contents page; exhibition names lead to their study pages.

What counts as an exhibition: typologies and periodisations

How the texts define, classify and periodise exhibitions. 19 concepts from 13 texts

Typological and periodising approaches ask what kind of event an exhibition was before they ask what it meant. They sort fairs by organiser, purpose and format, and they place each event in a sequence, so that one case can be read against a category and a phase. Mandell's split between state-directed universal expositions and business-run exhibitions is the clearest case of a category doing analytic work (Mandell 1967; Mandell 1967p. 7). Benedict, Park, and Rydell with Findling and Pelle each divide the history of fairs at one event: New York 1939, Seoul 1915, and the Spanish-American War of 1898 (Benedict 1983p. 59; Parkp. 21; Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000).

The core texts are Findling and Pelle's two reference works, whose terms and chronology frame the others (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 8; Findling & Pelle 1990); Benedict's anthropology of fairs, whose essays include the Panama Pacific Exposition of 1915 (Benedict 1983p. 60); and Denton's museum types, which carry the same sorting into museums (Denton 2014p. 10).

Periodisation by turning point

Several texts divide the history of fairs at one event and describe what changed afterwards. Benedict makes the New York World's Fair of 1939 a break: "The New York World’s Fair of 1939 represents a watershed in international" (Benedict 1983p. 59). Afterwards fairs were no longer the venue for important congresses, gave no prizes, and became trade shows and amusement parks (Benedict 1983p. 60).

Park places the Seoul 1915 exhibition at the start of colonial exposition culture. Some thirty large and small expositions followed between 1915 and 1940 (Parkp. 21), and the 1915 exhibition's features recur in the Chosŏn Exposition of 1929 and the Great Chosŏn Exposition of 1940 (Parkp. 21). Park's conclusion is that "new era of expositions had begun" in modern Korea (Parkp. 21).

Rydell, Findling and Pelle divide American fairs at 1898. Before the Spanish-American War, fairs were organised by a wealthy, business-oriented elite to show Anglo-Saxon heritage; from 1898 to 1916 they displayed the new colonial empire and presented American paternalism as benefiting its subjects (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Maloney's garden history uses a similar bracket: a "golden period" of exposition landscaping, running from 1870 to 1940 (Maloney 2012p. 6; Maloney 2012p. 199). Mathur's three moments, imperial, nationalist and postcolonial, give her case studies a sequence, though not a chronology (Mathur 2007p. 26; Mathur 2007).

Shifts in the aims and forms of fairs

Hotta-Lister describes a move from novelties, fine arts and new technology (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 4) to themed displays and entertainment (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 4). Educational exhibits were presented as entertainment, and exhibits of colonial peoples, the live exhibits, became standard (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 5). The author applies this to London 1910 at the White City (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 5).

The book reads the medium as moving from trade to public relations, and its stages run from the lauding of firsts, through nationalist propaganda, to marketplace dynamics (Allwood et al. 2001; Allwood et al. 2001p. 194). Paris 1878 and the Festival of Britain of 1951 are cited as fairs held to restore national pride after war (Allwood et al. 2001). Findling and Pelle describe a parallel shift from one large building, such as London 1851's Crystal Palace, to thematic and national pavilions, with fine art and amusements added (Findling & Pelle 1990).

Typologies by organiser, category and terminology

Mandell separates the French universal expositions, which the government ran as its own projects, from exhibitions elsewhere, which businessmen arranged with subsidies (Mandell 1967). French exhibitions were always state-directed (Mandell 1967p. 7), and after 1900 the Comité français des expositions grew to control French policy (Mandell 1967p. 119).

Findling and Pelle use the terms world's fairs, exhibitions, expositions and expo interchangeably, though they differ (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 8). Following Kenneth Luckhurst, they hold that exhibitions are "solely for displaying or exhibiting goods," whereas fairs connote their sale (Findling & Pelle 1990). The BIE passage in the Encyclopedia separates major events with a general theme from smaller, specialised ones (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 412). Allan and Reid note that specialised expositions multiplied and forced the BIE to tighten its timing (Allwood et al. 2001p. 195), and they call the specialised event, on the face of it, the ideal type (Allwood et al. 2001p. 196).

Displays organised by classification and theme

Chandler's account of the Paris 1867 palace shows products grouped by nature and by nationality, with a Group X arranged by makers' intentions (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 37; Findling & Pelle 1990p. 38). The text reads this as carrying the 1855 classification further, and as the legacy of Bonapartist reform (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 38).

Allwood defines the thematic exhibition: "The first example of a true thematic exhibition was not seen until 1867." (Allwood et al. 2001). Linked themes gave viewers more insight than miscellaneous objects with simple labels (Allwood et al. 2001), and Le Play's history-of-work gallery is traced forward to Expo 67 at Montreal (Allwood et al. 2001p. 32).

Henry sorts the displays of the Seoul 1915 exhibition into three techniques (Henry 2014p. 102; Henry 2014p. 104). The museological method classified goods on a uniform scale (Henry 2014p. 104). The dichotomizing technique set a precolonial past against a colonial present, and Henry contrasts its temporal logic with the "inherently spatializing effect of the museological method," (Henry 2014p. 104). Chu Yun-jŏng is credited with the decontextualizing vision (Henry 2014p. 104).

Museum types and their political roles

Denton organises the book by museum type, following an emic Chinese typology: "I have chosen to organize this book around museum types and not themes in part" (Denton 2014p. 10). Each type plays its own political role; memorial halls read as political modelling and military museums project state power (Denton 2014p. 10). Memorial halls appear in chapters 4 and 7 (Denton 2014p. 10).

Clifford sets out a schematic contrast. Majority museums articulate cosmopolitan culture, science, art and humanism, while "Tribal museums express local culture, oppositional politics, kinship, ethnicity, and tradition." (Karp & Lavine 1991). Tribal institutions aim at local audiences, and the art and culture distinction is often irrelevant or subverted within them (Karp & Lavine 1991). Denton's type is emic and tied to a national political order, whereas Clifford's is relational, defined by a museum's position towards majority power (Denton 2014p. 10; Karp & Lavine 1991).

Idea-driven exhibition

Crew and Sims make the research database, rather than the object, the final source of authority and authentication (Karp & Lavine 1991). Objects keep their place as evidence but lose their primacy (Karp & Lavine 1991). Objects are used generically, as representatives of the types that could have been used in a setting, as in the northern home room of Field to Factory (Karp & Lavine 1991).

Debates and limits

Benedict and Hotta-Lister disagree about what a trade event is. Benedict argues that the exhibitors' aim was ultimately trade, even where educational and artistic displays seem central (Benedict 1983). Hotta-Lister argues that the 1910 Exhibition was neither a failure nor a mere trade fair, and treats that proof as of cardinal importance (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 7). Findling and Pelle tie fairs to commerce (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 8), so the two accounts turn on whether a trade function excludes educational and political purpose.

Denton argues against much museum theory, which stresses the institution's power to impose ideology, and sets against it scholarship in which vernacular memory also counts (Denton 2014p. 13). Benedict rejects the view that ritual stabilises society and cites later writers who show that rituals can also drive change (Benedict 1983).

The texts also say what their approaches leave out. Benedict sets aside the images audiences form of exhibited people (Benedict 1983p. 43). Mandell notes that American historians have not studied the fairs of 1876, 1893 and 1904 (Mandell 1967p. 122). The book says there has never been a comprehensive study of the economic benefit to participants (Allwood et al. 2001p. 195).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask who organised and paid for a new event, and place it on Mandell's split before comparing its themes; this would show where political purpose and commercial aim diverged (Mandell 1967; Mandell 1967p. 7).
  • Trace the stated rationale of a new event through planning as trade, prestige, propaganda or marketplace (Allwood et al. 2001p. 194); this would show whether the official reason shifted.
  • Read the event's name against the exhibition/fair distinction (Findling & Pelle 1990); a sales function hidden by an official label would show.
  • Compare a new catalogue's ordering with Le Play's grouping by nature and nationality, and with the Group X of makers' intentions (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 37; Findling & Pelle 1990p. 38).
  • Read a new exhibition's halls against Henry's three techniques and ask which one dominated (Henry 2014p. 104); this would show how visitors were taught to see development.
  • Ask whether a new museum tells a universal or a local story, and whether its labels name owners, makers or the nation (Karp & Lavine 1991).
  • Ask which objects in a new show were used generically and whether the wall text says so (Karp & Lavine 1991); this would show how far the show rests on research rather than provenance.

Where to start reading

  • Benedict, Burton. The Anthropology of World’s Fairs: San Francisco’s Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915. London and Berkeley: Scolar Press, 1983. Benedict, for the 1939 break and the trade-show argument.
  • Findling, John E., and Kimberly D. Pelle, eds. Encyclopedia of World’s Fairs and Expositions. Jefferson, NC: McFarland, 2008. Findling and Pelle (Encyclopedia), for the terms and the BIE categories.
  • Findling, John E., and Kimberly D. Pelle, eds. Historical Dictionary of World’s Fairs and Expositions, 1851–1988. New York: Greenwood Press, 1990. Findling and Pelle (Dictionary), for the Paris 1867 classification and the shift to pavilions.
  • Mandell, Richard D. Paris 1900: The Great World’s Fair. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1967. Mandell, for the state versus business distinction.
  • Allwood, John, Ted Allan and Patrick Reid. The Great Exhibitions: 150 Years. London: Exhibition Consultants, 2001. Allwood, Allan and Reid, for the switch from trade to public relations and the specialised events.
  • Denton, Kirk A. Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2014. Denton, for the emic museum typology and the memorial halls.
  • Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991. Karp and Lavine, for Clifford's majority and tribal museums and the idea-driven exhibition.
  • Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014. Henry, for the three display techniques of the Seoul 1915 exhibition.

Exhibitions as machines of knowledge and rule: the exhibitionary complex and its relatives

Bennett's exhibitionary complex, Foucault's discipline and governmentality, and concepts that treat exhibitions as instruments for forming publics and subjects. 35 concepts from 19 texts

This family of approaches reads an exhibition as an instrument of rule. Its displays, routes and classifications are taken to order people and things, to form publics and to train subjects, rather than simply to show goods or knowledge. The question it asks is what an arrangement did to its visitors and to the people displayed, and by which mechanisms (Parkp. 2; Bennett 2004p. 5).

Its centre is the exhibitionary complex, Tony Bennett's term for a network of museums, exhibitions and retail sites (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 3; Giberti 2002). Filipová's introduction describes it as an idea that "analyses exhibitions as sites which install order among people and exhibits" (Filipová 2015p. 7). Denton (Denton 2014p. 12), Park (Parkp. 15), Henry (Henry 2014p. 3), Rydell, Findling and Pelle (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000) and Roche (Roche 2000p. 37) apply, test or qualify it for Chinese state museums, Seoul 1915, colonial Keijo, American fairs and sport.

The exhibitionary complex

Bennett's term covers museums, exhibitions, department stores, arcades and panoramas, which emerged alongside Foucault's carceral archipelago (Giberti 2002). Roche reads Bennett as reversing confinement: museums drew the public in to survey ordered objects, so that control came through entertainment and pleasure (Roche 2000p. 37). Denton keeps the contrast: "Bennett sees museums as making power visible to the public," whereas disciplinary institutions conceal it (Denton 2014p. 12).

The uses diverge. Filipová places the complex in Foucault's visualisation of discipline (Filipová 2015p. 7). Rezende reads Rio de Janeiro 1922 in Gramscian terms, as operating through the organisation of consent rather than coercion (Filipová 2015p. 171). Raizman and Robey credit Bennett with the phrase for "masking hegemonic ambitions under the guise of aesthetic appreciation" (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 3). Mathur uses it for display genres that moved objects and bodies into public arenas (Mathur 2007p. 12), and Dussel for the history of collecting (Lawn 2009p. 131).

Exhibitionary order and exhibitionary mode

Two texts use the adjective for different things. Peterson moves from Mitchell's exhibitionary order, in which the colonial fair displayed objects to be looked at, to a performative order of live performance and shared encounter (Peterson 2020p. 22). Hoffenberg's exhibitionary mode is another concept: a way of displaying commodities as more than inventories, arranged for classification, comparison and attraction, found in fairs, department stores and agricultural shows (Hoffenberg 2001p. 79). Hoffenberg attaches it to no theorist in these passages, so it should not be merged with Bennett's complex.

Governmentality and colonial rule

Bennett's analytics of government, drawn from Foucault, Dean and Rose, examines the technical mechanisms of classification and display through which conduct is shaped, rather than the ideology behind them (Bennett 2004p. 5). Henry applies the frame to colonial Keijo, where efforts to redirect colonised people's spiritual, material and civic affiliations were contested experiments of colonial governmentality, a framework first developed for liberal societies (Henry 2014p. 3). In wartime Keijo, the loyalty of the colonised was measured by counting shrine visits rather than by inquiry (Henry 2014p. 169). Bennett's reading of Dirks's ethnological state, in which administration kept subject populations at the archaic, is the colonial counterpart (Bennett 2004p. 10).

Machines, apparatus and self-regulation

Park reads Seoul 1915 as a cultural machinery whose effects exceed its political purpose (Parkp. 2). The exhibition was "a training machine, positioning visitors as" the new national subjects of its modern spectacle, and its rules on dress, hygiene and sanitary inspection aimed to make visitors discipline themselves (Parkp. 15). Denton's visitors, who see themselves from the side of power, come to regulate themselves (Denton 2014p. 12). Della Coletta applies Foucault's panopticism to De Amicis's guidebook to Turin, not to a fair (Della Coletta 2006p. 55). Sobe and Rackers's writing machine fuses human and non-human so that writing becomes automatic (Lawn 2009p. 87).

Exhibitions as schools

Lawn's materiality of education studies objects, captions, displays and technologies rather than temporary spectacle (Lawn 2009p. 10). London 1851 was a site where technologies of rule were formed (Lawn 2009p. 15). Coté reads Semarang 1914 as "an object lesson intended to instruct the learner in the advantages of" progress, its layout intended to educate like a textbook (Cotép. 33; Cotép. 17). Grosvenor reads London 1924 as a training school for future citizens (Lawn 2009p. 108). Fuchs traces school museums to fairs and to teachers' pursuit of professional status (Lawn 2009p. 51; Lawn 2009p. 66).

Classification and evolutionary time

Several of Bennett's concepts link classification to time. The evolutionary accumulator stores past times and acts on the present (Bennett 2004p. 106). The archaeological gaze names how Whewell and Huxley read the present as sedimented pasts (Bennett 2004p. 37). Pitt Rivers's typological method became a black box that secured a fit between the evolution of species and cultures (Bennett 2004p. 66). Centres of calculation act at a distance on peripheral sites (Bennett 2004p. 21). Giberti's Centennial installation was a tabular space, the grid Foucault proposed as the archaeology of Enlightenment knowledge (Giberti 2002).

Hegemony and consent

Rydell, Findling and Pelle describe "the rhetoric of power embodied in the exhibitionary complex", a power that organises an order for the good of all (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Rydell's Part One draws on Bennett's account of exhibitions forming "a complex of disciplinary and power relations" (Rydell 1993p. 10). Hur applies the same rhetoric to early fairs, placing China in the position of an inferior other at Paris 1867 and London 1886 (Hurp. 18).

Debates and limits

Hur argues that the cultural hegemony school, which reads fairs through their organisers' objectives, rests on a binary that does not fit China's ambiguous position, and calls for audience-oriented approaches (Hurp. 167). Filipová's volume denies that the complex carries over unchanged to regional fairs, where minority groups often turned exhibitions into sites of resistance (Filipová 2015p. 8). Hoffenberg finds commissioners in Australia and India making imperial knowledge more participatory and mediated, against Said and Cohn (Hoffenberg 2001p. 57).

Roche argues that Bennett underplays the performance involved in producing and consuming exhibitions (Roche 2000p. 34). Denton, against scholarship that pushes state discourse aside, wants the state back in the relation between state and people (Denton 2014p. 3). On these accounts the approach tends to leave out performance and the voices of those displayed; Henry notes that Korean voices silenced by censorship remain only partly recoverable (Henry 2014p. 13).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask whether a new pavilion makes its power visible or hides it, as Denton reads Bennett's contrast with disciplinary institutions, to see whether visitors were trained to regulate themselves (Denton 2014p. 12).
  • Compare a state's pavilion with its performance of the nation: Peterson's shift from exhibitionary order to performative order would show whether visitors were asked to look or to take part (Peterson 2020p. 22).
  • Trace who ran the display: read a state-run fair for its organisation of consent, then ask whether a minority-run event resisted that order, as Filipová's volume suggests (Filipová 2015p. 171; Filipová 2015p. 8).
  • Read the whole event as a machine, as Park does for Seoul 1915, asking which behaviours the organisers wanted visitors to adopt and which signs show that they did (Parkp. 2; Parkp. 15).
  • Trace one exhibited object through a fair, a museum and the press, asking at each step which institution gave it its meaning, as Cornish does for the Krishnanagar indigo model (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 136).
  • Test a propaganda exhibition's success by what it counted, as Henry shows colonial officials did with shrine visits, and ask whether it listened to visitors (Henry 2014p. 169).
  • Ask what exhibitors and visitors each expected an object to do, following Gosden and Knowles, for whom colonial relations were "a series of experiments, no two of which ever had quite the same outcome" (Gosden & Knowles 2001).

Where to start reading

  • Denton, Kirk A. Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2014. Denton, for the complex applied to a state museum and the question of who is made to see power (l. 687-691).
  • Filipová, Marta, ed. Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840–1940: Great Exhibitions in the Margins. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015. Filipová's introduction and Rezende's chapter, for the adaptation of the complex to regional and national fairs (l. 955-957; 7921-7930).
  • Park, Young-Sin. “Making ‘Modern’ Korean Subjects: The Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition of 1915.” Journal article. Park, for the cultural machinery and the training machine, read through displays and routes (l. 76-79; 829-831).
  • Lawn, Martin, ed. Modelling the Future: Exhibitions and the Materiality of Education. Oxford: Symposium Books, 2009. Lawn's introduction, for the materiality of education and technologies of rule (l. 309-313; 557-559).
  • Bennett, Tony. Pasts Beyond Memory: Evolution, Museums, Colonialism. London: Routledge, 2004. Bennett, Pasts Beyond Memory, for governmentality and the classificatory mechanisms of museums (l. 678-679; 3397-3398).
  • Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014. Henry, for contested governmentality and assimilation in colonial Keijo (l. 737-739; 797).
  • Roche, Maurice. Mega-Events and Modernity: Olympics and Expos in the Growth of Global Culture. London: Routledge, 2000. Roche, for the critique of Bennett's model and its treatment of performance and sport (l. 2058-2061).

Spectacle, commodity and the world as exhibition

Debord's spectacle, Benjamin's phantasmagoria and aura, Mitchell's world-as-exhibition, and concepts about representation, vision and media. 49 concepts from 19 texts

This family of approaches reads the exhibition as spectacle: an ordered visual field in which goods, nations and peoples are arranged for a spectator who is invited to take what is shown for the real. Its questions are how such displays make their claims convincing, what they ask the visitor to do with the eye, and what they leave out. Mitchell's essay gives the shared starting point, in which the exhibition works "as a mechanism of order and meaning" (Mitchell 1989p. 218). Debord supplies the social theory, defining the spectacle as "a social relationship between people that is mediated" by images. Benjamin's phantasmagoria and aura run through the group and are applied to single fairs (Parkp. 18; Giberti 2002). The central texts are Mitchell (Mitchell 1989), Harvey on Seville 1992 (Harvey 1996p. 3), Della Coletta on Italian expositions (Della Coletta 2006p. 37), and Giberti on Philadelphia 1876 (Giberti 2002).

World as exhibition and certainty of representation

Mitchell presents the world as a set of models, each claiming to show a reality beyond it (Mitchell 1989p. 218). Their certainty depended on a deliberate difference in time and place between model and real, as in the Egyptian street at Paris 1867 (Mitchell 1989p. 223). Harvey, who says Mitchell follows Heidegger, describes the move to "the world conceived as though it were an exhibition" (Harvey 1996p. 3). In Mitchell's labyrinth, what seems outside the exhibition is only more representation: "What matters about this labyrinth is not that we never reach the real" (Mitchell 1989p. 236). Della Coletta applies Heidegger's phrase to fairs whose displays had to be realistic and spectacular (Della Coletta 2006p. 37).

Spectacle and phantasmagoria

Debord's spectacle is a social relationship mediated by images, not a deliberate distortion of the visual world. Giberti applies Debord's formula to Philadelphia 1876, dividing the spectacle into a diffuse form, a surfeit of goods, and a concentrated form, a mass gathering (Giberti 2002). Giberti traces the phantasmagoria from the magic lantern through Marx's commodity fetish to Benjamin, for whom display was the source of value (Giberti 2002). Park, on Seoul 1915, describes the exhibition as a phantasmagoria into which people entered in order to be distracted (Parkp. 18), a phrase he credits to Benjamin (Parkp. 18); its shop area resembled a department store (Parkp. 18).

Aura and authenticity

Shepherdson-Scott describes a replica temple at Chicago 1933, openly known as a replica, which Chinese makers rendered so that "the aura of the authentic" served as a marketing hook (Shepherdson-Scottp. 559). Giberti uses Benjamin's sense of aura as the authority of the artwork, threatened at Philadelphia 1876 by commodity exchange and protected by the Group 27 judges (Giberti 2002); in the model room a singular object gained an aura of authenticity (Giberti 2002). Della Coletta reads cult and exhibition value as merging at Agra, where aura increases through display (Della Coletta 2006p. 262). The word carries three senses: a manufactured authority, a threatened one, and one that display increases.

Modes of looking

Giberti opposes two visual regimes: the Cartesian, which the vitrine embodies by separating subject from object, and the contextual, embodied in the mannequin and model room (Giberti 2002). The Centennial was designed for both the focused gaze and the distracted glance (Giberti 2002), and the model room lowers the boundary of display to invite the spectator into a scene (Giberti 2002). Alpers names the museum effect, the isolation of an object for attentive looking, and argues: "The museum effect, I want to argue, is a way of seeing" (Karp & Lavine 1991). She would work with the effect rather than overcome it (Karp & Lavine 1991).

Make-believe, fun and simulation

Rydell's preface takes make-believe to involve "the power to assert a reality that one can persuade others to occupy" (Hollengreen et al. 2014), and sets this against the fair movement from the 1851 Crystal Palace onward (Hollengreen et al. 2014). Thomas, after Bateson, defines fun as the pleasure of an is/is-not construction, in which something is presented as what it is not (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 426). Telotte uses cinematizing, after Paul Virilio, for the convergence of reality effects with reality, and reads Disney's place at New York 1964 in that light (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 411). Demeter reads Disney's Carousel of Progress, in General Electric's Progressland at New York 1964, through Baudrillard's hyperreal (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 87p. 92). Harvey separates simulation technologies, which need no context and simply produce effect, from representational technologies, and applies the distinction to Seville 1992 (Harvey 1996p. 125).

Exposition as medium and display of status

Geppert describes the exposition as a meta-medium, a specific means of communication that encompasses other communicative technologies (Geppert 2010p. 3); new technologies were swiftly absorbed into it (Geppert 2010p. 92). Massidda, drawing on McLuhan's claim that electric media abolish the spatial dimension, reads television as a cool medium that left no space for the expo mega-event (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 190). Allan and Reid describe the traditional world exposition as the dominant medium of international cultural exchange, now with less impact (Allwood et al. 2001p. 193). Allwood treats showing off as the motive of every international exhibition, a trait that is the life-blood of commerce and industry (Allwood et al. 2001). Samuel calls New York 1964 the ultimate trade show, where businesses spent about three hundred million dollars on exhibits (Samuel 2007).

Construction through representation

Bell treats European images of Maori as ideologically grounded objects, a central feature of the construction through representation of the indigenous subject (Bell 1992p. 6). Celik describes non-Western peoples at nineteenth-century fairs placed in settings and activities that seemed to belong to another age, forming tableaux vivants, spectacles that fixed societies in history (Çelik 1992p. 19–20). Peterson's regime of images is a different concept from Giberti's visual regimes: a systematically ordered power-knowledge, drawn from Peter Jackson, that blends word and image to require surface calm, read in the Thai pavilion at Milan 2015 (Peterson 2020p. 274). Peterson sets his study against accounts of display as imperial and aims to turn the lens towards Asian self-representation (Peterson 2020p. 16).

Debates and limits

Mitchell rejects the commodity-fetish argument, because it uncovers misrepresentation but leaves representation itself unquestioned (Mitchell 1989p. 225). Giberti reads the technique of more as a possible commodity fetish, while also as an expression of industrial power (Giberti 2002). Harvey argues that visitors to Seville 1992 were more than consumers, which modifies Baudrillard's account of cultural change (Harvey 1996p. 27). Brown holds that the apparatus critique applies differently to Japan, which was never a colonial subject (Brown). Harvey holds that representational knowledge and embodied practice cannot be combined by adding perspectives (Harvey 1996p. 171). The texts also say what the approach leaves out: Giberti notes that the fair was more than a visual experience, with its fragrance, din and music (Giberti 2002), and that its audience brought an agenda of its own (Giberti 2002).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Trace the claim to the real: find where a new exhibition says visitors have reached the real, and what displays follow, to see whether the claim closes the labyrinth. Mitchell's labyrinth models this (Mitchell 1989p. 236).
  • Compare model and referent: for each pavilion, record what visitors were told was real and whether the display showed the difference. Mitchell's time-and-place gap models this (Mitchell 1989p. 223).
  • Ask who made a replica shown at another fair, and whether its authenticity was staged through the makers' nationality. Shepherdson-Scott's Chicago 1933 case models this (Shepherdson-Scottp. 559).
  • Sort displays into those that separate viewer from object and those that place it in a scene. Giberti's vitrine and model room are the pair (Giberti 2002).
  • Read a fair's guides and mascot material for passages that show one thing while saying another. Thomas's is/is-not test models this (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 426).
  • Ask which social conditions of production a technology display hides, and whether it gives context or only effect. Harvey's distinction models this (Harvey 1996p. 125).
  • Read a national pavilion's self-representation for its own agency, against its promotional texts and visitors' accounts. Peterson's Milan 2015 study models this (Peterson 2020p. 16).
  • Compare which other media a fair absorbed and how each shaped the others' effects. Geppert's meta-medium models this (Geppert 2010p. 92).

Where to start reading

  • Mitchell, Timothy. “The World as Exhibition.” Comparative Studies in Society and History 31, no. 2 (1989): 217–236. the frame of order, certainty and the labyrinth.
  • Harvey, Penelope. Hybrids of Modernity: Anthropology, the Nation State and the Universal Exhibition. London: Routledge, 1996. that frame applied to Seville 1992, and the split between representational and simulation technologies.
  • Giberti, Bruno. Designing the Centennial: A History of the 1876 International Exhibition in Philadelphia. Lexington: University Press of Kentucky, 2002. visual regimes, the model room and the phantasmagoria at Philadelphia 1876.
  • the spectacle as social relation, and detournement as a method.
  • Park, Young-Sin. “Making ‘Modern’ Korean Subjects: The Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition of 1915.” Journal article. the phantasmagoria of the shop floor at Seoul 1915.
  • Shepherdson-Scott, Kari. “Conflicting Politics and Contesting Borders: Exhibiting (Japanese) Manchuria at the Chicago World’s Fair, 1933–34.” Journal article. the aura of the authentic as a marketing claim at Chicago 1933.
  • Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991. the museum effect as a way of seeing.
  • Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020. the regime of images and Asian self-representation at Milan 2015.

Empire, race and people on display

Concepts for colonial display, racial science and the exhibition of human beings. 45 concepts from 22 texts

These approaches read the exhibition as an instrument that ranked peoples, put them on show and taught visitors who held power. Their shared question is how a fair made empire and racial hierarchy look natural, progressive or benevolent, and whom it was built to persuade. Rydell states the link most directly: "But at the fairs, the idea of technological and national progress became laced with scientific racism." (Rydell 1984) Greenhalgh (Greenhalgh 1988) and Benedict (Benedict 1983) make the display of people central, while Bell (Bell 1992) and Hale (Hale 2008) carry the question into images, trademarks and official notices. Hotta-Lister (Hotta-Lister 1999) shows one state using a fair to justify its imperial role (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 83).

The texts disagree about how far visitors were persuaded. Hoffenberg (Hoffenberg 2001p. 57) and Mathur (Mathur 2007p. 7) place the meaning of displays in a contest among commissioners, visitors and colonised participants, which leaves the audience a share in the message.

Racial ranking and social evolution

Ranking peoples on one scale of progress is the most widely used idea here. Rydell (Rydell 1984) ties it to a racial blueprint that the Chicago Midway gave scientific sanction (Rydell 1984). Kwon (Kwon) calls the scale social Darwinism and says Korean intellectuals accepted it from the 1890s (Kwonp. 21). Burris (Burris 2001) calls it social evolutionism, a single hierarchy in which the ability to transform nature measured a society's place (Burris 2001p. 64). Rydell, Findling and Pelle (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000) show the scale in space, with the more Anglo-Saxon nations placed centrally (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Armstrong (Benedict 1983) applies Social Darwinism to gender, making strength and mastery male and women passive in the public art of San Francisco 1915 (Benedict 1983p. 118). The label does not mean one thing. Kwon uses it to explain how Korean critics read Osaka 1903 and Tokyo 1907 as a racial and national struggle (Kwonp. 22), while Armstrong's use concerns figures and gender, and the two should be kept apart.

Displays of people: types, villages and panoramas

Greenhalgh's human showcase is the key case. From 1889 to 1914 people were placed in reconstructed tableaux while paying audiences looked on, and they are sorted into imperial, educational, commercial and ambassadorial types that overlap (Greenhalgh 1988p. 82). Benedict holds that "The display of people is a display of power." (Benedict 1983p. 52) The power relation in such displays is not necessarily real but idealised by the exhibitors (Benedict 1983p. 45). Kwon's native-village model, which he finds in the Japanese displays, joined civilisational stages to freak-show curiosity (Kwonp. 19). Qureshi shows that mock villages at London 1899 turned performers into walk-through displays and changed the terms of contact (Qureshi 2011p. 255). Santesso's living panoramas set backdrop, animals and people in one landscape (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 45p. 46).

Stereotype, binary and the ideological image

Bell treats images as ideological objects. Representations can be sites where ideology is articulated, though art is not reducible to ideology (Bell 1992p. 5). A stereotype fixes a subordinated group in one picture, and its mask admits only one reading (Bell 1992p. 227p. 229). Mathur calls the colonial stereotype "a fundamentally ambivalent form of representation" (Mathur 2007p. 5). Hale's uncivilized type and dual image show fixed opposites in trademarks and notices, with Africa both primitive and rich in labour (Hale 2008p. 25p. 45). Binary logic is explicit in Della Coletta, for whom imperial culture defined nations through binary opposites in a fixed hierarchy (Della Coletta 2006p. 4p. 11), and in Thomas, who calls anthropology a discourse of alterity that treats difference as prior to any similarity (Thomas 1991p. 3p. 27).

Propaganda, power and the imperial economy

Several texts treat the fair as an argument made to a public. Greenhalgh holds that the state generated pride in empire so that the British would feel at home with Africa, Asia and India, with the Great Exhibition as an early instance (Greenhalgh 1988p. 53). Hotta-Lister dates a turn to "propagandistic defence of empire, a move away from the complacent" (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 84), and reads London 1910 as a platform on which Japan could justify its imperial role (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 83). Rydell, Findling and Pelle find an allegory of imperial conquest in a revolver displayed at London 1851 (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Prasch places colonies in a division of labour in which they supplied raw goods (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 28). Samuel finds in GM's Futurama "a ringing endorsement for what could be called corporate colonialism" (Samuel 2007).

Kinship, settlers and the civilising claim

Rydell's coloniale moderne joins modernistic architecture to imperial policy that stressed benefits to colonizer and colonised alike, and so made imperialism seem as basic to modernity as architecture and science (Rydell 1993p. 62). Hale traces the French colonial family from a parental to a fraternal image while the hierarchy beneath stayed the same. In his words, "the real role France played in the empire was of parents leading a family." (Hale 2008p. 176p. 161) His civilising mission allowed colonised peoples only a limited progress, so exhibits set exotic groups beside assimilated ones (Hale 2008p. 13p. 39). Settler communities give the imperial triad another form. Hoffenberg's tripartite empire of England, India and Australia uses Australia to stand for settler societies, including Canada and Southern Africa (Hoffenberg 2001p. 129). Markwyn applies settler colonialism to the racial assumptions behind the Woman's Pavilion at San Antonio 1968 (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 145), and Rice, drawing on Belich, describes New Zealand tightening its ties to Britain (Filipová 2015p. 232).

Salvage, collecting and objects as evidence

Gosden and Knowles reject the salvage paradigm, under which collectors thought "they were collecting vanishing examples of dying cultures" (Gosden & Knowles 2001). The predicted collapse did not come, because people drew on local resources to make a new way of life (Gosden & Knowles 2001). Colonialism reordered the moral world of New Guineans, and gifts and commodities cannot be cleanly separated (Gosden & Knowles 2001). Bell's old-time Maori is a figure about to vanish, a record Lindauer's tableaux were taken to provide, though Bell reads them as monuments to an idea of the past (Bell 1992p. 205p. 208).

Debates and limits

Greenhalgh rejects the view that imperialism underlay every human display, since two of her four types were not necessarily imperial or immoral (Greenhalgh 1988p. 82). Hoffenberg answers the Said and Cohn model, arguing that commissioners in Australia and India made imperial knowledge a participatory process that could challenge British authority (Hoffenberg 2001p. 57). Kwon disputes the Yomiuri shimbun's account of the 1907 display, which put the controversy down to a woman's freedom at work rather than to discrimination against Koreans (Kwonp. 31). Samuel objects that Rydell, Findling and Pelle describe the 1964 Fair as large, rambling and unfocused, and say nothing of its attendance or of how visitors felt (Samuel 2007).

What the approach tends to leave out, by the texts' own account, is the audience. Samuel says the Fair's story has largely left out individual visitors' experiences (Samuel 2007), and Benedict sets aside the images the audience formed of exhibited people (Benedict 1983p. 43).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask who was ranked by race and who by class or nationality at a new fair, and compare its anthropology section with its midway. This would show whether the ladder was racial, as Rydell reads Chicago (Rydell 1984), or a social ladder of nations, as Kwon's reading implies (Kwonp. 21).
  • Sort the people shown at a new fair into imperial, educational, commercial and ambassadorial displays, and check whether a fifth type, such as a labour display, is needed (Greenhalgh 1988p. 82).
  • Trace the layout and colour of a new fair as a sequence, and ask whether its guidebooks give the same order, as Greenhalgh does for Buffalo 1901 (Greenhalgh 1988p. 96).
  • Ask whether a new fair's displays of people claimed power as a real relation or an idealised one, which would show whether its ranking was presented as fact or as performance (Benedict 1983p. 45).
  • Code a new exhibition's notices for paired opposites such as clean and dirty, and check whether an official display of the same region uses them, following Hale's Manichean allegory (Hale 2008p. 29).
  • Check where colonial goods sat in a fair's plan against their catalogue entries, to see whether they were shown as raw materials or as manufactures, after Prasch (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 28).

Where to start reading

  • Greenhalgh, Paul. Ephemeral Vistas: The Expositions Universelles, Great Exhibitions and World’s Fairs, 1851–1939. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1988. the human showcase and naturalisation of empire chapters, for how displays of people were sorted and aimed at a metropolitan public.
  • Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. the introduction and Midway pages, for the racial blueprint and the argument that fairs legitimated upper-class authority.
  • Benedict, Burton. The Anthropology of World’s Fairs: San Francisco’s Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915. London and Berkeley: Scolar Press, 1983. lines 2570-2879, for displays of people as power.
  • Bell, Leonard. Colonial Constructs: European Images of Maori, 1840–1914. Auckland: Auckland University Press, 1992. the introduction, for images as ideology, the stereotype and the mask.
  • Gosden, Chris, and Chantal Knowles. Collecting Colonialism: Material Culture and Colonial Change. Oxford: Berg, 2001. the first chapter and the moral-universe chapter, for collecting and the meaning of objects.
  • Hale, Dana S. Races on Display: French Representations of Colonized Peoples, 1886–1940. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 2008. the race and trademark sections, for the colonial family and the uncivilized type.
All 45 concepts recorded under this theme, by text
Bell, Leonard. Colonial Constructs: European Images of Maori, 1840–1914. Auckland: Auckland University Press, 1992.
ideology of colonialismBelltheoretical framing

The images are read for their ideological correlatives: their links with the ideology of colonialism. Representations do more than reflect that ideology, since they can be sites where it is articulated, though the author insists that art is not reducible to ideology. (Bell 1992p. 5)

“representations could be prime sites for the articulation of ideology” p. 5

Draws on Thomas Metcalf; Said; Barthes

Used for Applied to Gilfillan's lithograph Interior, displayed at the Great Exhibition among New Zealand products (line 2904-2911), and to Chevalier's Hinemoa, which Bell says is 'as enmeshed ideologically' as Strutt's paintings (line 5780-5782).

London 1851London 1879

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For one exhibition, a researcher could ask where the ideological work is done (the catalogue, the venue, the subject chosen, the figure's pose), then test the same checklist on an exhibition in another colonial setting.

exotic picturesqueBellanalytic concept

A mode in which Maori figures are made into picturesque types, combining genre-painting conventions (peasants, harvesters, travellers) with the exotic non-European. Bell places it alongside the French Orientalist repertoire of Arabs with horses or camels. (Bell 1992p. 87)

“It remains an Orientalist cum genre-type painting; its subject a mixture of the conventionally picturesque peasant and exotic non-European.” p. 87

Used for Applied to Strutt's Maoris Beaching Their Canoes (Fig. 48), which Bell reads as a composition modelled on European peasant and Orientalist types rather than a documentary record of a market landing at Onehunga (line 3680-3701).

Melbourne 1853

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For a case-study image, a researcher could identify which European genre its figures are borrowed from, then ask whether its subjects are being shown as types or as particular people before using it as ethnographic evidence.

'old-time' MaoriBellperiodisation

A figure of the Maori past, set apart from contemporary Maori, whom Europeans treated as about to vanish under progress. Bell says Lindauer's tableaux were seen as records of that vanishing, though they are better read as monuments to an idea of the past. (Bell 1992p. 205)

“the standard European view of traditional Maoridom as either of the past or something the last remnants of which were about to vanish” p. 205

Used for Applied to Lindauer's Partridge series (Tohunga under Tapu, Digging with the Ko, Happy Days) and set against The Time of Kai, the one contemporary scene, which Bell reads as breaking the idealised order (line 8476-8483).

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a case-study image was presented as a record of a people 'about to vanish', and then trace which later catalogues or reviews kept that label and which contested it.

stereotypeBellanalytic concept

A fixed, one-sided picture of a subordinated group that confirms the dominant group's views and can take on an ideological role. Bell pairs it with the 'mask': a closed image that allows one dominant reading, unlike an open face. (Bell 1992p. 227)

“Stereotypes often develop about subordinated or suppressed social and ethnic groups that are the” p. 227

Used for Applied to Dittmer's Mana, the portrait of Te Heu Heu Tukino, where Bell says the individual features were 'transformed into a mask' and the politically active chief was made into a dejected stereotype (line 9186-9197, 9266-9273).

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For a portrait in a case study, a researcher could check what the sitter's known public role is missing from the picture and whether the image permits only one reading.

Benedict sorts the display of people into types (technicians, craftsmen, curiosities or freaks, trophies, specimens) and says that display of people is a display of power, a symbolic performance in which the power relation is not necessarily real but idealised by the exhibitors. (Benedict 1983p. 52)

“The display of people is a display of power.” p. 52

Armstrong reads the public art of the 1915 fair through Social Darwinism, the application of Darwin's evolutionary laws to society, which in her account made strength, mastery and conflict male and made women ethereal, subdued or passive, with racist tendencies as well as sexist ones. Burris, John P. Exhibiting Religion: Colonialism and Spectacle at International Expositions, 1851–1893. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 2001.

The idea that human societies form a single hierarchy of progress, a chain of being comparable to the one in nature, in which the demonstrated ability to transform nature measures a society's place. The text calls it a distorted 'bastard child' of evolutionary theory, and says it was popular because it could explain cultural differences in the West's favour. (Burris 2001p. 64)

culture and civilisation as separate categoriesBurrisanalytic concept

A split between 'culture', applied to peoples seen as savage or primitive and handed to anthropology, and 'civilisation', applied to peoples seen as having developed world religions and handed to the study of religion. The text says the exposition did not draw this line precisely but modelled it in the way it exhibited cultures and religions. (Burris 2001)

Used for Applied to the Great Exhibition's international juries and to the 1893 Parliament, where peoples defined ethnically were excluded and the remaining civilisations gathered as the 'ten great world religions'.

The basic division between 'savage' and 'civilized' societies that the exposition used to order cultures. The text says it was tied to the 'primitive' category, which by 1893 defined peoples by culture or race while civilisations were defined by religious affiliation. (Burris 2001p. 24)

The text's term for a display system in which colonial and non-Western peoples were shown through an ethnological approach and placed in a division of labour in which colonies supplied raw goods, with the division justified by free trade. (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 28)

Gosden, Chris, and Chantal Knowles. Collecting Colonialism: Material Culture and Colonial Change. Oxford: Berg, 2001.
salvage paradigmGosden, Knowlescritique

The idea that collectors were gathering vanishing examples of dying cultures before modernisation erased them. The authors present it as a belief held by collectors, which in fact increased production of the objects it sought to record. (Gosden & Knowles 2001)

Used for The Field Museum expedition of Lewis (who worked for an institution founded on the Chicago 1893 exposition) and the collecting of Blackwood and Speiser; the authors show its predictions of collapse failed.

cargo cult as a search for access to powerGosden, Knowlesanalytic concept

Cargo cults are read not mainly as a desire for Western goods but as an attempt to find the source of the spiritual power that the authors say Melanesians thought whites possessed; objects are central to a moral and political relationship with whites. (Gosden & Knowles 2001)

moral universe of colonialismGosden, Knowlesanalytic concept

Colonialism reordered the moral world of New Guineans, who had to decide which relationships were proper and how to gain access to white wealth; the authors argue that gifts and commodities cannot be cleanly separated and that objects had no fixed value. (Gosden & Knowles 2001)

Greenhalgh, Paul. Ephemeral Vistas: The Expositions Universelles, Great Exhibitions and World’s Fairs, 1851–1939. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1988.
human showcaseGreenhalghanalytic concept

Between 1889 and 1914 people from colonised and other non-Western regions were displayed on exhibition sites in reconstructed tableaux, going about their supposed daily business while paying audiences looked on, so that human beings were turned into objects of display. The text sorts these displays into imperial, educational, commercial and ambassadorial types that overlap. (Greenhalgh 1988p. 82)

social Darwinian site arrangementGreenhalghanalytic concept

Social Darwinism placed races on an evolutionary chain, with Western 'Aryan' peoples at the top and Aboriginal and African peoples at the bottom. At Buffalo in 1901 the layout, colour scheme and sculpture of the whole site were arranged to suggest a progression from less civilised to more civilised humanity, so that visitors would walk through an evolutionary flow. industry and empireGreenhalghtheoretical framing

Taking Hobsbawm's phrase for the British economy, Greenhalgh treats industry and empire as the two forces that transformed the world after about 1760. Pride in empire was artificially generated by the state so that the British public would feel at home with Africa, Asia and India as their own; the Great Exhibition is read as one of the earliest effective examples. The text treats “race” as a category that French officials and writers redefined as political situations changed, and as deciding a people’s potential for civilisation, with Europeans at the top, then Asians, then Arabs, then sub-Saharan Africans. A term the text takes from Abdul R. JanMohamed for a split in which opposing moral qualities are tied to race and complexion, so that whiteness signals cleanliness and goodness and blackness filth and evil. Kinship terms the French used for the link between metropolitan France and its colonies: a parental, often maternal, image in which France raised adopted children, joined after the First World War by a fraternal image of union and brotherhood. A phrase imperialists used to stress the strength and potential number of colonial soldiers. The French claim that colonized peoples could progress towards French civilisation through contact and tutelage. The text holds that the peoples could be civilised only in this limited way, while only white Europeans could be truly civilised, and that exhibits had to show exotic groups beside assimilated ones to prove the mission was working. The text’s term for the official and commercial image of black Africans as a race whose qualities are the opposite of white ones. Laziness is condemned while commitment is praised as white, and the text notes that no comparison is drawn between black and white weaknesses. (Hale 2008p. 25)

Orientalism, self-representation and the non-Western exhibitor

Said's Orientalism and its critics, and concepts for how Asian and colonised exhibitors represented themselves and answered being displayed. 54 concepts from 17 texts

Approaches in this family ask how an exhibition represented non-Western peoples and states, and what those represented did in response. Most start from Said's Orientalism. Hanson applies it as a knowledge-producing discourse that supported colonial expansion in the cultural realm (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 15), and Çelik describes the fairs as presenting the Orient as a three-dimensional living model (Çelik 1992p. 93–94). Other texts test the frame rather than adopt it. Peterson takes Asian national pavilions from 1915 to 2015 as sites where states controlled their own representation (Peterson 2020p. 22; Peterson 2020p. 16). Kwon, Hur and Park ask how audiences in Korea, China and colonial Seoul received displays, and Hur proposes audience-oriented approaches in place of theories that treat fairs as hegemonic propaganda or as a stage for resistance (Hurp. 168; Kwonp. 30; Parkp. 2). Shepherdson-Scott, Brown and Coté examine the sponsors behind displays of Manchuria, Japanese gardens and colonial Java (Shepherdson-Scottp. 541; Brown; Cotép. 6).

Orientalism and the contrapuntal reading

Said's framework is the one most texts inherit, but they apply it at different scales. Hanson uses it for the Tunisian Arab tent and bazaar at London 1851 and for Cairo Street at Chicago 1893, reading the controlling gaze of the mezzanine viewers as part of the Orientalist network (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 15; Raizman & Robey 2018p. 24). Mitchell borrows Said's term citationary for writing that adds to itself through reference, so that the East is never a place but a further set of representations (Mitchell 1989p. 231; Mitchell 1989p. 236). Hale uses Orientalism more narrowly, for Western stereotypes applied to North African trademarks and to the North African sections of Paris 1900 (Hale 2008p. 27; Hale 2008p. 48).

A contrapuntal reading supplies the method for reading these frames against their silences. Della Coletta reads imperial expositions against their silenced contradictions (Della Coletta 2006p. 11), Mathur applies the method to the imperial archive of portraits (Mathur 2007p. 82), and Çelik reads specific cases side by side to show overlapping histories (Çelik 1992p. 11–12).

Cultural self-definition and state self-presentation

Çelik's Muslim states used national pavilions and local elements to define their own cultures, against both European homogenising and Ottoman suzerainty, at Paris 1867 to Paris 1900 (Çelik 1992p. 11–12; Çelik 1992p. 137–138). Peterson's "performative order" replaces the "exhibitionary order" of colonial display, in which Asia was looked at rather than empowered (Peterson 2020p. 22). Following Chen Kuan-Hsing, Peterson treats Asia as a product of history and Western imagination, and asks for a critical distance from it (Peterson 2020p. 17; Peterson 2020p. 291). Shepherdson-Scott's authentic sovereignty treats Manchukuo's payment of 62 percent of the pavilion budget at Chicago 1933 as a performance of independent agency for a foreign audience, drawing on Duara (Shepherdson-Scottp. 545; Shepherdson-Scottp. 542). Aesthetic categories were also used for self-description: Yamaguchi's mitate treats an object as merging with a classical reference (Karp & Lavine 1991), and Goswamy's rasa locates aesthetic delight in the viewer and organised the Paris 1986 exhibition into nine sections (Karp & Lavine 1991).

Responses to being displayed: national shame and the press

Kwon's Korean responses start from Northeast Asian Solidarity, a discourse the text calls Japan-centred and which Korean intellectuals held as a hope until the 1905 Protectorate Treaty (Kwonp. 30; Kwonp. 36). The slogan of common race and common culture made the 1903 Osaka display a betrayal, and in 1907 Tokyo the Korean press framed the Crystal Pavilion affair as "national disgrace", a collective insult rather than a women's-rights matter (Kwonp. 23; Kwonp. 36; Kwonp. 31). Hur's Chinese press treats displays as a diplomatic and national matter. The "trauma of exhibition" from Osaka 1903 recurred at St. Louis 1904 and was read through as national shame (Hurp. 73; Hurp. 86). Chinese writers turned guochi, "national humiliation", inward against the Qing government (Hurp. 165; Hurp. 94). Hur calls this an audience-oriented reading, tied to China's own political context (Hurp. 168).

Displayed people as participants and subjects

Coté's native at Semarang 1914 was an object, but also a participant in the exhibition, and the educated Javanese viewer could take in its knowledge without accepting its colonial vision (Cotép. 34; Cotép. 36). Park's Korean subject, produced at Seoul 1915, is divided between disciplined citizen, consumer and colonised subject (Parkp. 19; Parkp. 21). Park draws on Foucault's disciplinary apparatuses and the Panopticon, and reads visitor responses knowing that the press censored much of its coverage (Parkp. 2; Parkp. 1; Parkp. 15).

Mathur reads the men displayed at London 1886 and Tulsi Ram's petitions as subaltern subjects who challenge the official archive (Mathur 2007p. 17; Mathur 2007p. 73). Boone reads mimicry, after Bhabha, as a strategy that can serve power or resistance, applied to a 1915 San Diego photograph of Mexican gardeners in suits (Boone 2019p. 191).

Colonial modernity and exhibitions under colonial rule

Coté defines colonial modernity by two strands, a reformist faith in progress and what he calls the Foucauldian sense of surveillance and discipline at the colony's boundaries, and reads Semarang 1914 as staging both (Cotép. 6). Maclaine Pont's utopian plan separated Western buildings in view from eastern forms hidden along a path; the author treats it as a vision that the built exhibition could not convey (Cotép. 14; Cotép. 15). Hur's semi-colonial China shows a related pattern: the foreign-staffed Imperial Maritime Customs became an index of semi-colonial status and selected the Chinese exhibits, including the bound-foot shoes that angered Chinese critics (Hurp. 5). Hotta-Lister's Island Empires frame gives Japan and Britain an equal footing at London 1910, while Brown argues that Japan was never a colonial subject but a successful coloniser (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 2; Brown).

Intermediaries, screens and paired claims

Shepherdson-Scott shows the South Manchuria Railway Company acting as the screen that presented Manchuria to American visitors as an economic project (Shepherdson-Scottp. 541). The same pamphlets make dual claims, honouring the Open Door while asserting Japanese dominance (Shepherdson-Scottp. 551). A life-size family diorama with no father presents Japan as the region's patriarch (Shepherdson-Scottp. 549; Shepherdson-Scottp. 550). Peterson's "nationalising the sell" describes a neoliberal nationalism in which the national pavilion sells a product, here packaged food beside devotion to the King at Milan 2015 (Peterson 2020p. 279; Peterson 2020p. 293).

Fair gardens and fixed national images

Brown treats the official Japanese gardens at American fairs from 1876 onward as ideological tools that presented a timeless, pre-modern Japan (Brown). The naturalizing device linked Japanese culture to the living garden, so that a contested policy appeared to be an inherent feature of the nation (Brown). The 1939 fairs in San Francisco and New York share a feminine land of tradition that became the core image of Japan, while a masculine, westernising Japan appeared in the halls (Brown).

Authenticity, ahistoricism and collage

Sigur shows that Japanese officials used the Western demand for the authentic national pavilion, arranging the Hôôden exhibits at Chicago 1893 for aesthetic unity rather than chronology, and resting the authentic result on invented pedigrees (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 104). The Hôôden's neoclassical exterior, by Kuru Masamichi, is for Sigur neoclassicism in Japanese, claiming parity with the West's idealised heritage (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 95; Raizman & Robey 2018p. 99).

Çelik's Islamic settings at the fairs collapse "different periods and regions" into single structures, which made Islamic cultures appear timeless (Çelik 1992p. 57–58). Designers claimed accuracy through accuracy by collage of fragments, so that the Rue du Caire at Paris 1889 mixed archaeological claim with salvaged parts (Çelik 1992p. 57–58).

Debates and limits

The texts disagree most over whether the displayed could speak for themselves. Karp and Lavine argue that exhibitors cannot represent cultures, though they may be tactful impresarios (Karp & Lavine 1991), whereas Peterson takes national pavilions as self-representation and sets out to turn the lens that Benedict and Greenhalgh used (Peterson 2020p. 16). Kwon criticises earlier research on the 1903 Osaka display for focusing on the Japanese organisers rather than the Korean responses (Kwonp. 20). Hur rejects the binary that places hegemonic producers against uncivilised colonial subjects, which both the cultural hegemony school and its counter-hegemony opposite rely on, and denies that China exerted counter-hegemonic influence (Hurp. 167). Shepherdson-Scott qualifies Duara's sovereignty argument by insisting on the coercive forces in Manchukuo, such as displacement and forced labour (Shepherdson-Scottp. 542). Coté argues against Foucault's account of state power for failing to reach the imperial periphery (Cotép. 7). Brown's Japan is not a colonial subject, so critiques of Orientalism apply to it differently (Brown). The approaches also leave gaps: Peterson relies on English-language sources and cannot reach the intentions of Asian officials (Peterson 2020p. 29), and Brown leaves open whether propaganda altered history in less obvious ways (Brown).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Trace the intermediary: identify which company, agency or donor stood between a national pavilion and its visitors, and ask whether its name changed what the display claimed. This models Shepherdson-Scott's screen at Chicago 1933 (Shepherdson-Scottp. 541) and Peterson's "nationalising the sell" (Peterson 2020p. 279).
  • Read a stated principle beside a claim of advantage in the pamphlets and speeches of any foreign company or state that exhibited abroad, to see whether the two claims are made together. Shepherdson-Scott's dual claims model this (Shepherdson-Scottp. 551).
  • Compare the press vocabulary for an insult at one fair with the vocabulary used at a later one, to see whether the earlier controversy shaped the later reporting. Hur's "trauma of exhibition" models this (Hurp. 73).
  • Read the local press and readers against the organisers' programme, asking what the displays meant to them and whether that differs from the intention, as Hur does for Osaka and St. Louis (Hurp. 168).
  • Trace where each element of a reconstructed street or pavilion came from, and whether its claimed authenticity rests on one source or a patchwork, as Çelik does for the Rue du Caire (Çelik 1992p. 57–58).
  • Ask whether visitors were addressed as spectators or as participants, and whether the design gave the colonised a role, as Coté does at Semarang 1914 (Cotép. 34).

Where to start reading

  • Kwon, Hyeokhui. “An Analysis of Korean Intellectual Responses to the Exhibition of Koreans at Japanese Expositions: Nationalism and the Discourse on Northeast Asian Solidarity at the Turn of the Century.” Journal article. the Korean press's answers to the 1903 and 1907 displays, and the "national disgrace" framing.
  • Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020. the "performative order", Asia as method and the commercial turn in national pavilions.
  • Shepherdson-Scott, Kari. “Conflicting Politics and Contesting Borders: Exhibiting (Japanese) Manchuria at the Chicago World’s Fair, 1933–34.” Journal article. the screen, dual claims and authentic sovereignty in the Chicago 1933 Manchuria pavilion.
  • Brown, Kendall H. “Fair Japan: Japanese Gardens at American World’s Fairs, 1876–1940.” Journal article. how garden and gesture fixed a timeless national image across the 1939 fairs.
  • Park, Young-Sin. “Making ‘Modern’ Korean Subjects: The Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition of 1915.” Journal article. the conflicted Korean subject, and the reading of Seoul 1915 against colonial propaganda.
  • Hur, Hyungju. “Staging Modern Statehood: World Exhibitions and the Rhetoric of Publishing in Late Qing China, 1851–1910.” Doctoral dissertation. audience-oriented reception of the Chinese exhibits, read through the press at Osaka and St. Louis.
  • Coté, Joost. “Staging Modernity: The Semarang International Colonial Exhibition, 1914.” Journal article. colonial modernity, the native as participant, and the gap between plan and building at Semarang 1914.
  • Çelik, Zeynep. Displaying the Orient: Architecture of Islam at Nineteenth-Century World’s Fairs. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992. the ahistorical, collaged and self-defining Islamic pavilions of the nineteenth-century fairs.

Nation, memory and invented tradition

Anderson's imagined communities, Hobsbawm and Ranger's invented traditions, Nora's lieux de mémoire, and concepts about national image and memory. 37 concepts from 19 texts

This family of approaches asks how a nation is made visible to the people who visit an exhibition, and what the display selects, stages or leaves out of the past. Its vocabulary comes from Anderson's imagined communities, Hobsbawm and Ranger's invented traditions, Nora's lieux de mémoire, and a looser language of national image and official memory. Its authors treat a national display as a construction rather than a neutral record. Rezende reads the statistical pavilion at Rio 1922 as a way of imagining Brazil (Filipová 2015p. 172). Boone argues that world's fairs use the past to imagine a present and future nation (Boone 2019p. 6).

Four texts stand at the centre. Denton applies Nora and Hobsbawm to state museums in China (Denton 2014p. 11; Denton 2014p. 27). Coté reads Semarang 1914 through Anderson (Cotép. 34). Rydell, Findling and Pelle treat American fairs as an extension of post-Civil War reconstruction (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Rezende and Boone then apply the same questions to a single pavilion and to a neglected national history.

Imagined community and imagined simultaneity

Rezende takes Anderson's proposal that "communities are to be distinguished by the style in which they are imagined" and asks how Brazil was displayed at Rio 1922 (Filipová 2015p. 172). Raizman and Robey use the idea as the thread of their volume: national identity is built by selecting products and displays from among groups and sub-groups (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 7). Coté reads Semarang 1914's Native Section, which gathered the colonised population of every region under one view, as a 'nation in embryo' (Cotép. 34). Hoffenberg moves the idea from print to the body: exhibitions gave a shared envisioning and physical participation, as at Melbourne 1880 (Hoffenberg 2001p. 3).

Invented tradition

Several texts apply Hobsbawm and Ranger to different objects. Filipová reads fine-art displays from Paris 1855 onward as an invented tradition that reinforced state ideologies (Filipová 2015p. 12). Denton treats invention as a modern severance from the past, which grows when rapid change weakens old patterns, and applies it to museums of premodern China (Denton 2014p. 27). Roche takes invented traditions as the official traditions of host-state nationalism, produced through cultural inclusion policies (Roche 2000p. 9; Roche 2000p. 35). Boone reads Philadelphia 1876 as a selection that left no room for Spain (Boone 2019p. 8). Coté's 'discourse of tradition' at Semarang 1914 fixed craft and architecture as 'traditional', and let colonial science 'embalm' the native (Cotép. 34).

Lieux de mémoire and pasts beyond memory

Denton takes Nora's term for sites that exist because a living milieu of memory has been lost, and treats state museums as such sites, which impose a collective national memory (Denton 2014p. 11). Boone applies the frame to Chicago 1893, where the Spanish replicas were set against the present rather than linked to it (Boone 2019p. 119). Her 'ex-position' removes events from history and places them in an artificial realm of state-sponsored memory (Boone 2019p. 6). She also follows Connerton: embodied action carries social memory as much as words and images (Boone 2019p. 113). Bennett's 'pasts beyond memory' are a different object, the deep pasts that geology and palaeontology made visible from the 1840s (Bennett 2004p. 1).

Official, vernacular and popular memory

Denton takes Gillis's distinction between 'official' and 'vernacular' memory, and argues that in China the two are intertwined, since individual memories are mediated by state discourse (Denton 2014p. 13; Denton 2014p. 14). Samuel's contrast is starker. The New York Fair of 1964 and 1965 had "two constructions of its past": an official memory of a costly enterprise and a popular memory of an experience most visitors enjoyed (Samuel 2007).

National profile and national image

Greenhalgh's nation projects a national disposition through architecture, decor, artefacts, industrial produce and statistics (Greenhalgh 1988p. 112). The English version was 'Olde Englande', a fabricated pre-industrial image applied to English culture in general (Greenhalgh 1988p. 122). Kargon, Fiss, Low and Molella see fairs displaying "the various national versions of modernity" (Kargon et al. 2015p. 3). Mandell argues that what changed after Paris 1900 was less France than the image France held of itself (Mandell 1967p. 120). Findling and Pelle define national boosting as stressing what made the host look better than its rivals (Findling & Pelle 1990).

Staged pasts

Smith reads Old London and Old Edinburgh as reconstructed host-city streets, and argues that "the historic city displayed a vision of the past mediated by contemporary discourses of power, belief and politics" (Filipová 2015p. 203). Boone's 'Spanish Fantasy Heritage', a term from McWilliams, names the romantic history that idealised Spanish roots at San Diego 1915 (Boone 2019p. 169).

Nationalising synthesis, settler and frontier belonging

Rydell, Findling and Pelle argue that Chicago 1893 combined an economic case for overseas expansion with a racial case for innate hierarchy (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Coté reads Semarang 1914 as settler nationalism, since a privately organised show may have expressed the settlers' own pride (Cotép. 27). Badger reads Chicago 1893 against Turner's frontier thesis and the anxiety about cultural continuity (Badger 1979p. 123). Ganz's 'Melting Pot' favoured acculturation over total assimilation (Ganz 2008).

Postsocialism, neoliberalism and commodified nostalgia

Denton's 'postsocialism' names a period starkly different from, yet still connected to, the socialist past (Denton 2014p. 7). He uses 'neoliberalism' for the market reforms of the 1990s and reads the downplaying of class in market-era revolutionary museums as tied to it (Denton 2014p. 7; Denton 2014p. 86). Red tourism is, in his words, "revolutionary tourism is a form of commodified nostalgia" (Denton 2014p. 216). Miller's nostalgia is a different use, applied to craft displays that looked to the past against the Fair's forward-looking exhibits (Weimann 1981).

Debates and limits

The sharpest disagreements concern state control. Denton rejects the view of PRC museums as monolithic state propaganda, since exhibits are negotiated among curators, historians, cadres and officials (Denton 2014p. 14). Hoffenberg argues against Said and Cohn that commissioners made imperial knowledge participatory, so nationalism succeeded by permeation rather than imposition (Hoffenberg 2001p. 57; Hoffenberg 2001p. 27). Roche objects that Foucault's surveillance model, if over-generalised to museums, misreads exhibitions, which drew the public in (Roche 2000p. 37). He also says Bennett's exhibitionary complex underplays performance (Roche 2000p. 34).

What the approach leaves out, according to the texts, is the wider world. Greenhalgh does not examine the hundreds of exhibitions outside Britain, France and the United States (Greenhalgh 1988p. 2). Bennett's museums are confined to Britain, Australia and the United States (Bennett 2004p. 2).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask which categories a statistical display at a regional fair used to describe its own population, and for whom. Rezende's Pavilion of Statistics at Rio 1922 models this (Filipová 2015p. 172).
  • Compare two national pavilions at one fair: list the national character each claims, then see where their versions of modernity diverge. Kargon, Fiss, Low and Molella model this (Kargon et al. 2015p. 3; Kargon et al. 2015p. 6).
  • Trace which objects were newly given a national past, and which older traditions were left out. Denton's museums of premodern China model this (Denton 2014p. 27).
  • Test whether a fair's chosen history left out its neighbours' histories, using another fair's programme. Boone's reading of Philadelphia 1876 models this (Boone 2019p. 8).
  • Sort a fair's exhibits into those that look forward and those that look back, and check which women's or craft displays fall on the backward side. Miller's split at Chicago 1893 models this (Weimann 1981).
  • Set a fair's official record against visitors' recollections, and see where its two constructions of the past diverge. Samuel's New York 1964 contrast models this (Samuel 2007).
  • Ask which bodily experiences a fair offered, and whether visitors' accounts record them. Boone's use of Connerton at Chicago 1893 models this (Boone 2019p. 113).
  • Read a new museum's nostalgia or silences about class against its city's market, asking what present visitors are invited to enjoy. Denton's commodified nostalgia at red tourism sites models this (Denton 2014p. 216).

Where to start reading

  • Filipová, Marta, ed. Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840–1940: Great Exhibitions in the Margins. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015. Filipová's introduction, and Rezende's use of Anderson at lines 7921–7985.
  • Denton, Kirk A. Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2014. Denton's introduction (lines 196–1325), for lieux de mémoire, official and vernacular memory, and neoliberalism.
  • Boone, M. Elizabeth. “The Spanish Element in Our Nationality”: Spain and America at the World’s Fairs and Centennial Celebrations, 1876–1915. University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2019. Boone's introduction (lines 590–1124), for the ex-position and the Spanish Fantasy Heritage.
  • Roche, Maurice. Mega-Events and Modernity: Olympics and Expos in the Growth of Global Culture. London: Routledge, 2000. Roche on the national and inter-national dimensions of mega-events (lines 916–939).
  • Samuel, Lawrence R. The End of the Innocence: The 1964–1965 New York World’s Fair. Syracuse: Syracuse University Press, 2007. Samuel on official and popular memory (lines 174 and 2306–2307).
