Agency, contact and reception: who makes the meaning

Pratt's contact zone, reception and audience approaches, and concepts that give exhibited people, brokers and visitors a part in making meaning. 42 concepts from 18 texts

These approaches ask who takes part in making an exhibition's meaning. They set aside what a fair was meant to show and ask what visitors, go-betweens, performers and displayed people each did with it. Some treat the visitor as a reader who completes the display; some treat the fairground or colonial city as a contact zone where organisers and local people met; some ask what choices exhibited people could make at all. Pratt's contact zone, reader-response criticism and performance theory supply much of the vocabulary (Henry 2014p. 11; Rydell 1984).

Rydell is the clearest case of the first move, applying Norman Holland's reader-response schema to the American fairs of 1876 to 1915 (Rydell 1984). Hoffenberg and Kaiser keep the visitor in view while questioning how far organisers controlled what was seen (Hoffenberg 2001; Kaiserp. 54). Henry, Qureshi and Peterson apply Pratt's term or the question of agency to Keijo, London and Asian pavilions (Henry 2014p. 11; Qureshi 2011p. 153; Peterson 2020p. 16).

Reader-response and the absorbed visitor

Rydell borrows Norman Holland's schema, in which a reader builds a structure for himself and becomes absorbed in it. Visitors who were doing the fair made the exposition part of their lives, which for Rydell explains why the fairs shaped many individual and collective beliefs (Rydell 1984). On this account the reader experiences "more than the objective external creation of the artist" (Rydell 1984).

Hoffenberg adopts a modified version of the method for the exhibitions of England, Australia and India, treating them as social texts authored by commissioners and read by visitors, and drawing on visitors' memoirs and diaries (Hoffenberg 2001). "These were truly texts: events and experiences, opening social visions as much as enframing them" (Hoffenberg 2001). Kaiser's version is narrower: visitors could and often did read colonial messages very differently from what organisers intended, which he tests against newspaper accounts of ordinary visitors (Kaiserp. 54). Henry reads Keijo's shrine festivals of the 1920s and 1930s through the different places participants held in society, using social semantics, a term she attributes to an unnamed interpreter of the postlinguistic turn before turning to Gabriel Spiegel (Henry 2014p. 12).

Contact zones, brokers and translation

Pratt's contact zone names places where people separated by geography and history meet. Henry applies it to Keijo's roads, shrines and palace grounds, where officials and local elites promoted assimilation and residents negotiated its meanings (Henry 2014p. 11). Qureshi applies it to London as a whole (Qureshi 2011p. 45). Johnson applies it to the places where Europeans and Burmese people worked together on Cuffe's year in Burma, a collaboration shaped by colonial assumptions (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 38).

Withers adds brokers and go-betweens: administrators of galleries, lecture halls and museums mediated between the makers of imperial knowledge and its publics (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 251). His translation goes beyond linguistic equivalence and changes meaning for each readership (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 253).

Agency and effective consent

Qureshi separates agency from freedom. Displayed peoples in London learned English, refused demands and negotiated payment, and so kept some control within restrictive conditions (Qureshi 2011p. 153). Against this she sets a stricter test, drawn from Herzog and Gerber, in which consent counts as effective choice and consent only if a person chose among meaningful options without compulsion and with adequate information (Qureshi 2011p. 136). She judges that the African prisoners recruited for London 1886 could hardly meet it, and says consent is culturally and historically specific (Qureshi 2011p. 136). Peterson turns the lens to the agency evidenced in Asian self-representation (Peterson 2020p. 16).

Re-fusion, affect and performative culture

Peterson organises his case studies around three modes of performance: cultural shows, guides who perform national identity, and metrics-driven performance (Peterson 2020p. 22). The guides' work is re-fusion, presenting a nation's culture so that it looks unified to a foreign visitor, who leaves with an affect rather than facts (Peterson 2020p. 23). Affect is the feeling that passes between bodies and things in an in-between space, and Peterson applies it to the Korean pavilion at Milan 2015 (Peterson 2020p. 24; Peterson 2020p. 228).

Gosden and Knowles use performance in another sense. Colonial culture held together through acts, because links between black, white and Asian were not recognised and existed only as performed, through dress, flag ceremonies and census lines (Gosden & Knowles 2001). Bauman and Sawin show participants choosing a frame for their own activity, with demonstration the most workable (Karp & Lavine 1991).

Wonder and resonance

Greenblatt separates two engagements with displayed objects. Resonance is an object's power to reach out beyond its formal boundaries to a larger world; wonder is its power to stop the viewer and hold attention on a unique object (Karp & Lavine 1991). Cornish applies the pair to the Krishnanagar indigo model at Kew, London 1886, reading wonder at a miniature world alongside resonance with known images of indigo production (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 137).

Posited intention and contested frames

Baxandall describes an exhibition as a field of three agents, makers, exhibitors and viewers, whose contact happens between object and label (Karp & Lavine 1991). His key concept is posited intention: the purposefulness a viewer attributes to an object, a culturally conditioned goal rather than a mental event in the maker's mind (Karp & Lavine 1991). Lavine and Karp call exhibiting a contested terrain, since communities dispute who controls the presentation of their culture (Karp & Lavine 1991).

The public as a process, and exhibition fatigue

Hoffenberg's participation rather than coercion holds that exhibitions shaped social order by inviting people to take part, and he reads the London 1871 and Sydney 1874 shows as socialisation (Hoffenberg 2001p. 27). He asks readers to "conceptualize the public as a process": a social body formed through participation, not a fixed condition (Hoffenberg 2001p. 247). Geppert's exhibition fatigue (Ausstellungsmüdigkeit), from the 1880s, names a rationale that questioned large expositions, which he calls a "peculiarly Victorian emotion" (Geppert 2010p. 207; Geppert 2010p. 4).

Debates and limits

The texts disagree about control. Rydell reads the fairs as hegemonic, upper-class productions that used evolutionary ideas of race to justify exploitation, and he claims they explain how those ideas became popular (Rydell 1984). Hoffenberg argues against Said and Cohn that commissioners made imperial knowledge participatory, which could challenge British authority (Hoffenberg 2001p. 57), and Kaiser says the imperialist reading misses an exchange that was not one-sided (Kaiserp. 54). Rydell himself allows that lower-class acquiescence may have been far less than total (Rydell 1984). Badger asks whether contrasts were organic choices or "as a series of either/ors" (Badger 1979p. 123).

Others attack the frame. Geppert rejects Bennett's exhibitionary complex as presuming a consolidation that was not historically given (Geppert 2010p. 10). Mitchell argues that the exhibition's effect of an external reality is itself a mechanism of power, which the commodity-fetishism critique leaves untouched (Mitchell 1989p. 225). By the texts' own account, the approach tends to leave out the performers' side: showmen, spectators and performers left few records of their encounters (Qureshi 2011p. 9), and English-language archives cannot reach the intentions of Asian officials (Peterson 2020p. 29).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Sort the performers at a new fair (dancers, guides, staff measured by visitor numbers or sales) into Peterson's three modes to see which one the national display relies on (Peterson 2020p. 22).
  • Trace a visitor's own account of "taking it in" in diaries, letters or souvenir books, and compare its frame with the exhibits' frame, to see whether the absorbed visitor shared the organisers' reading (Rydell 1984).
  • Map where a foreign collector and local staff worked together on a survey or display, and ask how far those contacts shaped what was recorded and shown (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 38).
  • List the options a performer actually had, and the information available, before asking whether consent was given; this applies Qureshi's test to a contract or court case (Qureshi 2011p. 136).
  • Read a pavilion's sequence for resonance and wonder, asking whether it opens with a spectacular object and moves to its context, and whether that order matches the visitor's path (Karp & Lavine 1991).
  • Apply auto-anthropology, Strathern's term for "anthropology carried out in the context which produced it", to an exhibition staged by one's own institution, asking how its organisers' concepts match the analyst's own categories; Harvey did this for Seville 1992 (Harvey 1996p. 12).

Where to start reading

  • Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. Rydell's reader-response argument and his hegemonic conclusion, and the gaps he flags
  • Hoffenberg, Peter H. An Empire on Display: English, Indian, and Australian Exhibitions from the Crystal Palace to the Great War. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001. Hoffenberg on exhibitions as social texts, participation, and the public as a process
  • Qureshi, Sadiah. Peoples on Parade: Exhibitions, Empire, and Anthropology in Nineteenth-Century Britain. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2011. Qureshi on agency, effective consent and London as a contact zone
  • Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014. Henry on contact zones and social semantics in everyday colonial sites
  • Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991. Karp and Lavine, for Greenblatt's resonance and wonder, and Baxandall's three agents
  • Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020. Peterson on re-fusion, affect and the three modes of performance
  • Kaiser, Wolfram. “The Great Derby Race: Strategies of Cultural Representation at Nineteenth-Century World Exhibitions.” Article. Kaiser, a short statement of alternative readings against the imperialist interpretation

The author uses the term broadly for texts that carry the codes of exposition displays (encyclopedic arrangement, the gaze, realist and spectacular modes) into the fiction, the guides and the journalism of the period. (Della Coletta 2006p. 5)

“what I broadly term exposition narratives” p. 5

Used for Salgari's jungle cycle and the ethnic inventories in his novels, and Gozzano's Indian letters and reportage on the 1911 exposition.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could assemble a corpus of novels, travel letters and press pieces that echo one case-study fair, to test whether the fair's codes appear outside the fairground.

Denton, Kirk A. Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2014.
narratological methodDentonmethod

Denton reads museums as stories told in a visual language made of photography, text, painting, sculpture, maps, film, architecture and digital media. Each medium sets up its own kind of communication with the spectator, and together they give form to stories of the past. (Denton 2014p. 14)

“These various visual building blocks give form” p. 15

Used for Exhibit-by-exhibit analysis throughout the book. In the introduction the Road to Revival exhibit is read as a story that stresses national humiliation and the party's role in revival.

Beijing 2011

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could list each element of a new exhibition (panels, dioramas, maps, architecture, screens) and ask what story each tells and what identification it asks of visitors.

Finnegan, Diarmid A., and Jonathan Jeffrey Wright, eds. Spaces of Global Knowledge: Exhibition, Encounter and Exchange in an Age of Empire. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015.
bottom up perspectiveFinnegan, Wrightmethod

Each case study uses local specificity to shed light on global structures and processes, so that global processes appear as lived and experienced phenomena rather than abstract historiographical concepts. (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 11)

“the volume is characterised by a ‘bottom up’ perspective, which uses local specificity to shed light on global structures and processes” p. 11

Used for All eleven chapters, which the editors describe as empirically grounded case studies combining detailed archival research with thematic and conceptual reflection; Wright's Belfast museum is the example of a 'global space' built from local collecting.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could start from one object, site or person and ask what it shows about the wider network it belonged to, rather than starting from a global thesis.

empirical globalism (global imaginary)Mayhewanalytic concept

The 'global imaginary' is Malthus's implicit understanding of the structure and subdivisions of the world. The 1803 Essay displayed an 'empirical globalism' only hinted at in 1798: far more geographical evidence, but the same binary geography, now sharper. (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 170)

“the Essay of 1803 would display an empirical globalism only hinted at in 1798” p. 177

Draws on Hume; Robertson; Smith; C.A. Bayly

Used for Malthus's first (1798) and second (1803) editions of the Essay on the Principle of Population, and the colonies and 'forced' populations of China and India that complicated the binary of positive and preventive checks.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether an exhibition's geographical claims rest on the sources it cites, and whether its evidence grows while its categories stay fixed.

contact zoneJohnsonanalytic concept

Johnson uses 'contact zones' for the places where European and Burmese people met and worked together. Cuffe's knowledge of Burma, though shaped by colonial assumptions about class, gender and race, was a collaborative exercise carried out along these zones. (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 38)

“was consistently a collaborative exercise conducted in dialogue with and along the contact zones between European and Burmese populations” p. 38

Used for Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe's year in Burma, 1901-1902: her paintings and letters, the expedition to Yado over the Karen hills, the survey at Thandaung, and the Burmese labour and guides that made it possible.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could look for the places where a foreign collector and local staff worked together on a survey or display, and ask how far those contacts shaped what was recorded and shown.

resonance and wonderCornishtypology

Following Greenblatt, visitors engage with objects in two ways: resonance, where the displayed object points beyond itself to a larger world and the visitor comes to see it as representing an idea; and wonder, a sensory response to objects of high visual impact. Both are used by museums as exhibitionary strategies. (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 137)

“is a sensory response to objects of high visual impact” p. 138

Draws on Stephen Greenblatt

Used for Visitors' responses to the Krishnanagar indigo model at Kew, which Cornish reads as wonder at a miniature, unknown world together with resonance with known images of indigo production.

London 1886

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For a given display, a researcher could ask which objects drew visitors by wonder and which by resonance, and whether the labels encouraged one response or the other.

brokers and go-betweensWithersanalytic concept

Administrators of art galleries, lecture halls, public theatres and museums were also cultural producers and scientific 'brokers' and 'go-betweens', mediating between imperial knowledge's makers and empire's diverse publics. Withers proposes institutions as a line of enquiry for this reason. (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 251)

“scientific ‘brokers’, ‘go-betweens’ mediating between imperial knowledge’s” p. 251

Draws on Jon Klancher; Simon Schaffer, Lissa Roberts, Kapil Raj and James Delbourgo

Used for Institutions in general, and civic natural history museums in particular, which collectively exhibited the fruits of empire; Withers asks how these bodies were trained and what they could say.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could identify the curators, secretaries and commercial agents behind an exhibition and ask how each mediated between the makers of its knowledge and its visitors.

translationWithersanalytic concept

Translation is more than linguistic equivalence: it embraces movement over space and an almost ontological transformation as well as linguistic change, so that even books in one language change their meaning according to their readers. (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 253)

“‘Translation’ is more than linguistic equivalence since the term embraces movement over space” p. 253

Draws on James A. Secord

Used for Withers's third line of enquiry, languages, which he applies to the volume's translated texts, notably Livingstone's German and French editions in Henderson's chapter and the translation of missionary medicine in Hunter's.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the editions, captions or translated labels of one exhibition catalogue to see how its meaning shifted for each readership.

Geppert, Alexander C. T. Fleeting Cities: Imperial Expositions in Fin-de-Siècle Europe. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010.
presentation, representation and perception (Chartier)Geppertmethod

Each chapter is organised around three modes drawn from Roger Chartier's concept of representation: the construction and politics of competing realities, the organised display of a group's self-image, and the perception, reception and appropriation that generate meaning. In the chapters these become subsections on construction/politics, site/sights and reading/meaning. (Geppert 2010p. 15)

“inspired by the conceptual triad of ‘presentation’, ‘representation’” p. 15

Draws on Roger Chartier

Used for Structures each of the five case chapters, so that planning and politics, the site, and reception are treated in turn for each fair.

Berlin 1896Paris 1900London 1908London 1924Paris 1931

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A new case could be organised in the same three strands, so that the organisers' intentions, the physical site and the visitors' reactions each get their own sources.

exhibition fatigue (Ausstellungsmüdigkeit)Geppertcritique

Introduced in the 1880s, the German term Ausstellungsmüdigkeit ('exhibition fatigue') names a rationale that questioned the principle of holding large expositions, from visitors' physical and mental exhaustion to commercial doubts about cost. Geppert treats it as a discourse with institutional effects, and as the key to why the medium lasted after it had lost its novelty. (Geppert 2010p. 4)

“peculiarly Victorian emotion: ‘exhibition fatigue’.” p. 4

Draws on Max Eyth's diaries

Used for Applied to the German debates from the 1880s, the French and British responses, and in the conclusion to the 1900 and 1931 fairs and the blocked Anglo-German exhibition at the White City.

Berlin 1896Paris 1900London 1908Paris 1931

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a given fair drew complaints of overload or cost, who voiced them (visitors, officials, critics or organisers), and whether they led to any institutional control.

Gosden, Chris, and Chantal Knowles. Collecting Colonialism: Material Culture and Colonial Change. Oxford: Berg, 2001.
radically performative cultureGosden, Knowlestheoretical framing

Colonial culture held together through acts rather than through representations: because the links between black, white and Asian were not recognised, they existed only as they were performed, through dress, comportment, flag ceremonies and census lines, and objects were central because social effects were realised through material means. (Gosden & Knowles 2001)

“In a radically performative culture, objects will be crucially important”

Draws on Judith Butler; speech-act theorists

Used for White colonial dress regulations, patrol flag ceremonies and head-tax census lines, and cargo-cult drilling and flagpoles that mirrored colonial acts.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For a staged display or ceremony, one could ask which material forms were meant to make a relationship real for the audience, and how the audience answered back through their own use of the same forms.

Harvey, Penelope. Hybrids of Modernity: Anthropology, the Nation State and the Universal Exhibition. London: Routledge, 1996.
auto-anthropologyHarveymethod

Strathern's term for 'anthropology carried out in the context which produced it', which draws on concepts that belong to the society under study rather than on difference or culture shock. (Harvey 1996p. 12)

“anthropology carried out in the context which produced it” p. 12

Draws on Strathern (1987a, 1987b)

Used for Applied to Expo'92, a 'prime candidate' because its organisers and visitors were already working with the same cultural and social concepts that anthropologists use.

Seville 1992

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The approach could be used on an exhibition staged by one's own institution or nation, asking how its organisers' concepts match the analyst's own categories.

Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014.
contact zonesHenryanalytic concept

Henry borrows Mary Louise Pratt's term for places where subjects separated by geography and history meet. In Keijo, major roads, shrines, palace grounds and other public sites functioned as contact zones where officials and local elites promoted assimilation and residents negotiated its meanings. (Henry 2014p. 11)

“functioned as contact zones insofar as government officials and” p. 11

Draws on Mary Louise Pratt

Used for Namsan's shrines, Taihei Boulevard, the Kyŏngbok Palace expositions and neighborhood sanitation sites, treated as places of popular encounter with Japanese rule.

Keijo 1915Keijo 1929Keijo 1940

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term lets a researcher treat a fairground, a parade route or a festival as a place where officials, traders, visitors and critics meet and contest meanings. It asks who used the site, and for what, rather than only what it was designed to show.

social semanticsHenrymethod

Henry analyses cultural events through what she calls social semantics, a reading that looks both at the semiotic structures used to stage a celebration and at how participants, placed differently in society, understood it differently. Gabriel Spiegel's idea of resignifying meanings to make sense of events is the basis she cites. (Henry 2014p. 12)

“one interpreter of the postlinguistic turn has called “social semantics.” p. 12

Draws on Gabriel Spiegel

Used for Shrine festivals and their processions in the 1920s and 1930s, read through the varied responses of Japanese settlers, wealthier Koreans and poor newcomers, including pickpockets.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For an exhibition, one could ask how the same displays were read differently by settlers, elites and working visitors, and whether those readings can be traced in newspapers or police records.

Hoffenberg, Peter H. An Empire on Display: English, Indian, and Australian Exhibitions from the Crystal Palace to the Great War. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001.
social textHoffenberganalytic concept

Exhibitions are treated as texts: authored by commissioners through their guidebooks, classifications and use of space, and read by visitors in varied and sometimes contested ways. The shared reading made the nation and empire into interpretive communities. (Hoffenberg 2001)

“These were truly texts: events and experiences, opening social visions as much as enframing them.”

Used for The popular exhibitions of England, Australia and India between 1851 and 1911 as a whole; the author's reader-response method is applied to visitors' memoirs and diaries.

London 1851London 1862London 1911

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could list the route, guidebook and classification that a given fair offered its visitors, then look for diaries or press reports showing where visitors departed from that reading.

participation rather than coercionHoffenberganalytic concept

Exhibitions shaped social order by participation and not coercion, creating a sense of natural order, consensus and hierarchy. The author follows Edward A. Ross's 1901 sense of social control rather than the later meaning of the term. (Hoffenberg 2001p. 27)

“Exhibitions were not mere mirrors of the political and social order but agents of change” p. 27

Draws on Edward A. Ross

Used for Visitors to the London and Sydney shows of the 1870s, whose participation in exhibition life is read as a mode of socialisation and mobilisation for national and imperial objectives.

London 1871Sydney 1874

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For another case, one could ask which participatory acts (buying, touring, joining a parade) organisers relied on to produce consent, and whether visitors and the press read those acts the same way.

the public as a processHoffenbergtheoretical framing

The Victorian public is conceived as something made through participation at the shows, a social body being formed rather than a fixed condition. Exhibitions helped create that public, rather than only reflecting opinion that already existed. (Hoffenberg 2001p. 247)

“conceptualize the public as a process” p. 247

Draws on Mary Poovey; Donald Horne

Used for Ceremonies, tourism and pageants at the British and colonial shows, notably the Delhi Durbar Art Exhibition of 1903 and the 1911 Festival of Empire at Sydenham.

Delhi 1903London 1886London 1911

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask what a given fair's ceremonies and souvenirs did to make visitors feel like a public, and whether that public was made across several shows rather than at one.

Hollengreen, Laura, Celia Pearce, Rebecca Rouse and Bobby Schweizer, eds. Meet Me at the Fair: A World’s Fair Reader. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2014.
performismHellier-Tinococritique

Hellier-Tinoco uses 'performism' for the all-encompassing agendas, strategies, practices and processes that construct and shape concepts of peoples, bodies, activities and places through display and reproduction. (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 74)

“Here I use “performism” to refer to the all-encompassing agendas, strategies, practices, and processes that entailed constructing and shaping concepts of peoples, bodies, activities, and places through display and reproduction.” p. 74

Used for Two Mexican exhibits, a 3D film of the Janitzio Night of the Dead at Hannover 2000 and a suspended mask from Jarácuaro at Shanghai 2010, which present the P'urhépecha as timeless and authentic.

Hannover 2000Shanghai 2010

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace how a people's ritual or craft was reshaped for tourism at a given fair, following the same object through posters, guidebooks and later campaigns.

Kaiser, Wolfram. “The Great Derby Race: Strategies of Cultural Representation at Nineteenth-Century World Exhibitions.” Article.
alternative readingsKaisercritique

The argument that visitors could read the messages of exhibits, including colonial displays, very differently from the meaning intended by organisers and governments, so that intercultural exchange was not one-sided. (Kaiserp. 54)

“the visitors could and often did “read” the message of cultural inferiority of colonial peoples very differently” p. 54

Used for The human displays of colonised peoples in re-created native villages brought to Paris and St. Louis, where newspapers reported visitors' surprise at the intelligence and friendliness of the people on show.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could look for visitor letters, diaries or press reports from a given fair to see whether the readings they record match the organisers' intentions.

Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991.
exhibition as a field of three agentsBaxandalltheoretical framing

Baxandall proposes that an exhibition be understood as a field in which three distinct terms are active: the makers of objects, the exhibitors of made objects, and the viewers, each playing a differently structured game. Contact between them happens in the space between object and label. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“makers of objects, exhibitors of made objects, and viewers of exhibited made objects.”

Used for Used to analyse an anthropological display in which a Kota mbulu-ngulu guardian figure from Gabon is placed beside a Fang bieri and a 1907 Picasso, and to follow a viewer moving between object and label.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could map who the makers, exhibitors and viewers are for a given fair pavilion, and where in that setting the label and the object meet. That map can be compared across fairs that differ in their labelling.

framing of participant activityBauman and Sawinanalytic concept

The contextualising question participants ask of their own activity, 'What is it that is going on here?', and the frames they adopt in answer, such as performance, demonstration, instruction, exhibition or work; demonstration proves most workable because it allows process without finished products. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“a basic contextualizing question that lies at the heart of frame analysis”

Draws on Prague School (poetics)

Used for Applied to the 1987 Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife, where fiddlers, fishermen, a polka band, a string band and a Finnish singing group had to decide what they were doing on the Mall.

Washington 1987

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a demonstration or living display at a fair, which frame the performers themselves used, and how far the public's frame matched theirs.

in situ and in contextKirshenblatt-Gimbletttypology

Two approaches to the ethnographic object: in situ, a metonymic part standing for an absent whole, often enlarged by mimetic recreation; in context, the object set within a theoretical frame through labels, charts, catalogues and classifications. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“distinguish in situ from in context, a pair of terms that calls into question the nature of the whole”

Draws on Oleg Grabar

Used for Applied to period rooms, ethnographic villages, reenacted rituals and photo-murals as in-situ approaches, and to labels, typologies and docents as in-context approaches, with human display at the Midway and Skansen.

Chicago 1893Washington 1985

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could sort a given display into in-situ and in-context elements and ask which one carries the claim about the culture and which one carries the claim about the theory.

posited intentionBaxandallanalytic concept

The purposefulness a viewer attributes to an object: not mental events in the maker's mind but culturally conditioned goals or functions, pursued with culturally enabled resources in culturally determined circumstances. The viewer constructs an intentional description, and if deprived of information, probably makes it up. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“He works primarily with intention—intention not of course in the sense of mental events in the maker’s mind, but a posited purposefulness”

Used for Applied to the Kota figure and its label, where the label offers an explanatory rather than descriptive reading of the object's head and headdress.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could list the functions a label implies for a foreign object and ask which of them a visitor is left to supply on their own.

resonance and wonderGreenblatttypology

Two models of display experience: resonance is the power of an object to reach beyond its formal boundaries and evoke the cultural forces that produced it; wonder is its power to stop the viewer and hold attention on a unique object. Both have histories, and most exhibitions combine them. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“By resonance I mean the power of the displayed object to reach out beyond its formal boundaries to a larger world,”

Used for Applied to the State Jewish Museum in Prague, whose resonance depends on a felt intensity of names and voices; to Renaissance cabinets and Durer's account of Mexican objects as wonder; and to the Musee d'Orsay as a case of resonance overtaking wonder.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a given fair or pavilion, whether the display begins with wonder (a spectacular object) and moves to resonance (its context), and whether that order matches the visitor's path.

contested terrainLavine and Karptheoretical framing

Every exhibition draws on the cultural assumptions of its makers, so exhibiting is a contested field in which communities and institutions dispute who controls the presentation of a culture. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“The very nature of exhibiting, then, makes it a contested terrain.”

Used for Applied to the 1984 Te Maori exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum, where Maori elders rejected the catalogue's background, and to Hispanic Art in the United States, faulted for thin presentation of Hispanic culture.

New York 1984Houston 1987

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could list which groups had a say in a given national or colonial display, and whether the controversy was over the objects, the catalogue text or the claim to represent a whole people.

museum as temple and museum as forumLavine and Karptypology

Two stances on the museum: as temple, a timeless and universal reference model against which to compare individual perceptions; as forum, a place for confrontation, experimentation and debate. The editors argue that the museum is now a forum, and that the question of who participates in it has been neglected. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

“the traditional one of the museum as temple and a newer one of the museum as forum.”

Draws on Duncan Cameron

Used for Applied to the general case for museums and the art museum's curatorial authority, which the editors argue persists in a modified universalist aesthetics even as curators claim their view is one of several.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a given display, whether it behaves as a temple (a fixed standard) or a forum (open to contest), and who was invited to the forum.

Lawn, Martin, ed. Modelling the Future: Exhibitions and the Materiality of Education. Oxford: Symposium Books, 2009.
imaginaryEscolano Benitoanalytic concept

The repertory of texts, icons and realities about unknown and exotic peoples, shown at the universal exhibitions and then carried into school manuals, murals and pedagogical museums. It is a culture of stereotypes that later pupils absorbed. (Lawn 2009p. 32)

“realities established an ‘imaginary’, i.e. a culture.” p. 32

Used for The chapter applies it to school manuals, a Spanish arithmetic textbook, a Barcelona publisher's cover, and Danish and Senegalese classrooms, and to Vallin's 1878 map and comparative table of popular instruction in Europe.

Paris 1867Paris 1878London 1862

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could look for the same stereotypes about a colonised or distant people in the school readers of the country that held a fair and ask who was shown as modern and who as backward.

circumstantial paradigmEscolano Benitomethod

A method of reading school objects and their images as signs and traces, in the manner of a detective or physician, using suspicion, clues and conjecture to reach the meanings the objects carry. The text names this as Ginzburg's proposal and treats historical research as semiotic practice. (Lawn 2009p. 44)

“particularly useful the circumstantial paradigm that the author of The Cheese” p. 44

Draws on Carlo Ginzburg; Umberto Eco; Pier Paolo Sacchetto; Jurij Lotman

Used for The chapter uses it to read school manuals, classroom murals and the 1878 Vallin map as material testimony about the imaginary of distant peoples.

Paris 1878Paris 1867London 1862

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The method could be applied to a fair's surviving catalogues or school objects to ask which clues show what the organisers wanted visitors to conclude.

Mitchell, Timothy. “The World as Exhibition.” Comparative Studies in Society and History 31, no. 2 (1989): 217–236.
participant observationMitchellanalytic concept

The European traveller's double position: he wanted to immerse himself in the Orient and at the same time to stand apart from it. Mitchell argues that disguise or a photographer's cloth gave the observer an apparent objectivity, and that the modern tourist, Orientalist and anthropologist inherited this way of treating the world as a representation. (Mitchell 1989p. 232)

“The curious double position of the European, as participant-observer,” p. 232

Draws on Edward Said; Pierre Bourdieu

Used for Gerard de Nerval, taken into the labyrinthine streets of Cairo by a French photographer with a daguerreotype, and Edward Lane, who dressed as a Muslim to observe Egyptians unobserved.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a fair's guidebooks or official guides claimed the same position of seeing without being seen, and what authority that position was given.

Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020.
three modes of performancePetersontypology

The text separates three modes of performance in pavilions: cultural shows (choreographed dance and ritual performed on or around the grounds), guides who perform national identity in a prescribed way, and the metrics-driven performance of neoliberal productivity, which Asian states increasingly use to present themselves as high-achieving. (Peterson 2020p. 22)

“Performance has three primary modes of operation” p. 22

Draws on Jeffrey Alexander; Jon McKenzie

Used for Used as the organising scheme of the case studies. The third mode is applied in the conclusion to China's pavilion at Milan 2015 as the 'ultimate performance-obsessed state'.

San Francisco 1915New York 1939Brisbane 1988New York 1964Milan 2015

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could sort the performers at another fair (dancers, guides, workers measured by visitor numbers or sales) into these three modes to see which one the national display relies on.

re-fusion (guides)Petersonanalytic concept

Taking Alexander's account of social performance, the text describes the cultural labour of pavilion guides as 're-fusion': presenting a nation's culture so that it looks unified and fused to a foreign visitor, who leaves with an affect rather than a set of facts. (Peterson 2020p. 23)

“It is this process of ‘re-fusion’ that constitutes the cultural labour of these” p. 23

Draws on Jeffrey Alexander

Used for Applied to the guides of the Thai pavilion at Milan 2015 and, in the conclusion, to the Chinese pavilion, where the guides are described as crowd control and the performers as the only impactful bodies.

Milan 2015

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a pavilion's guides are selected and scripted to appear unified, and whether their role is to inform, to perform, or simply to manage crowds.

affect and the affective encounterPetersonanalytic concept

The text uses 'affect' for the feeling a visitor carries away from a pavilion, generated by sensory and bodily encounter rather than by information. Peterson takes the definition from Seigworth and Greg, in which affect arises in 'in-between-ness' and passes between bodies and things. (Peterson 2020p. 24)

“Increasingly affect and affective encounters, the stickiness” p. 24

Draws on Seigworth and Greg

Used for Central to the Korean pavilion at Milan 2015, where the text argues that the galleries maximised affect but never reached taste or smell. It is also applied to the Japanese garden at San Francisco 1915 and to the Philippine pavilion at New York 1964.

San Francisco 1915New York 1964Milan 2015

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could describe a pavilion's sensory sequence (sound, image, touch, food) and ask which affects it aims to produce and whether the visitor's body is engaged or only looking.

Qureshi, Sadiah. Peoples on Parade: Exhibitions, Empire, and Anthropology in Nineteenth-Century Britain. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2011.
urban spectatorQureshianalytic concept

An individual who assigns worth to observing the street and who is left deliberately undefined by gender, class, ethnic origin or intellectual ability, offered as an alternative to the flaneur. (Qureshi 2011p. 16)

“an individual who assigns worth to observing the street” p. 16

Draws on Walter Benjamin

Used for Writers' accounts of London's streets: Punch's 1849 print of Regent Street, Eliza Lynn's 'Passing Faces' (1855) and Henry Mayhew's London Labour and the London Poor.

London 1849London 1855

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask who the implied viewer of a particular fair or exhibition was, without assuming a gender or class, and how the street or the press trained that viewer.

intercultural contact zoneQureshianalytic concept

The proposal that London itself, with its Jewish, Asian, black and other foreign residents, be understood as a space of intercultural contact, so that displays of foreign peoples were not read through colour alone; the text names Mary Louise Pratt's definition in note 119. (Qureshi 2011p. 45)

“would allow the city to be reconceptualized as an” p. 45

Draws on Mary Louise Pratt

Used for The metropolis as the setting for encounters between residents and the shows, in place of encounters only abroad.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be applied to a host city of a fair to ask which migrant or resident communities met visitors and performers outside the official grounds.

effective choice and consentQureshianalytic concept

A framework, drawn from Herzog and Gerber, in which consent counts only where a person chose among a significant range of meaningful options without compulsion and with adequate information; the text also says consent is culturally and historically specific. (Qureshi 2011p. 136)

“A person may only be said to have made a free” p. 136

Draws on David Gerber; Don Herzog

Used for Performers recruited for London shows, including the African prisoners recruited for the Colonial and Indian Exhibition, whose cases the text judges highly unlikely to meet these criteria.

London 1886

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher on another case could list the options a performer actually had and the information available before asking whether consent was given.

agencyQureshianalytic concept

The capacity of displayed peoples to maintain some control within restrictive situations, through learning English, refusing demands or negotiating payment; the text separates agency from freedom and says it must not be conflated with it. (Qureshi 2011p. 153)

“displayed peoples created ways to maintain their agency” p. 153

Used for Performers in London shows, including the court cases of the Zulu chiefs and everyday acts such as refusing to undress or refusing a sum of money regarded as unfair.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): Documents such as contracts and court cases could be read for the small choices performers made, rather than only for whether they were exploited.

arenas for the production of intercultural and natural knowledgeQureshitheoretical framing

The shows are treated as places where intercultural encounters and claims about natural history were both made, which were then debated by scientists, showmen and audiences. (Qureshi 2011p. 6)

“arenas for the production of both intercultural and natural knowledge” p. 6

Used for London's shows as sites of ethnological observation, including John Conolly's 1855 presidential address to the Ethnological Society of London, which called for the displayed peoples to be studied.

London 1855

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a given fair, which knowledge was produced on site, by whom, and which of it reached scientific journals.

Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.

Networks, circulation and comparison: beyond the single fair

Concepts for studying exhibitions as connected, transnational and competitive systems, including centre and periphery. 30 concepts from 18 texts

Approaches in this family treat an exhibition as one point in a system of connections: borrowed models, objects and personnel, rivalry between states, and relations between a capital and its margins. They ask how a fair was assembled from elsewhere, how it was compared with other fairs, and where it stood in relation to centres of power. The question is how a fair operated across borders and scales, not what one fair meant.

Geppert's 'exhibitionary networks' and Raizman and Robey's 'networks of exchange' (Geppert 2010p. 4; Raizman & Robey 2018p. 7) sit at the centre, with Filipová's regional cases (Filipová 2015p. 3) beside them. Boone (Boone 2019p. 9) and Hur (Hurp. 172) widen the frame beyond one nation, while Finnegan and Wright (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 5) and Lawn (Lawn 2009p. 18) ask what kind of knowledge and comparison such connections produced.

Exhibitionary networks and networks of exchange

Geppert argues that the 'exhibitionary complex', coined by Tony Bennett, should be "replaced with that of ‘exhibitionary networks’" (Geppert 2010p. 4; Geppert 2010p. 10). Pavilions, villages and old-town sections moved between fairs through personal, professional and institutional ties, and he applies this to Berlin 1896, Paris 1900, London 1908 and London 1924 (Geppert 2010p. 15). Raizman and Robey read the fairs as "networks of exchange rather than as independent univocal displays" (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 7). Komatsu calls Vienna 1873, Philadelphia 1876 and Tokyo's Educational Museum 'nodes' that generated the image of modern education in Japan (Lawn 2009p. 83). Roche scales the idea to mega-events, which create 'hubs' and 'switches' in global flows (Roche 2000p. 218).

Transnational connection and hybridity

Syrjämaa sees exhibitions as a bunch of threads rather than a chain, an approach that "lays emphasis on hybridity, bricolage and cultural translation" (Filipová 2015p. 296; Filipová 2015p. 307). Helsinki 1876 drew its pavilion on Stockholm 1866 more than on Vienna, and its cottage interiors went on to Paris 1878 (Filipová 2015p. 296; Filipová 2015p. 307). Boone's 'transnational study' is distinct from national and personal hybridity, and applies to nine celebrations from 1876 to 1915, asking how the United States responded to Spanish displays (Boone 2019p. 9; Boone 2019p. 12). Hur places the late Qing public sphere beyond the nation, through Chinese-language publishers linking domestic and overseas readers (Hurp. 172).

Microcosm, barometer and summary

Badger calls the single fair "a focal point, a microcosm perhaps", through which a culture's experience at one moment can be examined, and tests Chicago 1893 on that basis (Badger 1979). Burris treats the nineteenth-century exposition series as a microcosm and barometer of wider developments in religion, applied to London 1851 and the 1893 Parliament of Religions (Burris 2001; Burris 2001p. 13). Mandell calls the great expositions "revelational, multi-sensuous summations of our culture" (Mandell 1967) and reads Paris 1900 as a weathervane of fin de siècle thought (Mandell 1967). Ratcliffe asks that exhibitions be used as windows on technology, culture or values (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 21).

Comparison, contest and global public space

Lawn makes comparison the organising idea of exhibitions: "Exhibition is the idea of comparison." (Lawn 2009p. 18) Kaiser's 'derby race', from Punch's 1851 cartoon, casts states as competitors at London 1851, Paris 1855, Philadelphia 1876 and Chicago 1893 (Kaiserp. 45). For Mandell, the Rue des Nations at Paris 1900 was a tour to rank nations by performance (Mandell 1967p. 78). Kaiser describes the fairs as "creating a global public space for the limited time span of the exhibitions" (Kaiserp. 45), a space that states filled with meaning while social groups occupied parts of it (Kaiserp. 54). Culture transfer, in his account, adapted imported institutions to domestic conditions rather than transferring them whole (Kaiserp. 49).

Objects in circulation: network of meanings and assemblage

Bell's 'network of meanings' links exhibitions, books and images, each image taking part in several discourses at once, among them entertainment, ethnology and the exotic picturesque (Bell 1992p. 25). Byrne's 'assemblage' treats fur traders' scientific work as bearing the markers of the networks and places that formed it (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 91). Gosden and Knowles read four New Britain collections as products of one colonial field of mutual influence (Gosden & Knowles 2001).

Centre, periphery and regional modernity

Filipová's volume "turns attention to what may be called regional modernity" (Filipová 2015p. 3), where fairs helped consolidate municipal identities (Filipová 2015p. 3; Filipová 2015p. 15). Its marginal events were not simple copies: regional fairs modified practices to suit local agendas (Filipová 2015p. 15). Hopson's regional history of Nagoya 1937 is an intervention against Tokyo-centred accounts of 1930s Japan (Hopsonp. 139). Bird reads the power annex at the edge of Paris 1878 as a 'displaced centre' in Freud's sense, marginal in position yet central to the whole (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 303).

Networks of knowledge

Finnegan and Wright define global knowledge as knowledge moving between and beyond dispersed territories, and as the pursuit of patterns that actors took to be worldwide (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 5). Nikolaou's networks of knowledge are 'webs' of linkages and intermediaries, through which consuls joined Cypriot sites to the British Museum (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 41; Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 55). Hunter's medicine at the Dublin University Mission was moulded from two sources and altered by local people (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 224). Millar treats the ship as a space in its own right, whose layout shaped what was collected (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 104).

Debates and limits

Several texts argue against the approach as others use it. Geppert calls Bennett's term misleading, since it assumes a consolidation that was not historically given (Geppert 2010p. 10). Filipová's contributors resist the view that the exhibitionary complex carries over unchanged to regional exhibitions (Filipová 2015p. 8). Hoffenberg argues that Said and Cohn suggest a hegemonic model, and that Australian and South Asian commissioners made imperial knowledge more participatory and multilateral (Hoffenberg 2001p. 57). Hur rejects both the cultural hegemony school and its counter-hegemony opposite, and treats Habermas's public sphere as a particular Western European practice (Hurp. 167; Hurp. 171).

Against readings of convergence, Gosden and Knowles say connection changed the parties without making them alike (Gosden & Knowles 2001). Finnegan and Wright warn that global history flattens the topography of knowledge-making (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 8).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Trace which pavilions, villages or personnel recur from earlier fairs, and test whether their similarity comes from personal or institutional ties rather than the host city; this is Geppert's model (Geppert 2010p. 4; Geppert 2010p. 15).
  • Compare a regional fair with its metropolitan models element by element, and ask which were modified for a local agenda; this follows Filipová's focus on adaptation (Filipová 2015p. 15).
  • Ask which groups beyond the exhibitors and displayed people, such as suppliers or interpreters, shaped the display, and treat it as a joint product; this extends Gosden and Knowles (Gosden & Knowles 2001).
  • Read the service infrastructure at a fair's edge, its boilers and power plants, as where what the displays hide is put; this is Bird's reading of Paris 1878 (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 303).
  • Trace how a fair's coverage travelled between overseas and domestic newspapers, to test whether a national press framing was in fact transnational; Hur's reading models this (Hurp. 172).
  • Compare the foreign models shown at one fair with the policies adopted afterwards, to see how they were adapted locally; this is Kaiser's culture-transfer test (Kaiserp. 49).
  • Ask Badger's question of a new case: how far does this fair represent its society, and what would a second fair show? (Badger 1979)
  • Ask whether a fair's knowledge moved beyond the organising empire or only reproduced it, as Finnegan and Wright frame it (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 5).

Where to start reading

  • Geppert, Alexander C. T. Fleeting Cities: Imperial Expositions in Fin-de-Siècle Europe. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010. Geppert, for the 'exhibitionary networks' argument and his critique of Bennett's term (l. 690, l. 981–982, l. 1091–1093).
  • Raizman, David, and Ethan Robey, eds. Expanding Nationalisms at World’s Fairs: Identity, Diversity, and Exchange, 1851–1915. London: Routledge, 2018. Raizman and Robey, for networks of exchange as the volume's organising frame (l. 531–532, l. 806).
  • Filipová, Marta, ed. Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840–1940: Great Exhibitions in the Margins. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015. Filipová, for regional modernity, marginality and the critique of copying (l. 734–735, l. 1327–1328).
  • Hur, Hyungju. “Staging Modern Statehood: World Exhibitions and the Rhetoric of Publishing in Late Qing China, 1851–1910.” Doctoral dissertation. Hur, for the transnational public sphere and the case against the hegemony model (l. 8549, l. 8804–8812).
  • Boone, M. Elizabeth. “The Spanish Element in Our Nationality”: Spain and America at the World’s Fairs and Centennial Celebrations, 1876–1915. University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2019. Boone, for a transnational frame applied across nine celebrations (l. 902–903, l. 1061–1062).
  • Badger, Reid. The Great American Fair: The World’s Columbian Exposition and American Culture. Chicago: Nelson-Hall, 1979. Badger, for the single fair as a test of representativeness (l. 254–261).
  • Finnegan, Diarmid A., and Jonathan Jeffrey Wright, eds. Spaces of Global Knowledge: Exhibition, Encounter and Exchange in an Age of Empire. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015. Finnegan and Wright, for the definitions of global knowledge and the critique of flattening (l. 565–566, l. 745–746).
  • Roche, Maurice. Mega-Events and Modernity: Olympics and Expos in the Growth of Global Culture. London: Routledge, 2000. Roche, for hubs and switches and the critique of Castells (l. 11063–11064, l. 11823–11824).

Objects in motion: collecting, classification and material culture

Concepts from anthropology and the history of collecting for what happens to things when they are shown. 15 concepts from 7 texts

This family of approaches treats an object as something that changes through what happens to it: production, exchange, display, classification and storage. Its question is what a thing becomes once it enters an exhibition or a collection, and what showing or sorting did to its meaning. Thomas states the premise most directly, placing the identity of a thing in its later history of use rather than in its fixed material form (Thomas 1991p. 4).

Thomas's Entangled Objects (Thomas 1991p. 4) supplies most of the concepts, though it reaches fairs only in one chapter on Sydney 1879 and Melbourne 1880 (Thomas 1991p. 176). Gosden and Knowles's Collecting Colonialism (Gosden & Knowles 2001) builds object biography from colonial New Guinea collections, and Mathur's India by Design (Mathur 2007p. 23) applies a biographical method to people and objects shown at London 1886. The fair-centred texts are Benedict's classification account (Benedict 1983p. 27), the Hollengreen and Rouse introduction with its curiosity-cabinet analogy (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 2), Hoffenberg on labour (Hoffenberg 2001) and Harvey on hybridity (Harvey 1996p. 28).

Biography and the social life of objects

Thomas's central claim is that "objects are not what they were made to be but what they have become" (Thomas 1991p. 4). He sets this against the museum habit of identifying a thing with its fixed form (Thomas 1991p. 4). Iron hatchets become useful and meaningful in a new way when a headhunting culture appropriates them (Thomas 1991p. 5). Thomas calls the process "Creative recontextualization and indeed reauthorship" (Thomas 1991p. 5), and applies it to European things in museum cases (Thomas 1991p. 5). At Sydney and Melbourne, Fijian material with very few weapons was reformulated into an image of craftsmanship (Thomas 1991p. 177).

Gosden and Knowles also use biography, with a caution: objects cannot narrate their own history, so the researcher must construct it from surviving materials (Gosden & Knowles 2001). Their objects-as-process view holds that an object is indicative of a continuing sequence of relations, which runs on in the museum (Gosden & Knowles 2001).

Mathur extends biography to people. Bodies on display, she argues, have their own biographies that refuse their containment as mere ethnic objects (Mathur 2007p. 23). She draws the method from Richard Davis and Tapati Guha-Thakurta (Mathur 2007) and applies it to the men of the 1886 display.

Classification and the synoptic display

Benedict holds that "Classification produced order, and an ordered world was the aim of the" expanding middle class (Benedict 1983p. 27). The scheme changed: London 1851 had four major categories (Benedict 1983p. 27), Paris 1855 added one for domestic economy aimed at the working classes (Benedict 1983p. 27), and by 1867 there were ten, with fine arts first (Benedict 1983p. 27).

Curran examines a museum's arrangement rather than a fair's catalogue. Klemm grouped objects by successive stages of culture, and Pitt Rivers arranged his collections by gradual development from one technological form to another (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 32; Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 33). Goode and Mason adapted these displays into the synoptic method (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 33), first shown at Cincinnati 1888 (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 33). Benedict studies the fair's official categories; Curran studies the order of one display.

Curiosity

Hollengreen and Rouse present the curiosity cabinet as a microcosm of wonders and anomalies (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 2). "The types of border crossings and associative mixes found in the curiosity cabinet" can also be found at the world's fair, on a vastly larger stage (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 2).

Thomas uses the word differently. Curiosity is an unstable desire, not authorised by any methodological discourse and set against scientifically controlled knowledge (Thomas 1991p. 127). Burke's 1757 account opens with children running after novelty (Thomas 1991p. 127). The two uses should not be merged: for Hollengreen and Rouse curiosity orders wonders that the fair inherits, while for Thomas it names a desire that collections objectified without method (Thomas 1991p. 127).

Mixture: hybrids and entanglement

Harvey calls the nation state, the universal exhibition and social anthropology hybrid institutions, which seek pure origins while playing with mixing (Harvey 1996p. 176). Her concern is "the effects of the politics of exclusion within key modernist institutions" (Harvey 1996p. 28). Expo'92 in Seville is the case where their objectifying and deconstructing practices meet (Harvey 1996p. 176).

Thomas's term is entanglement: "My concern is with entanglement rather than colonial “penetration”" (Thomas 1991p. 205). It describes mutual but unequal contact in which local systems keep relative autonomy and capacity for resistance (Thomas 1991p. 205). Thomas also takes discovery in its older sense of exposing what is already known (Thomas 1991p. 206). Harvey's hybrid and Thomas's entanglement do different work and should not be swapped (Harvey 1996p. 28; Thomas 1991p. 205).

Commodity candidacy and the gift as foil

Thomas adopts Appadurai's three terms: commodity phase, commodity candidacy and commodity context (Thomas 1991p. 27; Thomas 1991p. 28). Phase concerns moves in and out of a commodity state, candidacy whether a thing is culturally seen as exchangeable, and context the arenas of exchange (Thomas 1991p. 28). Shell valuables, money, Fijian mats and second-hand cars are the obvious exchangeables (Thomas 1991p. 28).

Thomas treats the gift as a critical foil, not an ideal type that clan prestations approximate: "a foil for a range of differences and mutations" (Thomas 1991p. 15). He doubts that the postulated gift is anything other than the inversion of the commodity (Thomas 1991p. 15). In this theme only Thomas works with the gift this way (Thomas 1991p. 15).

Machines in motion

Hoffenberg reads the popular exhibitions as presenting a self-regulating, factorylike industrialism, which "did not require modern workers" (Hoffenberg 2001). Celebrations of self-acting machines, he argues, included the workers and families the technology was displacing, and the machines ran inside buildings built by striking labourers (Hoffenberg 2001p. 170). The strand is distinctive because it asks what a display of machinery hid.

Debates and limits

Gosden and Knowles reject the New Melanesian History associated with Thomas (1991), which stresses similarities created by shared colonial histories. For them the field of social relations changed the parties without making them alike (Gosden & Knowles 2001). They also reject the gift and commodity split, the idea of a bipartite colonial culture, and treat things as tools for social experiments whose outcomes were unknown (Gosden & Knowles 2001).

Harvey takes issue with anthropologists who distance themselves from the constructionist approach that representational knowledge entails (Harvey 1996p. 171). Expo visitors, she shows, were more than consumers (Harvey 1996p. 27). Mathur sets her biographical method against the joint statement of major museums defending universal museums and their retention of objects (Mathur 2007).

What the approach leaves out is also named by the texts. Gosden and Knowles say they attended less to what happened to objects once they reached the USA, Europe or Australia (Gosden & Knowles 2001). Thomas confines fairs to a single chapter (Thomas 1991p. 176). Hoffenberg says historians have ignored the active part visitors took in the exhibition (Hoffenberg 2001p. 247).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Trace an object through its later labels, catalogues, press coverage and reuse, rather than reading it only as evidence of its place of origin (Thomas 1991p. 4; Gosden & Knowles 2001).
  • Compare the items a colony sent to each fair with what it left out; Thomas's Fijian selection had very few weapons at Sydney and none at Melbourne (Thomas 1991p. 5; Thomas 1991p. 177).
  • Compare the category lists of a new case with its official catalogue, to see which groups were placed where and which were left out, as Benedict does (Benedict 1983p. 27).
  • Ask whether a fair's objects were arranged by stage of development rather than by place of origin, and what that arrangement leaves out; Curran's synoptic method is the model (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 33).
  • Ask whether machines were shown as self-acting and whether the workers who built or ran them appear in the official photographs (Hoffenberg 2001; Hoffenberg 2001p. 170).
  • Read a community's gift and debt relations with an exhibition as an open question, not a fixed classification: what was given, and what debts it created (Thomas 1991p. 15; Thomas 1991p. 206).
  • Ask, for a given exhibition, which local systems of exchange shaped what was shown, rather than treating the display as the only source of colonial meaning (Thomas 1991p. 205).
  • Follow one person through the file trail of an exhibition, setting petitions against the official story of the display, as Mathur does (Mathur 2007p. 23).

Where to start reading

  • Thomas, Nicholas. Entangled Objects: Exchange, Material Culture, and Colonialism in the Pacific. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1991. for the object concepts (biography, recontextualisation, commodity candidacy, the gift as foil).
  • Gosden, Chris, and Chantal Knowles. Collecting Colonialism: Material Culture and Colonial Change. Oxford: Berg, 2001. for object biography and objects as process, and the case against the gift and commodity split.
  • Mathur, Saloni. India by Design: Colonial History and Cultural Display. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2007. for biographical method applied to people on display at London 1886.
  • Benedict, Burton. The Anthropology of World’s Fairs: San Francisco’s Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915. London and Berkeley: Scolar Press, 1983. for the official category lists of the fairs from 1851 to 1893.
  • Hollengreen, Laura, Celia Pearce, Rebecca Rouse and Bobby Schweizer, eds. Meet Me at the Fair: A World’s Fair Reader. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2014. for the curiosity-cabinet model and the synoptic display in Curran's chapter.
  • Hoffenberg, Peter H. An Empire on Display: English, Indian, and Australian Exhibitions from the Crystal Palace to the Great War. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001. for machines in motion and the labour kept out of fair displays.
  • Harvey, Penelope. Hybrids of Modernity: Anthropology, the Nation State and the Universal Exhibition. London: Routledge, 1996. for hybrid institutions and the Expo'92 case in Seville 1992.

Ritual, religion, performance and the mega-event

Anthropological and sociological concepts that treat fairs as rituals, festivals and staged events. 22 concepts from 8 texts

These approaches read an exhibition as a ritual, a religious celebration or a staged event. They ask what it did for those who entered it: how it confirmed a shared order, placed visitors and peoples within that order, and dramatised the authority of those who ran it. Most draw on anthropology or sociology. Benedict compares the fair with the potlatch as a contest of prestige (Benedict 1983). Rydell reads the American fairs of 1876 to 1916 as ideological wholes that confirmed the authority of corporate, political and scientific leaders (Rydell 1984). Gelernter reads New York 1939 as the rite of an American civic religion (Gelernter 1995p. 49), and Duncan calls the art museum a ceremonial monument (Karp & Lavine 1991). Roche treats expos as dramas and performances within a sociology of modernity (Roche 2000p. 12). Burris and Starr take narrower routes: religion as a field of study (Burris 2001), and allegory at San Francisco 1915 (Benedict 1983p. 135).

Ritual as contest: the mammoth ritual and the potlatch

Benedict defines a ritual as a symbolic statement whose symbols "stand ambiguously for a multiplicity of meanings" (Benedict 1983). Against the Durkheimian view of ritual as stabilising, he follows Gluckman and Cohen in treating it as a force for change too (Benedict 1983). A world's fair is one of a series of "mammoth rituals" in which power relations are expressed through a contest for advantage (Benedict 1983). The potlatch supplies the mechanism: a fair is an almost perfect example of Mauss's total prestation, and each escalating display puts rivals in debt (Benedict 1983p. 11).

Symbolic universes and the religion of fairs

Rydell takes the symbolic universe from Berger and Luckmann, who describe it as a structure of legitimation that gives meaning to social experience (Rydell 1984). He applies it to the expositions of 1876 to 1916 as one cumulative construct, moulded from ideas of race, nationality and progress into "symbolic universes" that confirmed the authority of the country's leaders (Rydell 1984). The fairs resembled religious celebrations and ritualistically affirmed faith in American institutions (Rydell 1984). Henry Adams is his source for the comparison, and Rydell calls the closing of San Francisco 1915 the fair's last rites (Rydell 1984).

Civic religion, the community of faith and the religious idiom

Gelernter describes the American civic religion as a faith held on emotional rather than rational grounds, whose utopian promise, he says, came true after the Second World War (Gelernter 1995p. 49). In 1939 America was "a community of faith", held together by distinctions such as clothes for home and clothes for the fair, whatever their moral weight (Gelernter 1995p. 92). Religion, for Gelernter, is "a matter of seeing: in the civic religion at its height the future was visible to the faithful (Gelernter 1995p. 369). Samuel finds the idiom in science at New York 1964, where an exhibitor called the displays sermons of science" (Samuel 2007), and a religious group's films of nature were among the fair's most compelling presentations (Samuel 2007).

The museum as ceremonial monument

Duncan calls the art museum a ceremonial monument: it is not a neutral sheltering space but works like temples and shrines (Karp & Lavine 1991). Visitors follow a prescribed route through a programmed narrative, the history of art, which purges history of social and political conflict (Karp & Lavine 1991). The idea draws on Alan Wallach and Victor Turner (Karp & Lavine 1991). Duncan's case is the Louvre, which the revolutionary government declared a public museum in 1793 to dramatise the new republic (Karp & Lavine 1991). The museum then gives citizenship a content without redistributing real power (Karp & Lavine 1991).

Mega-events, drama and the performance complex

Roche's mega-events are large, dramatic, mass-popular spectacles with international implications, a definition Hopson adopts for Nagoya 1937 (Hopsonp. 138). Roche's dramatological perspective reads the event core as drama and performance, attending to ritual, theatre and charisma (Roche 2000p. 12). Human displays at expos, in his view, belong to a "performance complex" as much as to Bennett's exhibitionary complex (Roche 2000p. 40). He faults Bennett for underplaying performance and for missing the link between expos and sport (Roche 2000p. 34). Hopson finds Nagoya 1937 complex enough to permit alternative interpretations, resistance and even discord (Hopsonp. 138). Samuel's global holiday, the name of Coca-Cola's pavilion at New York 1964, describes a festival that mixed real exchange with promotion (Samuel 2007).

Event zones and cultural citizenship

Roche divides a mega-event into three zones: the event core, read dramatologically; an intermediate zone, read as critical political sociology; and an event horizon, read as a long-run sociology of modernity (Roche 2000p. 12). The intermediate zone links events to the political and economic uses made of them by elites, classes and publics, and to cultural citizenship and inclusion (Roche 2000p. 12). Cultural citizenship concerns who was offered membership of the public and on what terms, and it is the stake of symbolic struggle over inclusion (Roche 2000p. 12). Time-structure, the experience of past, present and future as directional, is said to be restored by bounded mega-events, against the timeless present Castells describes (Roche 2000p. 222).

A field of religion, dual reification and the carnival

Burris uses the expositions to identify what allowed a field of religion to become a distinct, differentiated and permanent feature of Western thought (Burris 2001). His cultural history reads that formation across all levels of Western society and the colonial world (Burris 2001). Dual reification names the mutual support of social evolutionism and the fairs: the hierarchy of cultures on display gave the theory a living example (Burris 2001p. 64). The midway shows the hierarchy's consequences. At Chicago 1893, peoples lined up along it were given the message that they "belonged only in the carnival" (Burris 2001). Peoples deemed exotic were kept on the midway, not in the main fairgrounds (Burris 2001p. 85).

Allegory as a veil to be decoded

Starr reads the San Francisco 1915 sculpture and murals as allegory, veils over truths that guidebooks helped visitors decipher (Benedict 1983p. 135p. 136). Americans, on his reading, did not reject allegory. Tocqueville's literalism is better read less strictly, so long as one did not linger over the veil (Benedict 1983p. 135). The effort to decode made much of the art stilted, and its shortcomings can be traced to an obsession with lofty meanings (Benedict 1983p. 136).

Debates and limits

Several authors dispute the approach at its root. Benedict argues against the view that ritual only stabilises society (Benedict 1983), and against any claim that education or art was the fairs' chief purpose, since the exhibitors' aim was ultimately trade (Benedict 1983). Historians who doubt that Darwinian ideas reached popular culture through elite authority are answered by Rydell, who sees the fairs as a partial but crucial explanation of that popularisation (Rydell 1984). Hopson rejects a cynical reading of Nagoya 1937 as a misappropriation of capitalist peace (Hopsonp. 137). Samuel rejects the view that New York 1964 was a failure and its conservatism a liability (Samuel 2007).

Roche faults functionalist accounts, which see mega-events as reproducing social systems, for missing long-run change and resistant responses (Roche 2000p. 20). He also argues that Bennett underplays performance (Roche 2000p. 34), and that a Foucauldian account over-generalised to expos misreads them (Roche 2000p. 37). Burris calls a Foucauldian archaeology of the Congress Auxiliary papers untenable (Burris 2001p. 190).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Compare each new fair's towers, statues and gifts with its rivals', and ask who was left in debt, to see whether the rivalry ran between cities or nations; Benedict's potlatch model asks this (Benedict 1983p. 11).
  • Ask which symbols a regional or colonial exposition used to hold its visitors within one frame of meaning, and whether they formed a closed set, as Rydell argues for the American fairs (Rydell 1984).
  • Ask which civic creed a different exhibition presumed of its visitors, and whether its promises were shown as achieved or still to come (Gelernter 1995p. 49p. 369).
  • Read a new museum's route, ceiling and room order as a programmed sequence, and ask which national story it tells and who is counted as citizen (Karp & Lavine 1991).
  • Ask what a new event asked its audience to do, not only what it displayed, and whether the crowd was part of the spectacle (Roche 2000p. 40).
  • Plot where each people was placed on a new fair's grounds, to test whether a midway placement changed how its religion was judged (Burris 2001p. 85).
  • Trace a host city's intermediate zone from the bid through the build to the years after, and ask at whose expense the gains came (Roche 2000p. 12).

Where to start reading

  • Roche, Maurice. Mega-Events and Modernity: Olympics and Expos in the Growth of Global Culture. London: Routledge, 2000. the event zones, the dramatological and performance concepts, and the critique of Bennett.
  • Benedict, Burton. The Anthropology of World’s Fairs: San Francisco’s Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915. London and Berkeley: Scolar Press, 1983. the ritual and potlatch models, and Starr's allegory essay.
  • Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. the symbolic universe and the religious reading of the fairs.
  • Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991. the museum as ceremonial monument and its programmed route.
  • Burris, John P. Exhibiting Religion: Colonialism and Spectacle at International Expositions, 1851–1893. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 2001. dual reification and the carnival midway.
  • Gelernter, David. 1939: The Lost World of the Fair. New York: Free Press, 1995. civic religion and the community of faith.
