Space, architecture, city and landscape

Concepts for reading sites, buildings, gardens, midways and the relation of fair to city. 34 concepts from 17 texts

This family of approaches reads a world's fair as designed space: its grounds, halls, gardens, amusement zones and relation to the host city. It asks what a layout, a route or a planted site made visitors see, and what it said about nation, class and progress. Rydell's reading of the Midway shows the method. Classified under the Department of Ethnology, the Midway becomes part of the exposition's own argument rather than a sideshow (Rydell 1984). Geppert treats the site as socially produced space, using Lefebvre's triad to separate what each fair said about itself from its built and lived site (Geppert 2010p. 222). Gilbert, Park, Celik and Henry ask the same spatial questions of Chicago 1893, Seoul 1915, Islamic pavilions and colonial Seoul (Gilbert 1991p. 15; Parkp. 9; Çelik 1992p. 137–138; Henry 2014p. 10).

The fair's two zones: White City and Midway

Rydell gives Chicago 1893 two foundations, the White City and the Midway Plaisance, and reads the Midway's ethnological displays as scientific sanction for a view of the nonwhite world as barbaric (Rydell 1984). In a later book he pairs the same contest with the 1958 American Pavilion at Brussels, which he reads as the "triumph of the Midway as an organizing principle" (Rydell 1993p. 214). Benedict reads the amusement zone as a parody of the main pavilions, with gigantism turned into toys (Benedict 1983p. 53). Gilbert describes "two Chicago fairs coexisting in Jackson Park", one of control and one of fantasy, which the audience itself had to reconcile (Gilbert 1991p. 15).

Walking the site: tour, route and lived space

Gelernter's method is the walk: "My most important goal is not to make an argument but to lead a tour" (Gelernter 1995p. 54). Park's Seoul 1915 exhibition offered a numbered route of twenty stops through new Western-style pavilions (Parkp. 9), staging a contrast with old space (Parkp. 6). Geppert applies Lefebvre's spatial practices (perçu), representations of space (conçu) and spaces of representation (vécu) to five expositions, separating official statements from the site and lived experience (Geppert 2010p. 222). Henry's social space stresses a lived, contested use that often exceeded colonial plans (Henry 2014p. 10). Gilbert defines touring as creating a familiar environment within a strange place, and notes that the planners saw the balance as key to success (Gilbert 1991p. 21).

The fair and its host city

Geppert notes that exhibitions were increasingly described as "cities within the city" as their sites grew (Geppert 2010p. 233), and that the official guide called Kairo and Old Berlin complete cities (Geppert 2010p. 233). Hopson presents Nagoya 1937 as a city-branding event that showed Nagoya as an industrial and cultural centre of the empire (Hopsonp. 137). Maloney credits Chicago 1893 as the catalyst of the City Beautiful movement (Maloney 2012p. 79), and shows Manning carrying its civic planning into Jamestown 1907 (Maloney 2012p. 119). For Geppert, transience is intrinsic: fairs were built for demolition (Geppert 2010p. 243).

Re-created and ideal places

Lukas defines place sampling as the desire to re-create another place, which at fairs became thematic space, with the re-created Streets of Cairo at Chicago 1893 as his example (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 399). Geppert borrows Bakhtin's chronotope for ensembles such as Old London, Vieux Paris and the Bastille reproduction at Paris 1889, which offered imaginary travel backwards in time (Geppert 2010p. 245). Brechin reads Panama Pacific 1915 as a Byzantine myth of perfection, an "artifice of eternity" that was everything San Francisco was not (Benedict 1983p. 105).

Style, type and national architecture

Mandell says that at Paris 1900 Binet pushed eclecticism to its limit, drawing on Mexico, the Near East, India and Angkor, and that "sources from all the world and all the ages. It could go no further" (Mandell 1967p. 74). Celik's rationalists sought scientific rules of composition, while intuitionists relied on feeling and fantasy, and the theory was often not articulated (Çelik 1992p. 137–138). Regional difference at the fairs was a stylistic affair, which did not extend to the types of buildings displayed (Çelik 1992p. 137–138). Greenhalgh shows historicist styles fading slowly, some remaining in the marketplace after critics had moved on (Greenhalgh 1988p. 145).

Gardens and landscape: naturalism, planning and ephemerality

Maloney traces a shift from Victorian carpet bedding to naturalistic planting (Maloney 2012p. 67). She argues that the original design intent of fair landscapes, and the technical constraints behind them, should be understood to support preservation (Maloney 2012p. 10). Fair grounds had to look mature within months (Maloney 2012p. 2), and fair gardens were ephemeral yet influential (Maloney 2012p. 2). Planning the whole site replaced piecemeal planting (Maloney 2012p. 80).

Planned futures: aerial views, megastructure and midcentury urbanism

Morshed finds an ascensional spirit in Binder's winning poster for New York 1939, where nine aircraft rise with the Trylon, and an aerial gaze in Petit's aerial drawing of the grounds (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 503). Riar's megastructure is a flexible framework enclosing a city's functions, and its pavilion seemed in photographs to dematerialise (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 255). Uva's midcentury urbanism, a dense business centre ringed by highways with suburbs of single-family homes, was implemented in New York between the two New York fairs (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 78).

Placement and boundaries: where a thing is shown

Bell argues that the venue sets how an image is read. The Egyptian Hall made Angas's watercolours entertainment, and Gilfillan's Interior at the Great Exhibition sat among minerals and manufactures rather than art (Bell 1992p. 15). Brown's heterogeneous space lets a nation hold several stages, from halls to leased land for a pavilion (Brown). Whitfield writes that "Frontiers can be crossed, or they can divide", and applies the point to Chicago 1893 (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 83).

Debates and limits

Gilbert accepts that the Fair exhibited racism, but doubts that its planners imposed it on an unwilling audience, and says whether they half succeeded in regulating the Midway needs more careful examination (Gilbert 1991p. 82). Rydell, by contrast, reads the midways as central to upper-class efforts to shape popular culture (Rydell 1984). Brown warns that it is tempting to split official from unofficial gardens, yet commercial gardens reinforced the rhetoric of the national pavilion (Brown). Geppert criticises Bennett's exhibitionary complex as misleading, since it assumed a consolidation that was not historically given (Geppert 2010p. 10). Celik notes that architectural historians had treated buildings in isolation, so she takes the fairs whole (Çelik 1992p. 5–6). What the approach leaves out, on Gilbert's own account, is the city of the workers who built the fair and stayed behind (Gilbert 1991p. 2).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Trace a new fair's numbered route against its pavilion sequence, and ask where any old-new contrast sits, in the layout or in the labels. Park does this for Seoul 1915 (Parkp. 6).
  • Ask which zone of a new fair held the concessions and what it taught that the main buildings did not. Rydell's Midway (Rydell 1984) and Benedict's parody of the pavilions (Benedict 1983p. 53) model the question.
  • Compare the official account of a host city with the built site and with how visitors moved through it. Geppert's triad (Geppert 2010p. 222) and Henry's social space (Henry 2014p. 10) supply the three terms.
  • Ask what past and what elsewhere a fair staged together, and what that implied about time and space. Geppert's chronotope (Geppert 2010p. 245) and Brechin's ideal walled city (Benedict 1983p. 105) show how to read a fair's own rhetoric.
  • Count the styles on show, and check which were already stale when they appeared. Greenhalgh (Greenhalgh 1988p. 145) and Mandell's count of sources at Paris 1900 (Mandell 1967p. 74) would allow eclectic and modern phases to be compared across fairs.
  • Ask what a new fair left on its site, and who argued for permanence. Geppert's account of transience (Geppert 2010p. 243) supplies the test.
  • Ask whether a fair's posters and guides offered an overhead view of its future, and who that view made the planner. Morshed's aerial gaze (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 503) models the question.

Where to start reading

  • Geppert, Alexander C. T. Fleeting Cities: Imperial Expositions in Fin-de-Siècle Europe. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010. for the Lefebvre triad, the chronotope and the cities-within-the-city idea
  • Gelernter, David. 1939: The Lost World of the Fair. New York: Free Press, 1995. for the tour as a method of reading a fair's layout
  • Gilbert, James. Perfect Cities: Chicago’s Utopias of 1893. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991. for the White City and the Midway read as one fair, and for touring
  • Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. for the Midway's place in the exposition's ideological plan
  • Maloney, Cathy Jean. World’s Fair Gardens: Shaping American Landscapes. Charlottesville: University of Virginia Press, 2012. for fair gardens as design history and the original-design-intent argument
  • Çelik, Zeynep. Displaying the Orient: Architecture of Islam at Nineteenth-Century World’s Fairs. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992. for the pavilions and regionalism as a stylistic affair
  • Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014. for social space as a way into colonial sites

cities within the cityGeppertanalytic concept

Over the nineteenth century expositions were increasingly described as 'cities within the city', and their subsections as little secluded cities. Progress, technology and the future

Concepts about the idea of progress, technological display, modernism and the futures that fairs promised. 29 concepts from 16 texts

The approaches in this theme treat a fair as a statement about the future: what it said progress was, for whom, through which machines and displays, and how later writers judged the promise. They share the premise that an exhibition is an instrument of ideology rather than a neutral record of achievement. Rydell reads the American fairs of 1876 to 1916 as ritual confirmation of economic growth and racial hierarchy (Rydell 1984). Ganz asks for what, and for whom, Chicago 1933 displayed progress (Ganz 2008). Gelernter places the realisation of the American utopia around 1976 and describes the present as a post-utopian twilight (Gelernter 1995p. 53). The question these texts answer is what future a fair promised and who was asked to believe it. Rydell's World of Fairs (Rydell 1993p. 110) and Ganz's study of Chicago 1933 (Ganz 2008) stand at the centre, with Molella and Knowles extending the question to New York 1964 (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 5).

Progress as ideology

Rydell defines progress as an ideology of economic development, presented as the answer to America's problems (Rydell 1984). Ganz says Chicago 1933's organisers replaced orthodox views with the belief that progress rides on technological innovation, which limited humankind's role to consumerism (Ganz 2008). Rydell, Findling and Pelle read the technological utopianism of the 1930s, with General Motors' Futurama as its emblem, as a vision in which technology and corporate capitalism made social problems seem to disappear (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Rydell's scientific idealism is the creed that the Science Advisory Committee wanted visitors to absorb, "more political than scientific, more ideological than philosophical" (Rydell 1993p. 96).

Technological sublime and the machine

Della Coletta takes David Nye's technological sublime, the awe produced by man-made technology, which at fairs becomes a collective experience of human skill rather than a solitary encounter with nature (Della Coletta 2006p. 37). She applies it to the bird's-eye view and to Salgari's Le meraviglie del Duemila (1907) (Della Coletta 2006p. 13). Molella draws on Henry Adams, who contrasted the dynamo with the Virgin in the art pavilions of Paris 1900 and proposed an animated dynamo as a compromise (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 97p. 98). Mumford's megamachine marks the Cold War's apogee of techno-science (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 98). Gelernter's New York 1939 is the case of art and technology joined: "Art ministered to technology." (Gelernter 1995p. 168)

Futures and periodisation

Rydell's future perfect describes New York 1939 exhibits that held out a future perfect society, wholly conditional on popular acceptance of the blueprints laid down at the fairs (Rydell 1993p. 118); the fair authorities placed their utopia in time rather than space (Rydell 1993p. 130). Hopson's new Pacific Age ties Nagoya 1937 to a national mission, and its rise to doubts about Western civilisation after 1914-18 (Hopsonp. 142). Gelernter's postutopian twilight is his periodisation of American utopia (Gelernter 1995p. 53). Demeter follows Bukatman in reading the Carousel of Progress's final scene as a retro-future, "futures past... now exhumed and aired" (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 94).

Hybrid, slow and postmodern modernity

Raizman and Robey introduce hybrid modernity for Carl von Diebitsch's architecture, modern industrial construction only superficially clothed in Islamic revivalism (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 11); Hedrick applies it to the kiosk's industrial materials and portability (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 43). Bennett's slow modernity describes evolutionary museums that organised past and present through long continuities rather than sharp breaks (Bennett 2004p. 187). Harvey's modern coherent subjects and postmodern diffuse consumers addresses Expo'92 visitors both as "modern coherent subjects" and as diffuse consumers (Harvey 1996p. 134).

Reactionary and fascist modernism

Kargon et al. take Herf's reactionary modernism, which under National Socialism reached the core of social transformation, not only its surface aesthetics (Kargon et al. 2015p. 42); they call Nazism's mixture pragmatic reactionary modernism (Kargon et al. 2015p. 56) and test the concept against the aborted Tokyo 1940 plans (Kargon et al. 2015p. 84). Fascist modernism is their reading of the planned E42 (Rome 1942) artifacts as an ensemble, where blending Roman authority with engineering was no contradiction to Fascist supporters (Kargon et al. 2015p. 111).

Planned programmes: culture, peace and cooperation

Labbé's culture technique joined technical training to general culture, a middle way that Dautry set between one-sided technical education and an exclusive culture-first approach (Kargon et al. 2015p. 9); Paris 1937 imagined France as a rational middle way (Kargon et al. 2015p. 29). Hopson's capitalist peace was the Nagoya 1937 vision of stability and prosperity through free trade rather than autarky (Hopsonp. 140p. 142). Ganz's cooperative progress organised exhibits around industrywide progress rather than competing products, though the plan did not win every exhibitor (Ganz 2008). Findling and Pelle trace fairs since the Crystal Palace to the aim of forwarding industrial civilisation (Findling & Pelle 1990).

Contested futures and whose progress

Rydell argues that America's world's fairs had always been "battlegrounds for control of the future" (Rydell 1993p. 157); African Americans tried to redirect that future toward social justice and economic equality, and he treats their response as audience response (Rydell 1993p. 156). Ganz takes up David Noble's questions, "Progress for what? What kind of progress? Progress for whom?" (Ganz 2008), and draws on Mary Beard's point that the fair left a fuller history of man than of women (Ganz 2008).

Order, containment and the dead circus

Gelernter's ought culture answers why dynamite could be left unguarded in 1939 New York: a life of obligation rather than desire (Gelernter 1995p. 210). Samuel's safe bubble describes Moses, heavily inspired by Walt Disney, creating a space virtually free from worldly concerns (Samuel 2007). Coté's progressivism gave colonial administrators an apparently neutral language and defined non-believers as uneducated, backward or native (Cotép. 8). Bennett's dead circus sets evolutionary museums against living spectacle; the expert is the impresario of a dead Punch-and-Judy show (Bennett 2004p. 12p. 13).

Debates and limits

The sharpest disagreement concerns whether a fair's official story can stand for its public. Samuel rejects histories that call New York 1964 a failure, since they leave out what visitors could see, hear and learn (Samuel 2007). Gelernter calls Rydell's book tendentious but says he learned a lot from it (Gelernter 1995).

Other critiques target rival models of power and consumption. Harvey argues against Baudrillard that Expo'92 visitors were more than consumers (Harvey 1996p. 27). Bennett accepts that McClintock is right about time, but argues that treating it solely as ideological misses the new ways the historical sciences posed of managing the self (Bennett 2004p. 26). Hopson rejects reading Nagoya's peace theme as a cynical misappropriation (Hopsonp. 137). Rydell, Findling and Pelle ask whether Expo 2000 at Hannover will escape the technological utopianism of earlier fairs (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). The gaps the texts name are visitor experience and the progress that went unrecorded (Samuel 2007; Ganz 2008).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask, as Ganz does of Chicago 1933, for what and for whom a new fair displays progress, and which groups' spaces it separated or integrated; this shows whose future was addressed (Ganz 2008).
  • Trace what a fair's future depends on: as Rydell does for New York 1939, ask who was said to hold the plans and what visitors had to accept (Rydell 1993p. 118).
  • Compare the vantage points a fair offered and the awe they were meant to produce, as Della Coletta does for the bird's-eye view (Della Coletta 2006p. 37).
  • Read an unbuilt or abandoned monument with its plans and approvals, as Kargon et al. read E42, to find where past and future were fused (Kargon et al. 2015p. 111).
  • Look for a modern structure under ornament and ask which audience each layer addressed, as Raizman and Robey and Hedrick do for Diebitsch (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 11p. 43).
  • Set a fair's peace or cooperation theme against its trade content, as Hopson does for Nagoya 1937, to see whether it is a programme or a backdrop (Hopsonp. 140p. 142).
  • Map which conflicts an exhibition kept off its grounds and who decided, as Samuel does for New York 1964 (Samuel 2007).
  • Test whether a display organises time as continuity or rupture, as Bennett does for evolutionary museums, then ask the same of a fair's account of its own past (Bennett 2004p. 187).

Where to start reading

  • Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. Rydell on progress as ideology and racial hierarchy at American fairs, 1876-1916.
  • Rydell, Robert W. World of Fairs: The Century-of-Progress Expositions. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993. Rydell on future perfect, battlegrounds for the future and scientific idealism in the 1930s fairs.
  • Ganz, Cheryl R. The 1933 Chicago World’s Fair: A Century of Progress. Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 2008. Ganz on Chicago 1933: progress for whom, and cooperative versus individual exhibits.
  • Della Coletta, Cristina. World’s Fairs Italian-Style: The Great Expositions in Turin and Their Narratives, 1860–1915. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2006. Della Coletta on the technological sublime and the bird's-eye view.
  • Molella, Arthur P., and Scott Gabriel Knowles, eds. World’s Fairs in the Cold War: Science, Technology, and the Culture of Progress. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2019. Molella on the dynamo and the Virgin, the megamachine and the Carousel's final scene.
  • Kargon, Robert H., Karen Fiss, Morris Low and Arthur P. Molella. World’s Fairs on the Eve of War: Science, Technology, and Modernity, 1937–1942. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2015. Kargon et al. on reactionary and Fascist modernism in the planned expositions of 1937 to 1942.
  • Samuel, Lawrence R. The End of the Innocence: The 1964–1965 New York World’s Fair. Syracuse: Syracuse University Press, 2007. Samuel on the safe bubble and popular memory against official history.
  • Bennett, Tony. Pasts Beyond Memory: Evolution, Museums, Colonialism. London: Routledge, 2004. Bennett on slow modernity and the dead circus.

Gender, class and the politics of consensus

Concepts about women's and workers' place at fairs, class, hegemony and the manufacture of consent. 41 concepts from 18 texts

These approaches read a world's fair as a political project: displays, speeches and plans that sought to persuade particular publics that an order of nation, class, race or sex was natural or progressive. They ask whom a fair was meant to win, whose meanings it fixed, and which dissent it had to absorb (Rydell 1993p. 214; Gilbert 1991p. 13).

Rydell's reading of the American fairs of 1876 to 1916 is the reference point: the expositions "performed a hegemonic function" and blurred class divisions among whites (Rydell 1984). Rydell, Findling and Pelle call this the 'cultural hegemony school', which reads fairs through their organisers' intentions (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000). Badger (Badger 1979), Gilbert (Gilbert 1991p. 13) and Kargon and co-authors (Kargon et al. 2015p. 2) apply related framings to single fairs, while Peterson (Peterson 2020p. 230) and Boone (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 9) take them to national self-presentation and cultural diplomacy.

Hegemony and consent

Rydell defines hegemony as the exercise of economic and political power in cultural terms, with force used only when that fails (Rydell 1984). Della Coletta uses the Gramsci-derived term for Turin 1911 and notes that its consensus is never wholly homogeneous, so subordinate discourses arise inside the fair (Della Coletta 2006p. 5; Della Coletta 2006p. 10). Gilbert finds that the institutions built to impose order on Chicago connected the groups it was meant to separate (Gilbert 1991p. 13; Gilbert 1991p. 82). Rydell's 1930s book adds that "some social groups have greater resources to define" reality than others (Rydell 1993p. 214). Thomas uses the word for colonial Fiji, where Gordon "depended upon hegemony, consent, and the fabrication of shared meanings"; that is an administration, not a fair (Thomas 1991p. 171).

Soft power and cultural diplomacy

Peterson takes 'soft power' from Joseph Nye, whose model he says derives almost entirely from American power, and applies it to all nations (Peterson 2020p. 230). Middle-power states at New York 1964 are read as exercising it (Peterson 2020p. 230). The Thai pavilion at Milan 2015 is instead "ultimately offered a coercive, hard-power experience", tied to domestic authority (Peterson 2020p. 263). Molella and Knowles use the term as a general frame, calling the Cold War fairs "conspicuous arenas for the exercise of soft power" without naming Nye (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 6). Boone takes cultural diplomacy from Claire Fox: dialogue among intellectuals brings understanding (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 196). Kaiser lists three state goals, a favourable national image, alliances and agendas, but argues that states did not control what visitors took from the fairs (Kaiserp. 46; Kaiserp. 54).

Propaganda and ideological struggle

Kargon and co-authors treat the years before the war as a propaganda war focused on ideological struggle (Kargon et al. 2015p. 2). At Düsseldorf 1937 Nazi consumer propaganda sold 'enticement' and 'deprivation' together, so that consumption became a civic duty (Kargon et al. 2015p. 31; Kargon et al. 2015p. 55). Mandell describes the Paris 1900 exposition as a truce that eased political tempers and kept rival parties silent on the Dreyfus Affair (Mandell 1967p. 103). Rydell, Findling and Pelle describe fairs as supplying 'ideological and cultural armor', whose weight grows when tied to transnational corporate capitalism (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000).

Order, reassurance and unity

Badger's Victorian belief in improvement without disorder is expressed as "faith that man could have his revolution and control it too" (Badger 1979). Chicago 1893 had to reaffirm it, and its disorder was read as dynamic progress (Badger 1979p. 123). The business generation of 1873 to 1897 wanted reassurance, and the Philadelphia 1876 Centennial looked back to the national past (Badger 1979p. 28). Badger reads the White City's planned unity as both a response to anxiety and an escape from conflict (Badger 1979p. 125; Badger 1979p. 126). Samuel argues that the 1964 fair's conservative tone, which critics treated as a flaw, gave visitors stability and reassurance (Samuel 2007).

Class, the middle class and popular culture

Rydell argues that nationalism and racism together obscured class divisions among whites (Rydell 1984). Gilbert describes the middle class as a growing group of nonmanual workers and professionals, and the elite that planned the 1893 Fair as 'of but not in' it (Gilbert 1991p. 4; Gilbert 1991p. 11). He treats commercial and popular culture as 'aspects of the same phenomenon' in the 1890s, and reads the 1893 exhibitions as anticipating a later eclecticism he calls 'postmodern' (Gilbert 1991p. 11; Gilbert 1991p. 15).

Women's place and separate display

Weimann treats whether women's work should be shown in a separate building or beside men's as the central dispute over Chicago 1893's Woman's Building; the Isabella faction opposed separation (Weimann 1981p. 51; Weimann 1981p. 55). The split between general reform and women's own equal rights divided the Isabella Association from the clubwomen (Weimann 1981p. 43). Equal footing without a separate exhibit left black women's groups out (Weimann 1981p. 111; Weimann 1981p. 123). Palmer argued that the home ideal of woman's sphere let manufacturers underpay women, a view Weimann records without adopting (Weimann 1981p. 250). Markwyn applies 'universal womanhood' to the women's pavilion at San Antonio 1968 (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 138; Molella & Knowles 2019p. 143). Ganz reports that in 1933 women's exhibits were integrated with men's (Ganz 2008).

Planners, experts and official reasons

Hoffenberg describes commissioners as a 'clerisy' of professionals applying administrative skill and scientific knowledge to public culture (Hoffenberg 2001). Greenhalgh finds the professed reasons, peace, education, trade and progress, largely constant from 1851 to 1940, with peace 'little more than a rhetorical exercise' (Greenhalgh 1988p. 16; Greenhalgh 1988p. 22). Kargon and co-authors apply Hofstadter's split between 'soft' idealists and "the tough-minded, practical" pragmatists (Kargon et al. 2015p. 58). Ganz presents Chicago 1933 as privately financed by business leaders (Ganz 2008). Skee's 'Cold War consensus' of advisers from RAND and SRI is traced through Harrison Price's attendance estimates (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 58; Molella & Knowles 2019p. 59).

Debates and limits

Gilbert accepts that the 1893 Fair exhibited racism but treats whether its planners imposed it on an unwilling audience as a separate question (Gilbert 1991p. 82). Kaiser holds that social groups occupied parts of the exhibition and read displays differently (Kaiserp. 54). Badger argues that a fair had to show American diversity, so any single theme is a selective reading (Badger 1979p. 122). Hur rejects the cultural hegemony school's binary of hegemonic producers and colonial subjects, which does not fit China, and asks for audience-oriented approaches (Hurp. 167). Rydell's own gap allows that lower-class acquiescence may have been far from total (Rydell 1984).

Peterson sets his work against studies that show colonised peoples as integral to imperial display (Peterson 2020p. 16). Greenhalgh rejects the idea that imperialism motivated every display (Greenhalgh 1988p. 82). The texts leave gaps in visitors' own experience (Samuel 2007), in women as a population group (Ganz 2008), and in the workers' city (Gilbert 1991p. 2).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask which groups a new fair addressed, and whether its planners saw one audience or several. Gilbert's middle-class and elite split would show whether the plan imagined one public (Gilbert 1991p. 4; Gilbert 1991p. 11).
  • Trace the four professed justifications in a new fair's official guide, and check which comes first. It would show what planners said the fair was for (Greenhalgh 1988p. 16; Greenhalgh 1988p. 22).
  • Separate messages to domestic visitors from those aimed at rival powers, and compare both with the press. The propaganda-war frame makes this a test of audience (Kargon et al. 2015p. 2).
  • Check whether a fair's unity was offered as fact or as reassurance, and for whom, by setting its plan against its critics (Badger 1979p. 125; Badger 1979p. 126).
  • Compare a women's section's stated purpose with whether it was placed separately or among the general categories, as Weimann's dispute does (Weimann 1981p. 55; Ganz 2008).
  • Read a fair's cultural-diplomacy claim against its reviews, and ask whether a stress on likeness hid differences visitors would notice, as Boone does for the 1910 tour (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 196).
  • Ask which groups had the means to write a fair's official account, and how dissenting press accounts were kept out of it (Rydell 1993p. 214).
  • Ask whether a national pavilion aims to attract its visitor or to direct them, and whether both occur, using Peterson's soft and hard power test (Peterson 2020p. 230; Peterson 2020p. 263).

Where to start reading

  • Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984. Rydell's hegemony argument in its introduction and conclusion.
  • Rydell, Robert W. World of Fairs: The Century-of-Progress Expositions. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993. the theaters of power and the power to define reality.
  • Rydell, Robert W., John E. Findling and Kimberly D. Pelle. Fair America: World’s Fairs in the United States. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 2000. the cultural hegemony school and the closing argument on armour.
  • Gilbert, James. Perfect Cities: Chicago’s Utopias of 1893. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991. Gilbert's Chicago, the Midway and the hegemony test.
  • Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020. Peterson's soft and hard power, with Milan 2015 as the contrast case.
  • Weimann, Jeanne Madeline. The Fair Women: The Story of the Woman’s Building, World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893. Chicago: Academy Chicago, 1981. the dispute over a separate Woman's Building.

Kaiser, Wolfram. “The Great Derby Race: Strategies of Cultural Representation at Nineteenth-Century World Exhibitions.” Article.
goals of cultural representationKaisertypology

Three main goals that states pursued with their cultural representations: a favourable national image abroad, the formation or strengthening of national and ideological alliances, and the setting of international or domestic agendas through culture transfer. (Kaiserp. 46)

“the creation of a favorable national image abroad” p. 46

Used for Applied to France (the Paris exhibitions of 1855 to 1900, against Britain and then Germany), to the United States at Philadelphia 1876, and to Japan at Philadelphia, Chicago and Paris.

Paris 1855Paris 1867Paris 1878Paris 1889Paris 1900Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could sort the national sections of a given fair under these three goals and check which goal dominated for each state, then compare the result with the fair's official rhetoric.

ideological alliance of republicsKaiseranalytic concept

The use of an exhibition to form a symbolic community of republics, which could sit alongside, and partly conflict with, the national alliances of monarchical Europe. (Kaiserp. 49)

“attempted to use their exhibitions for the symbolic formation of an ideological alliance of republics” p. 49

Used for The Philadelphia exhibition of 1876, commemorating American independence from monarchical Britain, and the Paris exhibition of 1889, which marked the centenary of the French Revolution and drew republican delegations.

Philadelphia 1876Paris 1889

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check which regimes sent delegations to a given fair, and whether the political language about a shared form of government matched the visits that actually took place.

cultural shieldKaiseranalytic concept

Japan's willingness to adopt Western systems of production, forms of government and high culture, which the text says gave it a shield against imperial intrusion, in contrast to China, which was not officially represented until 1904. (Kaiserp. 48)

“created a highly effective cultural shield against imperial intrusion” p. 48

Used for The Japanese sections at Philadelphia 1876, Chicago 1893 and Paris 1900, and the unofficial Chinese displays that the text presents as weak and conservative by comparison.

Philadelphia 1876Chicago 1893Paris 1900

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether a given country used its national section to present itself as ready for partnership with an imperial power, and compare cases where it did not.

Kargon, Robert H., Karen Fiss, Morris Low and Arthur P. Molella. World’s Fairs on the Eve of War: Science, Technology, and Modernity, 1937–1942. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2015.
ideological struggle (propaganda war)Kargon, Fiss, Low, Molellatheoretical framing

The 1930s fairs differ from their predecessors because they focused on ideological struggle; the text calls the years before the war a propaganda war, and says the war of ideas was significant for the outcome of the fighting. (Kargon et al. 2015p. 2)

“they focused their spotlights on ideological struggle” p. 2

Used for All five fairs of the 1930s, and Brussels 1958 as a continuation in which 'the battle was between the two major superpowers' (lines 4754-4757).

Paris 1937Düsseldorf 1937New York 1939Tokyo 1940Rome 1942Brussels 1958

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): For any fair, separate the messages aimed at domestic visitors from those aimed at foreign visitors and rival powers, and compare both with the press coverage.

'hard' and 'soft' New DealKargon, Fiss, Low, Molellatypology

Hofstadter's distinction, which the text uses for two kinds of New Dealer: the 'soft' idealists, often academics, social thinkers or urban planners, who wanted to serve 'the little people', and the 'hard' pragmatists, often lawyers, economists or businessmen. (Kargon et al. 2015p. 58)

“were the tough-minded, practical (Hofstadter called them pragmatic)” p. 59

Draws on Richard Hofstadter; Arthur Schlesinger Jr.

Used for The 1939 New York fair: Mumford and his allies saw the fair's public-education role as an opportunity, while designers such as Teague, Bel Geddes and Loewy read 'planning' and 'social' around the needs and wants of consumers (lines 2134-2137).

New York 1939

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): When a fair's planners split between reformers and business sponsors, ask which group controlled the main theme and which exhibits carried the reformers' message.

paradox of enticement and sacrificeKargon, Fiss, Low, Molellaanalytic concept

Nazi consumer propaganda promised future abundance while asking Germans to give up goods and accept shortages, so that consumption became a form of civic duty; the text says the regime sold both at once. (Kargon et al. 2015p. 31)

“sold the German people on the paradox of enticement and sacrifice simultaneously.” p. 31

Used for Schaffendes Volk in Düsseldorf: its advertising and displays, and the loan vouchers for young couples (lines 1323-1329), read as 'enticement' and 'deprivation' sold together (lines 1896-1897).

Düsseldorf 1937

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): On another regime's fair, look for the same pairing of an appeal to desire with a call for restraint, and check which social groups are asked to make the sacrifice.

Mandell, Richard D. Paris 1900: The Great World’s Fair. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1967.
political tranquillizer (the treve de l'Exposition)Mandellanalytic concept

The fair worked as a truce: its public and patriotic character eased political tempers, so that rival parties agreed to silence on the Dreyfus Affair and politicians were reluctant to disturb the peace it brought. (Mandell 1967p. 103)

“The Exposition of 1900 had served well politically” p. 103

Used for The Dreyfus Affair in 1899-1900: the press inquiry that called for silence, the 'truce of the exposition', and the amnesty that passed quietly. Mandell cites 1878 as a precedent ('The great tranquillizer was the Paris Exhibition', line 959).

Paris 1900Paris 1878Paris 1889

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether another fair held in a divided year had the same effect, by tracing whether press coverage and official statements fell silent on a dispute during the fair's run.

Molella, Arthur P., and Scott Gabriel Knowles, eds. World’s Fairs in the Cold War: Science, Technology, and the Culture of Progress. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2019.
soft powerMolella, Knowlesanalytic concept

The editors call the fairs of this era conspicuous arenas for the exercise of soft power. They say the US pavilions staked claims to the future through fashion, film and celebrity, in ways that went beyond missiles and computers. (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 6)

“claims to the future in ways that went beyond missiles and computers” p. 6

Used for The US pavilions across the Cold War fairs, as the editors' general frame; Uva applies the term to the display of household goods at New York in 1964.

Brussels 1958New York 1964

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which national pavilion at a given fair used consumer goods, film or celebrity to claim the future, and compare that with the objects-and-statistics displays described in Swift's chapter.

Cold War consensusSkeeanalytic concept

Skee uses the historians' term for a coalition of advisers, from RAND, SRI and other research institutes and consultancies, who mobilised against a Communist threat. Price and his peers used a quantitative, systems-oriented framework to bring business and political establishments together in support of Cold War American democratic capitalism. (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 58)

“in what historians have called the Cold War consensus” p. 58

Used for Harrison Price's attendance estimates and feasibility studies for Century 21 in Seattle, HemisFair '68 in San Antonio and the Louisiana World Exposition in New Orleans.

Seattle 1962San Antonio 1968New Orleans 1984

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a fair's attendance and cost projections came from consultants in the same network, and how their disclaimers allocated the risk of being wrong.

universal womanhoodMarkwynanalytic concept

Markwyn's term for the category the Woman's Pavilion promoted: visitors were shown women as individuals and as embodiments of a supposedly universal womanhood. She reads this as a hemispheric feminine solidarity, akin to other Cold War women's organisations' soft diplomacy through shared definitions of femininity. (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 138)

“of a supposedly universal womanhood” p. 138

Used for The Woman's Pavilion at HemisFair '68, which she compares with the Woman's Building at the Chicago fair of 1893 and with the Texas debate over the Equal Rights Amendment.

San Antonio 1968Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare how a women's pavilion defines its audience, as one category or divided by race, class or nation, and whether it addresses women as producers or consumers.

Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020.
soft power / hard powerPetersonanalytic concept

Using Nye's terms, the text treats state self-representation as a form of power: 'soft power' attracts and co-opts, while 'hard power' coerces. The text argues that all nations use soft power, and that a pavilion can also be a coercive, hard-power experience when it is tied to domestic authority. (Peterson 2020p. 230)

“ultimately offered a coercive, hard-power experience, one whose success” p. 263

Draws on Joseph Nye

Used for The Philippines and Indonesia in New York 1964 are read as middle-power soft-power exercises, Brisbane 1988 as a 'conscious, soft-power exercise' by China, and the Thai pavilion at Milan 2015 as a coercive, hard-power experience.

Brisbane 1988New York 1964Milan 2015

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a given pavilion, whether the aim is to attract (soft) or to direct the visitor's conduct (hard), and whether the two are present together.

Raizman, David, and Ethan Robey, eds. Expanding Nationalisms at World’s Fairs: Identity, Diversity, and Exchange, 1851–1915. London: Routledge, 2018.
cultural diplomacyBooneanalytic concept

Boone takes the guiding assumption of cultural diplomacy from Claire Fox: that dialogue and contact among intellectuals bring understanding and mutual respect. She argues that the 1910 reviews stressed similarity between the United States and its southern neighbours, which avoided political conflict, and that this was an odd way to achieve that dialogue. (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 196)

“dialogue and contact among intellectuals lead to greater understanding and mutual” p. 196

Draws on Claire Fox

Used for The touring exhibition of 120 paintings and 41 sculptures sent from the United States to Buenos Aires, Santiago and Montevideo, read through the reviews and the Caras y Caretas, Zig-Zag and Sucesos cartoons.

Buenos Aires 1910Santiago 1910Montevideo 1911

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): When an exhibit is offered as diplomacy, a researcher could ask whether the stress on likeness served the sponsor's aims and hid differences the audience would notice.

Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.
hegemonyRydelltheoretical framing

By hegemony Rydell means the exercise of economic and political power in cultural terms by the established leaders, who win the consent of the population to the direction imposed on social life; force is used only when cultural power can no longer maintain order. (Rydell 1984)

“World’s fairs performed a hegemonic function precisely because they propagated the ideas and values of the country’s political, financial, corporate, and intellectual leaders”

Draws on Antonio Gramsci

Used for The fairs as propaganda for the national leadership of the period; the conclusion reads the midways as efforts by elites to establish their cultural hegemony.

Philadelphia 1876New Orleans 1885Chicago 1893Atlanta 1895Nashville 1897Omaha 1898Buffalo 1901Saint Louis 1904Portland 1905Seattle 1909San Francisco 1915San Diego 1915

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which groups a local exhibition addressed as its audience, and whether the dissent it recorded (labour, the black press) marked the limit of the consent it sought.

muted class divisions among whitesRydellanalytic concept

Nationalism and racism together obscured class divisions within white society, so that the emphasis on white supremacy gave whites a shared national purpose and defused perceptions of class domination. (Rydell 1984)

“The emphasis on white supremacy as a utopian agency, moreover, muted class divisions among whites, providing them with a sense of shared national purpose.”

Used for The fairs of 1876 to 1916 set against the class warfare from the railroad strikes of 1877; at the Chicago Midway, Americans of any class could ‘study ethnography practically’.

Philadelphia 1876New Orleans 1885Chicago 1893Atlanta 1895Nashville 1897Omaha 1898Buffalo 1901Saint Louis 1904Portland 1905Seattle 1909San Francisco 1915San Diego 1915

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether a regional fair addressed workers, employers and exhibitors differently, and whether its racial displays did the same work of uniting whites across class.

Rydell, Robert W. World of Fairs: The Century-of-Progress Expositions. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993.
theaters of power (webs of signification)Rydellanalytic concept

The author states that the century-of-progress expositions were theaters of power and also what the anthropologist Sidney Mintz calls webs of signification that gave reality meaning during the Depression. The fairs are read as systems of meaning that legitimised the existing order rather than as neutral showcases. (Rydell 1993p. 11)

“progress expositions were theaters of power.” p. 11

Draws on Sidney Mintz

Used for The introduction applies the idea to the depression-era fairs as a group, and the conclusion applies it to the claim that the fairs helped secure elite cohesion.

Chicago 1933San Diego 1935San Francisco 1939New York 1939

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept invites a question about who a fair's meanings served: a researcher on a different exhibition could list its organising webs of meaning (speeches, guidebooks, architecture) and ask which groups they left out.

cultural and ideological repairRydelltheoretical framing

The author treats the depression-era expositions as exercises in cultural and ideological repair and renewal. They were designed to restore popular faith in the economic and political system, and to encourage Americans to share in controlled fantasies about modernizing the present. (Rydell 1993p. 10)

“exercises in cultural and ideological repair” p. 10

Used for The four main fairs of the 1930s, presented as the book's whole subject, and then the corporate-government alliance the later chapters describe.

Chicago 1933San Diego 1935San Francisco 1939New York 1939

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a given exhibition was built to repair a crisis of confidence, and look at what it promised to restore and to whom.

the power to define realityRydellanalytic concept

Rydell's conclusion argues that the expositions' organisers had more resources to define social reality than their critics, and that the fairs, by drawing on the authority of science, helped the national elites and middle-class Americans hold together around one definition of progress. He cites Donald Horne for the claim that some social groups have greater resources to define reality than others. (Rydell 1993p. 214)

“some social groups have greater resources to define” p. 214

Draws on Donald Horne

Used for The fairs of 1933-34 and 1939-40, read against the dissenting voices that the African American chapter documents.

Chicago 1933San Francisco 1939New York 1939

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept lets one ask, for any exhibition, which groups had the means to write the official account, and how dissenting accounts in the press or in the community were kept out of the official record.

Rydell, Robert W., John E. Findling and Kimberly D. Pelle. Fair America: World’s Fairs in the United States. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 2000.
ideological and cultural armorRydell, Findling, Pelleanalytic concept

The authors use the metaphor of armor for the ideological and cultural protection that world's fairs have built, comparable to the armor some dinosaurs evolved, and they ask whether that armor will help the human species survive or only give a false sense of security. (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000)

“they continue to provide us with ideological and cultural armor”

Used for The conclusion's reading of the whole fair history, from London 1851 to Chicago in 1893 and 1933-34, New York 1939-40, Seville 1992 and Hannover 2000.

London 1851Chicago 1893New York 1939-40Seville 1992Hannover 2000

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The metaphor can be turned into a question about a later fair or exhibition: which permanent buildings, museums or narratives it left behind, and whether they still shape how the city presents itself.

cultural hegemony schoolRydell, Findling, Pelletypology

The authors' first of six schools of writing on fairs, which examines them through the intentions of their organisers and managers, reading fairs as vehicles for winning popular support for national imperial policies. (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000)

“The first may be termed the cultural hegemony school.”

Draws on Antonio Gramsci; Robert Rydell; Tony Bennett

Used for The authors' survey of the scholarship, and their Chicago 1893 chapter, where Putnam and the fair board treated race in what the text calls a traditional hegemonic manner.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could use the school as a checklist of organiser-side sources (plans, instructions, board minutes) and then ask what the audience-centred schools would add for the same fair.

Samuel, Lawrence R. The End of the Innocence: The 1964–1965 New York World’s Fair. Syracuse: Syracuse University Press, 2007.
conservatism as an assetSamuelanalytic concept

The Fair's conservative, postwar tone, which critics treated as a flaw, gave visitors stability and reassurance during the cultural upheaval of 1964–65, and Samuel argues it was a key to the Fair's popularity. (Samuel 2007)

“the Fair’s conservative tone was thus not a liability, as critics have argued, but I believe a key asset”

Used for The Fair's architecture and entertainment, set by Moses's traditional taste, against the civil rights struggle, the Vietnam War and the 1965 counterculture named in the introduction.

New York 1964

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a given exhibition's conservatism was a commercial or political choice, and which audience it was meant to reassure.

Thomas, Nicholas. Entangled Objects: Exchange, Material Culture, and Colonialism in the Pacific. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1991.
hegemony in colonial rule (contrast with the theatre state)Thomastheoretical framing

Thomas describes Gordon's rule in Fiji as depending on hegemony, consent and the fabrication of shared meanings, not on violence or the denial of indigenous identity. Indirect rule celebrated Fijian chieftainship and made the Crown the apex of the hierarchy, and the text says Fiji was not a theatre state oriented to symbolic display. (Thomas 1991p. 171)

“Gordon’s approach was different: it depended upon hegemony,” p. 171

Draws on Geertz

Used for Applied to Governor Gordon's administration and the display of clubs and bowls at Government House in Levuka, which ordered Fijian culture into a totality for the colonial state, and to the ethnological interest in Fijian custom.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a colonial display works by consent or by coercion, by checking who was made a spokesperson for the exhibited culture.

Weimann, Jeanne Madeline. The Fair Women: The Story of the Woman’s Building, World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893. Chicago: Academy Chicago, 1981.
separate exhibit (a separate Woman's Building against an exhibit of merit)Weimannanalytic concept

Weimann treats whether women's work should be shown in a separate building or beside men's work as the central dispute over the Building. Some wanted women's work apart so that its extent would be seen; the most advanced thinkers wanted an exhibit of merit, not sex, with women competing beside men. The Isabella faction opposed separation. (Weimann 1981p. 51)

“Isabellas did not want women’s work to be separate from men’s.” p. 55

Used for The Board's first decision against a 'Woman's Department', which it reversed at its second session, and the Chicago press attacks on a 'special building' in December 1890.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): On another exhibition, ask whether women's work was argued for as a separate display or within the general categories, and who opposed each option.

woman's "sphere" (the home as the conservative ideal of woman's place)Palmer (in a speech Weimann reports)analytic concept

The conservative theory that woman's sphere is the home, and that wage work is unfeminine. Palmer argues that the theory lets manufacturers underpay women, so the Building's industrial exhibits answer it. Weimann records the argument as Palmer's and does not adopt it. (Weimann 1981p. 250)

“She plunged into the controversial area of woman’s “sphere” p. 250

Used for Palmer's speech on women's wage labour at the Exposition, which defends the Building's displays of women's industrial and professional handiwork.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a women's section presented its work as answering a home ideal, or as evidence of women's wage work, and which exhibits carried each message.

freemasonry (among women, abroad)Palmer (term), reported by Weimannanalytic concept

Palmer's name for a bond among women abroad, which she offered as a reason that forty-one countries answered the Board's circulars and appeals. Weimann reports the term, and the Commission's surprise at the response, without making it her own explanation. (Weimann 1981p. 139)

“Bertha Palmer spoke of “the freemasonry” among women” p. 139

Used for The Board's foreign correspondence and appeals to women in other countries, traced in the chapter on the state and foreign committees.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether an exhibition's international women's network was built through personal appeals across borders, or through governments, and which one the sources show.

chivalric chimeraWeimann (term from the Chicago Herald)critique

The Chicago Herald's label for the Board of Lady Managers, a body set up as a recognition of women that the editorial said gave them no real standing and cost the public money. Weimann uses the phrase as the title of the chapter on the Board's first months. (Weimann 1981p. 45)

“The Board created as a recognition of them is simply a chivalric” p. 55

Used for The Board's first meeting on November 18, 1890, its disputes with the Directory and the Commission, and the press's complaints about its expense.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could look for the press label given to an advisory women's committee in another exhibition, and test whether that body had a budget or any authority.

general reform against women's own equal rights (the split in the women's movement)Weimanntypology

Weimann's split within the women's movement: some women wanted to work for general reform, while others wanted to work primarily for their own equal rights. She uses this as the battle line between the Isabella Association and the Board's clubwomen and philanthropists, and between suffragists and philanthropists in the Board. (Weimann 1981p. 43)

“wanted women to work primarily for their own equal rights” p. 43

Used for The Board's divisions in 1890 and 1891, including the Isabellas against the clubwomen and philanthropists, and the Couzins quarrel.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): Test whether another women's committee split along the general-reform and equal-rights line, or along class or regional lines, and which split best explains its votes and resignations.

equal footing against separate treatment (race and the Woman's Building)Weimannanalytic concept

Whether black women's work should be shown on the same footing as white women's or in a separate exhibit. Weimann notes that most of the Board's women favoured the same footing and a smaller group separate treatment, and she shows that equal treatment without a separate exhibit left the black groups out. (Weimann 1981p. 111)

“was a white city in more ways than one” p. 123

Used for The black women's resolution of November 1890 and the Board's handling of the rival black organisations, including Mrs Cantrill's committee.

Chicago 1893

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): Check whether an 'equal treatment' rule for exhibitors left minority groups without their own space, and whether those groups had asked for separate space themselves.

Each text's framing, opponents, methods and gaps

Open a text for its overall stance, the positions it argues against, the sources and ways of working it relies on, and the gaps it names.

Allwood, John, Ted Allan and Patrick Reid. The Great Exhibitions: 150 Years. London: Exhibition Consultants, 2001.6 concepts

The book treats international exhibitions as a 'medium' whose motive has always been display and public relations: nations show off for trade and then for prestige, and the medium has declined as television and the internet took over its role. It is a narrative chronicle of 150 years of expositions (Allwood's original chapters, with Allan and Reid's new chapters 13 to 16 on the years after 1974), with an institutional and policy argument about the BIE, so its kind of history is diplomatic and administrative, with economic and cultural history in the background.

Argues against

  • critics who say Expo 2000 failed because of its city or its site (Berlin, or a site too large and antiseptic): The text says there are surely more fundamental reasons for the decline of the traditional world exposition, which had been overtaken by other media. p. 193
  • faith that the BIE can regulate the medium through the 1928 Convention: The authors say the BIE has shown itself incapable of the rigorous administration of the existing Convention, and that the medium has lost direction. p. 201
  • hosting a world exposition mainly to win urban and regional development funding: When that was the sole motivation, with scant resources of the organisers' own, the result was an indifferent exposition with few and often disgruntled exhibitors. p. 199

Sources and ways of working

  • Visitor and attendance figures, which the text says are recorded by turnstile clicks and reported as visitors though they count visits; the authors urge checking them against how they were counted. p. 198
  • Press and media coverage as a measure of public response to an event, read from German and foreign reporting of Expo 2000. p. 199
  • Economic impact studies, such as the study of Expo 98 printed in the BIE Bulletin, which the authors cite as useful for students of the medium. p. 183
  • Official post-event reports and their catalogues, some of which run to many volumes, held in host-city libraries and in the BIE and Bibliotheque Nationale. p. 215

Gaps it names

  • The economic benefit to participants of exhibiting at a world exposition: the text says there has never been a comprehensive study on it. p. 195
  • The smaller, specialized-type expositions: the text says there is no consensus of any sort on them. p. 201
  • Analytical research on the medium as a whole, which the bibliographic note says is more difficult to find than books on individual events. p. 215
  • What role the medium should play in international affairs in the future, which the authors call for an international conference to decide. p. 201

Contents and chapter overviews

Badger, Reid. The Great American Fair: The World’s Columbian Exposition and American Culture. Chicago: Nelson-Hall, 1979.8 concepts

Badger frames the world's fairs as an expression of the Victorian faith that industrialism, nationalism, urbanisation and science would bring improvement without disorder, and he takes the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 as a test case for how far a single fair represents its culture. His overall argument is that the fair reflected the conflicts and insecurities of the 1890s more than it shaped them, and that its impression of unity and order was a reassurance Americans wanted. It is a cultural history with substantial social, economic, urban and architectural history (finance, the city, the site and design, the Midway), and it draws on the press, visitors' accounts and attendance figures.

Argues against

  • Those who treat the great fairs of the earlier period as costly curiosities of no serious cultural significance: The fairs of the earlier period are prime sources for understanding an age in which they were taken seriously; dismissing them has hindered an accurate assessment.
  • Sullivan's followers and admirers, who read his symbolic account of Burnham and the fair as literal description: Badger finds no evidence that Burnham conspired against Sullivan, and argues that the stylistic retreat in architecture would have happened whether or not the fair had occurred. p. 118
  • Readings that take the fair as dramatic evidence for one view of American culture alone: The fair had to show the actual diversity of American culture, so any one theme is a selective reading and each side of the contrast can be supported from the same evidence. p. 122

Sources and ways of working

  • Newspaper reports, such as the Daily Inter Ocean, for the opening-day narrative of the crowd, the speeches and the ceremony
  • Accounts of foreign visitors, treated as the best vantage point on American cultural contrasts, drawing on Muirhead and the London Quarterly Review p. 119
  • Attendance figures and paid-admission counts, used to chart the Midway's popularity and the fair's rise p. 109
  • Architecture and sculpture read as statements about the culture, for example Sullivan's gilded gateway to the Transportation Building read as a symbol of the Gilded Age p. 117

Gaps it names

  • Whether the ethnic exhibits along the Midway actually encouraged viewers to see non-white peoples as barbaric; Badger raises the question and leaves it open p. 106

Contents and chapter overviews

Bell, Leonard. Colonial Constructs: European Images of Maori, 1840–1914. Auckland: Auckland University Press, 1992.8 concepts

Bell reads European visual representations of Maori, 1840-1914, as constructs made for European viewers, patrons and buyers, and as ideological objects rather than neutral records of Maori. The book is a cultural and art history of particular images and of how they were exhibited, sold and used to build a settler national identity; it says the images 'could be said to have participated in the making of history' (line 834-835) and claims they cast Maori as a dualism of savagery and romance that helped naturalise European possession.

Argues against

  • viewers, and some historians, who take representations of Maori as faithful records of the visible: 'Pure' visual documentation is impossible. Observational neutrality is a fiction. p. 2
  • James Cowan and Partridge, who presented Lindauer's paintings as objective and ethnologically accurate records: strict ethnological accuracy is not a primary feature of his paintings. p. 200
  • a view that Strutt's painting amounted to a positive celebration of Maoridom: Rather, Strutt constructed Maori in terms of conventional image types and idealising pictorial formulae in the interests of the 'good' picture. p. 87
  • ethnological interest in primitive peoples, presented as disinterested: was not a disinterested, ideologically neutral discipline. Rather, it can be seen as one aspect of European territorial and economic expansion p. 22

Sources and ways of working

  • contemporary newspaper and periodical articles, exhibition reviews, letters, private journals, catalogues and publicity tracts, read as evidence of attitudes and of how the images operated p. 4
  • photographs (Carnell, Hamilton, Mayall) compared with paintings to trace which photographic models a composition used p. 200
  • field sketches read by the conventions of the sketch, not judged as finished art p. 113
  • comparison of a painting with its European models and image types (for example the French Orientalist repertoire) p. 86

Gaps it names

  • Maori uses of and responses to the European images, which Bell leaves to another writer p. 256
  • material left unaccounted for in the narrative p. 8
  • social and political history, which the book does not attempt p. 2

Contents and chapter overviews

Benedict, Burton. The Anthropology of World’s Fairs: San Francisco’s Panama Pacific International Exposition of 1915. London and Berkeley: Scolar Press, 1983.9 concepts

Benedict treats world's fairs as modern secular rituals of competition, comparable to the potlatch, in which nations, companies and cities display goods, towers and allegorical symbols to win prestige and power. The essays on the 1915 Panama Pacific fair (Dobkin on politics and finance, Brechin on architecture, Armstrong on public art, Starr on allegory and its reception) are cultural, political and architectural histories of one exposition, read through the anthropological frame Benedict sets out. The book's overall claim is that 1915 was the last collective outburst of nineteenth-century optimism and that 1939 turned fairs into trade shows.

Argues against

  • the view that ritual is a stabilising force that keeps society in equilibrium, as in the Durkheimian tradition: rituals can also be forces fomenting change; there are rituals of rebellion as well as rituals of stabilization
  • the view that fairs' educational and artistic displays are their chief purpose: ultimately, the aim of the exhibitors was trade
  • Tocqueville's account of Americans as literal-minded and hostile to allegory: the 1915 allegory can be explained by taking less literally Tocqueville's account of American literalism p. 135

Sources and ways of working

  • oral histories taken from people who remembered the fair, gathered early in the research
  • diaries: six volumes kept by a boy of eleven who visited the fair, and unpublished diaries and letters read for fresher impressions than books
  • souvenirs, postcards, picture books and tape-recorded music lent by visitors and collectors
  • reading newspapers and magazines alongside guidebooks for the impressions of visitors and critics p. 151

Gaps it names

  • the images the audience is allowed or encouraged to form about exhibited people and the attitudes these produce among those exhibited, which Benedict says is beyond the scope of his study p. 43

Contents and chapter overviews

Bennett, Tony. Pasts Beyond Memory: Evolution, Museums, Colonialism. London: Routledge, 2004.9 concepts

Bennett frames late-nineteenth-century evolutionary museums of natural history, ethnology and geology (chiefly Britain, with Australia and the United States as contrasting contexts) as 'memory machines' that governed the self by making 'pasts beyond memory' operative in the present, within a Foucauldian framework of governmentality. It is a cultural and political history of liberal government and museums, and it also follows the same sciences into colonial administration, where indigenous people were denied historical depth and managed as if they were museum specimens.

Argues against

  • Anne McClintock's account of 'panoptical time' and 'anachronistic space', which treats museum time as solely ideological: Bennett says McClintock is right about the significance of time, but that the historical sciences also posed new ways of managing the self, so the question must be pursued as a temporal conscience within the person. p. 26
  • Donna Haraway's reading of the American Museum of Natural History as a private, ruling-class peephole: Although privately owned, the museum's links to city and state government, the Central Park commissioners and popular schooling made it a hybrid institution, so it cannot be read solely as an expression of a ruling-class ethos. p. 117
  • the view that modernity is marked by a radical break with the past (Latour's 'temporal conscience' of the moderns): Late-nineteenth-century theorists were preoccupied with how habit and inheritance carried the pasts beyond memory into the present, so the relation to the past was one of continuity. p. 26

Sources and ways of working

  • close reading of the arrangement of museum objects in typological series and of their exchange between institutions, with attention to how display and label worked together p. 66
  • photographs and reports read critically for what they show and what they leave out (Baldwin Spencer's Northern Territory photographs) p. 158
  • comparison across three national contexts (Britain, Australia, United States) as 'contrapuntal perspectives' p. 2
  • reading colonial administrative knowledge (Dirks's account of the 1901 Indian ethnographic survey) as a practice of government p. 71

Gaps it names

  • a broader picture of museum developments beyond Britain, Australia and the United States, which the author says still needs to be examined p. 2
  • the Postscript does not engage adequately with the relations between museums and government, and maps only directions for future work p. 11

Contents and chapter overviews

Boone, M. Elizabeth. “The Spanish Element in Our Nationality”: Spain and America at the World’s Fairs and Centennial Celebrations, 1876–1915. University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2019.8 concepts

Boone reads nine celebrations of 1876 to 1915 (five world's fairs or centennials in the US, Europe and Latin America, and the California fairs) through the Spanish displays at them, asking what was shown, refused or misread and how this helped invent a singular US national identity that left Spain out. Fairs are treated as exercises in using the past to imagine a present and future nation, and the overall argument is that recognising the 'Spanish element in our nationality' in all its complexity is needed for a more equitable present. It is a cultural and visual history of exhibitions, combining art history (paintings, ephemeral architecture, posters, photographs) with transnational, memory and national-identity studies.

Argues against

  • an English-only national history, which the text says challenges the integration of Spanish America into the history of the United States: Boone argues the 1876 centennial's selection of a single historical narrative 'left no room for Spain', and that Spanish-speaking America belongs in US history p. 10
  • the Black Legend, 'historical propaganda' that defined the Spanish as brutal conquistadors in search of wealth: The text says it has made recognition of Spanish contributions to the United States difficult, and that English-speaking Americans later transferred these anti-Spanish attitudes to Spanish-speaking Americans p. 11
  • the Colonial Revival's national history, in which English-speaking Protestants on the northeastern seaboard were the ancestral founders: Boone shows Spain's relevance kept south of the border, with England, the 'Madre Patria', always first, so that other European nations were allowed to speak and others, Spain among them, were asked to be silent p. 41
  • the claim, quoted from Tenorio Trillo, that historians of America have failed to move beyond the nineteenth-century model of the nation-state: Boone takes up his question of whether North American history could become the symbol of a new relationship between Mexico, Central America, Canada and the United States p. 5

Sources and ways of working

  • official catalogues and final reports published by government agencies, visitors' memoirs and daily news accounts in the local press, used as primary sources for each celebration p. 6
  • close examination of individual works (paintings, architectural spaces, posters, postcards and photographs), using formal, iconographic and comparative analysis p. 7
  • reading the displays alongside political cartoons, civic sculpture and popular parades produced in each exhibition year p. 8
  • treating photographs, illustrations and written descriptions as a further level of representation, since many people experienced the fairs only through reproductions p. 7

Gaps it names

  • Spain's nineteenth-century artistic production is largely unknown to English-speaking scholars, unlike its seventeenth-century golden age p. 3
  • the role of Spanish women in the period, for which the text says readers will find few sources, all of them in Spanish p. 4
  • the recovery and wider dissemination of nineteenth-century Spanish art, design and visual culture, and its relationship to the United States, which the text calls a work in progress p. 4
  • the schism between Spain and immigrant cultures from postindependence Latin America, which the text says continues to impede development of this history p. 11

Contents and chapter overviews

Brown, Kendall H. “Fair Japan: Japanese Gardens at American World’s Fairs, 1876–1940.” Journal article.9 concepts

Brown reads the Japanese gardens built at American world's fairs from 1876 to 1940 as official, performed images of a timeless, pre-modern Japan, and argues that these gardens were political tools that presented an imperial nation as the natural expression of an unchanging culture while Japan was industrialising, expanding and fighting wars. The overall argument is that the fair gardens were propaganda that outlasted the fairs as a popular image of Japan. It is a cultural and political history of exhibition, built on garden design, architecture, the popular press, photographs and official publications, with a landscape-studies orientation.

Argues against

  • the critiques of world's fairs as an apparatus of representation and of Orientalism: these critiques apply differently to Japan, because the Japanese were never colonial subjects; on the contrary, they were successful colonizers
  • the view that the Japanese garden is an aesthetic import devoid of political implications: that view is, paradoxically, a measure of the garden's continuing success as a form of propaganda
  • dividing fair gardens into official and unofficial representations: the commercial gardens helped to underscore the dominant rhetoric of the Japanese national pavilion
  • the conclusion that the propagandistic use of fair gardens had no positive political effects in the long term: the real question is whether such propagandistic efforts altered history in less obvious ways

Sources and ways of working

  • newspapers published during the run of the fairs, read beside the pictures and descriptions of the Japanese pavilions and gardens
  • official posters and exposition pamphlets, read for their slogans
  • photos and postcards of the gardens, read for the women figures who usually appear in them
  • the formal features of the gardens read together with the writings for and about them

Gaps it names

  • whether the propaganda altered history in less obvious ways, for example by delaying American actions to counter Japanese aggression
  • the degree to which Theodore Roosevelt's support for Japan in the Russo-Japanese War was influenced by the Japanese displays at the 1904 fair

Contents and chapter overviews

Burris, John P. Exhibiting Religion: Colonialism and Spectacle at International Expositions, 1851–1893. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 2001.8 concepts

Burris treats international expositions, from London 1851 to Chicago 1893, as the place where a field of religion took shape in Britain and the United States: the fairs ranked cultures by industrial capacity, displayed peoples as evidence of social evolution, and made religion a comparative category built on colonial hierarchies, which the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions then reproduced in its exclusions. The argument is deliberately not a single thesis. It is a cultural history of religion and anthropology that reads commerce, popular culture, display and the press together, and it resists a purely intellectual or elite-context account.

Argues against

  • a reading of the Great Exhibition as a plan by the Royal Commission to advance British colonialism and sell an unjust class structure at home: Burris says he does not explore that plan; hegemonic inclinations existed to some extent but must be placed within their own historical context p. 24
  • Richard Seager's suggestion of a Foucauldian archaeological analysis of the Congress Auxiliary papers: a casual aside that is untenable, because many congresses did not publish their proceedings and the surviving papers are too general and redundant p. 190
  • scholarship on the 'primitive' written off as 'nostalgic': the dismissal is not quite that simple, since primitiveness was defined by a lack of industry, which may have been a choice p. 177

Sources and ways of working

  • press coverage of the Great Exhibition, read for how it ranked nations and their cultures p. 32
  • the official catalogue and the reports of the international awards juries p. 59
  • anthropological analogy: expositions compared with potlatch ceremonies, after Benedict's reading of Mauss p. 14
  • published proceedings of exposition congresses, which the author notes are incomplete and general p. 190

Gaps it names

  • an extended study of the material context that shaped the formation of the field of religion, which the author says does not exist
  • the early history of a field of religion in Germany or France, which the author sets aside as a formidable undertaking
  • whether the 'primitive' has been adequately brought into consciousness in the field of religion today, which the author calls an open question p. 177

Contents and chapter overviews

Coté, Joost. “Staging Modernity: The Semarang International Colonial Exhibition, 1914.” Journal article.8 concepts

Coté reads the Semarang International Colonial Exhibition of 1914 as a settler-led, pedagogical showcase of ‘colonial modernity’, in which a reformist faith in progress and tighter surveillance of racial boundaries were staged for both European and Javanese audiences. His overall argument is that, because the colonised were also participants and not only objects, the exhibition produced ambiguities that could feed nationalism, so that 1914 marks ‘the beginning of the end of the future that was being celebrated’. It is a cultural and political history of colonial urban reform, read through architecture, displays, public health and attendance, rather than an economic or purely architectural history.

Argues against
