  • Explanations of low native attendance as native superstition, or as the ordinary native being too traditional for modern surroundings: Coté calls these colonial stereotypes that fitted easily with European suspicion of nationalism; the likeliest cause, he argues, was growing anti-colonial opposition. p. 31
  • Foucault’s account of state power, which does not extend to Europe’s imperial periphery (as Stoler argues): Colonial practices and discourses of governance originated in the colonies and significantly shaped the metropolis. p. 7
  • Maclaine Pont’s utopian reading of the native section as an encounter between separate but connected communities: The section was redolent with orientalist nostalgia for ‘the historical greatness of now declining cultures’, and the total vision was never implemented. p. 17

Sources and ways of working

  • Reading the layout, labelling and thematic arrangement of the exhibition as a pedagogical text, like a school textbook, drawing on the 600-page official account. p. 17
  • Setting the planning intentions and designers’ retrospective accounts against the built exhibits, the layout and the visitors, looking for the gaps between them. p. 11
  • Using contemporary press and guides as evidence of how the exhibition was read, for example the journalist Later’s guide to ‘read’ the exhibition and the De Locomotief reports. p. 21
  • Using attendance figures by group (Javanese and European visitors) to test who the exhibition actually reached. p. 30

Gaps it names

  • The share of native visitors who were the better off and educated, and how many came from Semarang as against other north-coast cities; the author says this remains unclear. p. 33
  • How the native spectator would have regarded the display of ‘native tradition’ and its evolutionary message, which the author raises as the more important question in hindsight. p. 26

Contents and chapter overviews

Della Coletta, Cristina. World’s Fairs Italian-Style: The Great Expositions in Turin and Their Narratives, 1860–1915. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2006.9 concepts

Della Coletta treats world's fairs and national expositions as a 'signifying practice' whose displays combine realist and spectacular codes to produce a binary, hierarchical picture of nations and empires, which the text calls 'formidable consensus-creating machines'. Her argument is that Italian expositions, 1860 to 1915, were tools of nation building (above all Turin's) and that their master narratives also carried counter-discourses and contradictions. This is cultural history with a strong literary-critical and postcolonial method: urban and exhibition history of Turin, read through close reading of Salgari's and Gozzano's texts.

Argues against

  • critics who separate popular adventure fiction from serious literature by a binary of high and low, elite and popular: popular and non-popular forms differ 'more a matter of shade and degree', and popular novels such as Salgari's can carry tension and innovation p. 125
  • the common critical view that formula narratives are intellectually unchallenging and flatly subservient to mainstream ideology: the author reads Salgari's novels as highlighting the cultural dissonances and ideological conflicts of their society p. 12
  • Borgese's edition of Gozzano's Verso la cuna del mondo, which unified the Indian letters into one narrative: the letters should be seen in the 'magmatic context of contemporary popular culture', as a montage of non-successive sketches rather than a unitary picture p. 13

Sources and ways of working

  • official exposition guides and catalogues, including the 'Visione generale' and bird's-eye view sections that gave the visitor the master narrative p. 37
  • reading the texts in their original publication sites (newspapers and periodicals such as La Stampa, La Donna, La Lettura) and not only in the later book edition p. 180
  • close reading of exposition pieces and fiction (De Amicis, Salgari, Gozzano) for their representational codes, including ekphrasis p. 241
  • tracing the sources and intertexts of a novel or travel text (Dumas's Memoirs of Garibaldi behind Sandokan) p. 13

Gaps it names

  • the letters on Indian topics that Borgese left out of his edition, which the author says the edition forces readers to overlook p. 179
  • Abruzzese's notion of the metropolitan landscape is left abstract and interchangeable; the author says he does not carry his analysis further p. 83
  • an equally important, if contradictory, facet of Salgari that Magris neglects p. 139

Contents and chapter overviews

Denton, Kirk A. Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2014.9 concepts

Denton frames museums and memorial sites in the PRC as politically directed spaces where the party/state tells the modern past as a story of national humiliation, revolution and revival. Their overall argument is that official memory has not stayed fixed but has adapted to market reform, nationalism and the decline of socialism, while still serving state legitimacy. The book is a political and cultural history of exhibitions, read narratologically through exhibit design, architecture and the museums' own publications, with some fieldwork.

Argues against

  • scholarship that treats people as active agents and pushes state discourse aside, a reaction against the Foucauldian discursive determinism that once dominated cultural studies: Denton wants to reintroduce the state into the state/people equation, since state narratives and official memory are not monolithic and still have power to persuade p. 3
  • a view that dismisses the state's presence in public memory as nothing but propaganda: that view fails to understand the complexity of the state/people relationship, since state historical narratives have changed in response to the market economy p. 4
  • much museum theory, which emphasizes the power of the institution to impose ideology and compel the spectator to identify with a civic and national character: other scholarship is less deterministic; vernacular memories and the varied experiences of visitors also count p. 13
  • a view of PRC museums as a monolithic state propaganda: PRC museums and their exhibits are the product of negotiations among curators, historians, cadres and officials, and so not simply a transparent vehicle p. 14

Sources and ways of working

  • close narratological reading of exhibits as stories told through a visual language p. 14
  • reading a museum's architecture, location and spatial setting as part of its meaning, e.g. a museum on Tiananmen Square p. 15
  • reading a museum's own journal, e.g. a special issue published alongside an exhibit to show how officials framed it p. 2
  • fieldwork at exhibitions and events, e.g. walking through the 2006 Human Rights exhibit on media day p. 6

Gaps it names

  • modern history museums have received little attention in the scholarship, which has focused more on fine arts museums such as the Palace Museum p. 10
  • how negotiation among historians, curators, cadres and officials shapes PRC exhibitions is not made public, so it is hard to study p. 14
  • alternative memories (independent films, unofficial memorial sites, online blogs) are present but small and hidden, and have yet to enter the mainstream the way they have in Taiwan p. 4

Contents and chapter overviews

Filipová, Marta, ed. Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840–1940: Great Exhibitions in the Margins. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015.9 concepts

Filipová's introduction treats exhibitions as a global medium whose smaller regional, provincial and colonial-margin cases (Budapest, Barcelona, Wolverhampton, Dunedin, Launceston, Nancy, Helsinki, Naples, Osaka, Rio de Janeiro) adapted it to local agendas such as regional identity, municipal promotion and nation-building rather than copying London or Paris. Its overall argument is that these marginal exhibitions show universal values combined with regional and national agendas, linking local 'regional modernities' to a global one. It is a cultural and political history of exhibitions, concerned with identity, art, urban space and the exhibition network, and it is an edited volume, so the framing varies by chapter.

Argues against

  • The view that the exhibitionary complex, developed for colonial and imperial exhibitions and the world fairs of developed nation-states, carries over unchanged to regional exhibitions.: Minority or regional groups often challenged state imperatives and turned exhibitions into sites of resistance and of claims to their own identities. p. 8
  • The model in which regional exhibitions are copies of London or Paris.: Small, regional events in many cases did not simply copy the larger exhibitions but rather modified and adapted practices to suit local agendas. p. 15
  • The 'century of progress' frame that starts at 1851 and closes at the New York World Fair of 1939.: The studies also look before 1851 and beyond 1939, to the prehistory of the great exhibitions and to events during the Second World War. p. 5

Sources and ways of working

  • Microhistories of one or a series of exhibitions, related to the macrohistory of local and global circumstances. p. 5
  • Reading the terms used in exhibition titles (regional, national, international, universal, commemorative) as evidence of political ambitions. p. 7
  • Analysing the typology of pavilions in the national section of the exhibition, as Rezende does for Rio 1922. p. 171
  • Tracing practices and persons (the people who organised and the models they used) as intertwined dimensions of transnational exchange. p. 296

Gaps it names

  • The volume does not offer an exhaustive list of 'marginal' exhibitions in the period, and it aims to initiate further research on aspects left aside. p. 15
  • Colonial exhibitions in remote locations (Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India, Brazil) have only recently attracted attention as sites of the adoption of the exhibition medium. p. 14

Contents and chapter overviews

Findling, John E., and Kimberly D. Pelle, eds. Encyclopedia of World’s Fairs and Expositions. Jefferson, NC: McFarland, 2008.2 concepts

This is a reference encyclopedia with no single thesis. The editors (Findling and Pelle) say the volume gives basic information and annotated bibliographies, with essays by named specialists on each fair, chronologically from London 1851 (lines 729-734; general bibliography, line 22723). Their preface traces the lineage from medieval fairs, English prize shows and French national exhibitions to the Crystal Palace of 1851 (lines 529-661) and says American fairs grew from European experience but gave more weight to civic pride and entertainment (lines 642-661, citing Reid Badger at line 654). The BIE foreword frames expos as platforms for innovation, public education and sustainable development (lines 349-526), so the volume reads as a mixed institutional, cultural and industrial history.

Argues against

  • Opponents of industrial development, capitalism and modernization (London 1851 essay, John R. Davis): The essay says they highlighted the exhibition's failure to represent the disadvantages and social costs of modernity and its inherent imperialist messages. It sets against this the view that economic historians since the 1960s have treated exhibitions as important routes for technology transfer. p. 13
  • The view that the Paris 1855 exposition was merely derivative of the Crystal Palace and two smaller fairs (Paris 1855 essay, Barrie M. Ratcliffe): The author says 'This is not the case'. The exposition was innovative in ways later emulated, and before 1851 France rather than Britain had the well-established tradition of national industrial exhibitions. p. 22
  • Observers who see modern fairs devoting too much of their resources to amusements (preface, the editors): The editors report this as a concern held by some observers, not as their own view. They note that amusement zones had become a staple at all international exhibitions by the first decade of the twentieth century. p. 7

Sources and ways of working

  • Annotated bibliographies for each fair, indicating where possible the location of relevant primary sources and the quality of secondary sources; the editors required these of authors. p. 8
  • Official catalogues and the unofficial guides that followed them, which the London 1851 essay treats as sources of varying authority. p. 13
  • Archival collections: Smithsonian records in Record Groups 70 and 192, National Archives records in Record Groups 46 and 223, and the Donald G. Larson Collection at California State University, Fresno. p. 436
  • Bibliographic survey: the general bibliography starts from Rydell's Books of the Fairs (1990) for primary and secondary material on world's fairs. p. 435

Gaps it names

  • The Paris 1855 essay's bibliography says very little work has been done on the 1855 exhibition and its significance, despite attention to the London 1851 exhibition. p. 26
  • The Dublin 1853 entry says there is only one secondary source on the exhibition (Alun C. Davies). p. 17
  • The Hanoi entry says sources from the Hanoi fair are limited (author of that entry not checked). p. 171

Contents and chapter overviews

Findling, John E., and Kimberly D. Pelle, eds. Historical Dictionary of World’s Fairs and Expositions, 1851–1988. New York: Greenwood Press, 1990.8 concepts

Findling and Pelle compile a reference dictionary rather than argue a single thesis. Their introduction traces fairs from medieval trade fairs, the Royal Society of Arts show of 1761, French national exhibitions and English mechanics institute shows to the 1851 Crystal Palace, whose aim 'to forward the progress of industrial civilization' the later fairs have not strayed far from (lines 600-601). It then argues that fairs moved from one large hall to thematic and national pavilions and added fine art and amusements, so that they came to show comparative national life-styles, with nationalism and civic pride as the main threads (lines 606-645). Inclusion: fairs were left out when they lacked sufficient international scope or had an overly specialised theme (lines 357-358), and the history is institutional, cultural and diplomatic narrative, organised chronologically with one signed essay per fair.

Argues against

  • Secondary sources that overlook the 1862 London exhibition or dismiss it as a failed Crystal Palace: Prasch says the exhibition is largely overlooked, and that the one work claiming it was more central than 1851 (Kroker) rests mainly on German national and economic development. p. 30
  • Studies of nineteenth-century exhibitions in general and of Paris expositions in particular: Ratcliffe says these have generally been written without consulting archives or attempting to use exhibitions as windows to study technology, culture, or values. p. 21

Sources and ways of working

  • Annotated bibliographies for each fair, giving the location of primary sources and the quality of secondary sources
  • Currency equivalents (French francs, U.S. dollars, Canadian dollars, Belgian francs per pound) to compare figures across years p. 2
  • Official reports and correspondence in federal archives (Congressional reports from U.S. commissioners, Smithsonian records, USIA collection) p. 412
  • Press supplements, e.g. the Argus 'Exhibition Supplement' for Melbourne 1880 p. 75

Gaps it names

  • Dublin 1853: modern scholarship is scant (Davies, Allwood only) p. 11
  • Paris 1855: the fine arts sections are the only facet examined seriously by scholars p. 21
  • London 1862: secondary sources have largely overlooked the exhibition p. 30
  • Fair statistics: substantial discrepancies abound in the literature on attendance, dates and accounts p. 375

Contents and chapter overviews

Finnegan, Diarmid A., and Jonathan Jeffrey Wright, eds. Spaces of Global Knowledge: Exhibition, Encounter and Exchange in an Age of Empire. Farnham: Ashgate, 2015.12 concepts

An edited volume on 'global knowledge' in the long nineteenth century, framing knowledge-making as shaped by imperial expansion and exchange. Exhibitions are one site among many: the editors name 'exhibitionary practices' (line 845) and the 'display language of world fairs' (line 1115), and the exhibition cases are Kew's indigo model (London 1886) and Haiti's display (New York 1853). The history is cultural and historical-geographical, built from empirically grounded case studies (archival, biographical and institutional) with a 'bottom up' method, and it treats global claims as things to test rather than assume.

Argues against

  • global histories that flatten the varied political and cultural topography of knowledge-making, as Warwick Anderson argues: The editors say the danger remains that global history flattens this topography, and prefer local concerns where local circumstances matter. p. 8
  • reconstructions made under the sign of the global, which reproduce a unifying construct (Stein and Cooter): Global history cannot help but return to a form of universal history; the editors call instead for critical studies of globalist ambitions. p. 8
  • transnational and global framings that elide the nation: Withers asks whether working with the local or the global has elided 'the national', and notes that transnational terms may instead produce the nation as the frame of reference. p. 252

Sources and ways of working

  • empirically grounded case studies that marry detailed archival research with broader thematic and conceptual reflection p. 11
  • small stories: following Hayden Lorimer, Nikolaou argues that small stories make better sense of big words, using the consuls' letters as the evidence p. 41
  • the geography of the book: linking the production, circulation and reception of texts, as Henderson recommends p. 231
  • reading categories of space and place as Rupke's 'assignments', shaped by the location of the historian p. 255

Gaps it names

  • a Francophone or German global knowledge in the nineteenth century, which Withers raises as unexplored, and whether having an empire was necessary for global knowledge p. 253
  • a 'global Livingstone', which Henderson calls a worthwhile question though one that could underplay local reception p. 243

Contents and chapter overviews

Ganz, Cheryl R. The 1933 Chicago World’s Fair: A Century of Progress. Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 2008.8 concepts

Ganz treats A Century of Progress (Chicago, 1933-34) as a privately financed, business-led fair whose organisers recast progress as a material, technological and consumer process, with science rather than people as its engine, and used that idea to generate Depression-era optimism. Her overall argument is that this official vision was contested by women, African Americans, ethnic communities and Midway entertainers, who pressed their own meanings of progress on the fair. It is a cultural and social history of an exposition, built on business, military and engineering history, and it reads gender, race, ethnicity and popular entertainment as parts of the fair's story.

Argues against

  • histories of women that record only the achievements of individual women, most of them white and educated: Beard argued that the fair received a fuller history of man without a comparable history of women, and that women should be recorded as a population group.
  • fair management's rhetoric of 'women's equality' used to justify integrating women's exhibits: Management provided no separate women's exhibit space, and integrated women's exhibits with those of men.
  • Charles Dawes's view that a woman's greatest contributions are made in the home: Ganz says his remarks show he had completely missed the woman-focused dynamic of the Chicago women's fairs.

Sources and ways of working

  • visitors' recollections of the fair, such as Donald Richie's childhood visit and John S. Van Gilder's memory of Sally Rand
  • court cases over the Midway, read through judges' remarks and rulings on whether the shows should close
  • comparison across earlier American fairs (1876, 1893, 1901, 1904, the Chicago woman's fairs of 1925-28) to set the 1933 fair's treatment of women in context
  • architecture, colour and lighting read as expressions of the fair's theme of progress

Gaps it names

  • a collective history of women as a population group, not only of individual women, in the history of the fair and of exhibitions
  • the fair itself is little recognised compared with government-sponsored Depression-era projects such as the Tennessee Valley Authority, because it was a privately run project

Contents and chapter overviews

Gelernter, David. 1939: The Lost World of the Fair. New York: Free Press, 1995.7 concepts

Gelernter reads the 1939 New York World's Fair as the 'credo in stucco and steel' of an American civic religion, a community of faith whose utopian promise of a better future was fulfilled after the war, so that the fair is now 'the shrine of a dead faith' and the future 'no longer exists' for us. It is cultural and moral history of a sociological cast, with intellectual and architectural history used as evidence, and it is written as a narrative tour of one fair day through diaries and recollections rather than as a sustained argument. The argument about why 1939 differed from the present is, by the author's own account, secondary to the tour.

Argues against

  • Robert Rydell's critical reading of the fairs in World of Fairs: Gelernter calls the book 'consistently tendentious' but says he learned a lot from it; in the epilogue he argues that the fuller story will not show that the charges of bigotry against the fair are false, because the fair mirrored an America that was complicated.
  • liberal and conservative accounts of the decline since the late 1960s: Gelernter says neither has explained why the degradation happened: liberals are at a loss, and conservatives who cite the Great Society and the counterculture have not answered the question. p. 368
  • critics who read the fair as overcommercialised: He accepts that the commercial tide ran strong at the fair, but holds that what really pains such critics is the character of American society itself, and aims to set the charge in context rather than argue it down. p. 364

Sources and ways of working

  • the period literature of the fair's own age, chiefly newspapers, magazines and guidebooks, which the preface says the book relies on mainly
  • diary extracts (Hortense Glassman's diary) used as the narrative's main voice, with the author's commentary between them p. 108
  • recollections and interviews with people who remember the fair, from which the characters' speech is reconstructed
  • close reading of the fair's own 1939 Guide as a text, treated as a document of the fair's self-presentation p. 169

Gaps it names

  • why the degradation of American life happened after the 1960s, which the author says no current explanation has answered p. 368
  • the causal link between the 'little oughts' of daily life and the social character of the late 1930s, which the author admits is unprovable p. 218
  • the other side of the 1930s story about Jewish prominence and anti-Semitism, which the author says we tend to know only one side of p. 291

Contents and chapter overviews

Geppert, Alexander C. T. Fleeting Cities: Imperial Expositions in Fin-de-Siècle Europe. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010.8 concepts

Geppert reads five imperial expositions (Berlin 1896, Paris 1900, London 1908, Wembley 1924, Vincennes 1931) as a 'meta-medium' with its own rules, grammar and transitory character, and as sites that wove into the urban fabric of Berlin, Paris and London. His argument is that the fairs formed overlapping transnational networks, so their similarities come from organisers' borrowing and mobility, and that the national 'identity' framing is too simple. It is a cultural and urban history of modernity that is also explicitly theoretical and historiographical, drawing on spatial theory and on Chartier's account of representation.

Argues against

  • Tony Bennett's 'exhibitionary complex', coined in 1988 with a Foucauldian perspective: The term was influential but misleading, since it assumed a consolidation that was not historically given but evolved over time; networks are the better description. p. 10
  • the national-identity reading of expositions, including the 'identity through non-identity' and metropole/colony opposition: 'identity' is a conceptually vague, highly charged and worn buzzword; the metropole/colony opposition is now insufficient, and the study treats identity as peripheral. p. 14
  • reading exhibitions as fleeting magnifying glasses on the society that produced them: Geppert proposes a prism: attention should first go to the medium's own rules and to reception, before a society's self-presentation. p. 12
  • single-exposition studies that ignore transnational entanglements: Such studies disregard the transnational and transatlantic entanglements and inter-urban competition, which shaped internal organisation. p. 12

Sources and ways of working

  • archival research combined with autobiographical accounts, personal correspondence, postcards, letters to the editor and oral history interviews, read for both reception and representation p. 12
  • comparison across cases: the five expositions are read as embodiments of a larger medium, not as isolated national displays p. 12
  • relational network analysis of personal, professional and institutional ties among organisers, critics and exhibitors p. 13
  • a biographical appendix (dramatis personae) of organisers, participants and critics, used to show transnational entanglements p. 240
  • a historiographical version of field reconnaissance (urban ethnography and town planning, after Kevin Lynch) to map each site p. 15

Gaps it names

  • Brussels, with its exhibitions of 1897, 1910 and 1935, is named as a dramatically under-researched exhibition hub p. 13
  • other European and American fairs (Barcelona 1888, Milan 1906, Turin, the American world's fairs) are left out of the sample and need study p. 14
  • the Berliner Gewerbeausstellung of 1896 is described as an under-researched counter-case p. 14

Contents and chapter overviews

Giberti, Bruno. Designing the Centennial: A History of the 1876 International Exhibition in Philadelphia. Lexington: University Press of Kentucky, 2002.9 concepts

Giberti frames the 1876 Centennial as an Enlightenment project of transparent classification (a dual system by country and by type, laid out as a grid in real space) that the organisers kept revising as conditions forced compromises, and that visitors experienced as distracted, commodity-oriented spectacle. The overall argument is that early world's fairs were perennially incomplete, and that their design problems (order, architecture, installation, display, evaluation) carried into Philadelphia's permanent institutions. It is a cultural and architectural history of visuality and material culture, using institutional, architectural and documentary evidence and drawing on cultural theory.

Argues against

  • Historians who read the new art institutions of the period as signs of cultural maturity: The text reads them as symptoms of a deep cultural anxiety about the value of things in the modern city.
  • The organisers' ideal of the exhibition as a clear series of precise object lessons: Many visitors perceived the exhibition not as a clear series of precise object lessons but as a blur of faintly received impressions.
  • The view that the audience was a passive surface on which the organisers could inscribe their intentions: The audience brought its own agenda, which included entertainment as well as education, pleasure, and instruction.

Sources and ways of working

  • The exhibition's literature (official reports, descriptive histories, illustrated surveys, and newspaper and magazine articles), read as the means by which its lessons were spread beyond the fairground
  • Visitors' accounts and critical and journalistic accounts, read for the impressions they record (Howells, Tozier)
  • Photographs read critically, since they privilege sight and show an emptied, constructed view
  • The official catalogue read for its ideological function as a screen of classification

Gaps it names

  • How audiences experienced the bazaar, museum and department store, which the text says is difficult to gauge from the sources
  • The non-visual experience of the exhibition (sound, smell, the din of the crowd), which the text says must be recovered to understand its full reality

Contents and chapter overviews

Gilbert, James. Perfect Cities: Chicago’s Utopias of 1893. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991.8 concepts

Gilbert reads the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and three other 'total urban environments' in Chicago (the guidebook city, the Pullman company town and Moody's evangelical campaign), as attempts by a Protestant middle class and elite to manage the city's cultural diversity and its commercial popular culture. His argument is that these attempts only partly worked: the audience had to reconcile the controlled White City with the commercial Midway, and popular culture kept escaping the planners' control. It is a cultural history of leisure and the imagination, not of work, combining biography, urban sociology, architectural and religious history, and the analysis of guidebooks, journalism and visitors' records.

Argues against

  • Readings of the Fair as a triumph of elite hegemony and racial control, notably Alan Trachtenberg's and Robert Rydell's use of hegemony theory: Gilbert accepts that the Fair exhibited racism, but asks 'whether the elite which planned it was trying to impose racism on an unwilling audience is another matter entirely', and says whether the planners even half succeeded 'requires much more careful examination'. p. 82
  • The cliche that middle-class Americans contributed to popular culture only through censorship boards and sneering disapproval: The middle classes of Chicago and elsewhere 'participated in and helped to create modern popular culture', on their own terms. p. 4
  • Histories of the Fair that assess only its architecture, the White City, and divide Chicago culture into reactionary and progressive camps: Such assessments leave out the Midway; the Fair has to be read as the White City and the Midway together. p. 80

Sources and ways of working

  • Guidebooks, itineraries and urban journalism read closely for their point of view and what they leave out (George Ade's detached sketches, Edwin Stine's inventories) p. 49
  • Official records of the Fair: the president's report, directors' minutes and committee structure p. 94
  • Census tables on occupations and city populations, with estimates flagged where census categories were combined p. 9
  • Family papers and private diaries, such as Hattie Pullman's diary, read for what they leave incomplete p. 161

Gaps it names

  • Whether the Fair's business elite succeeded in regulating the Midway and its audience: 'Whether they even half succeeded, however, is something that requires much more careful examination' p. 82
  • The workers' city: the book is 'not a book about work or workers' and does not venture into the city of the men and women who built the Fair's environment p. 2
  • The Midway as a neglected part of the Fair in earlier historiography, which Gilbert presents as only partly redressed by recent work p. 80

Contents and chapter overviews

Gosden, Chris, and Chantal Knowles. Collecting Colonialism: Material Culture and Colonial Change. Oxford: Berg, 2001.8 concepts

Gosden and Knowles treat colonial New Guinea as one social and cultural field in which Europeans and Melanesians influenced each other, so that museum collections are complete but particular outcomes of colonial relations rather than partial records of vanishing societies. Their argument is that objects were the medium of these relations and that their meanings changed continually between village, trade and museum, while forms often stayed stable. It is a historical anthropology of collecting and material culture: a cultural history of colonialism built from four collections, with economic, institutional and moral strands.

Argues against

  • acculturation: the local culture taken over and submerged by the incoming culture, or cultural loss: Such change has not brought convergence or acculturation but has created new forms of difference.
  • New Melanesian History (Thomas 1991), which stresses similarities created by shared histories of colonialism and exchange: Our view is different to any of these: the field of social relations has changed the parties without making them alike.
  • the gift and commodity split: New Guineans have gifts and Europeans commodities, a bipartite colonial culture: Things in New Guinea were tools to create a series of complex social experiments whose outcomes were unknown.
  • the salvage paradigm, which predicted that people would lose the will to live or embrace Western values: Instead, a much more remarkable thing happened. People drew on their local cultural resources to fashion a new way of life.

Sources and ways of working

  • archival work on patrol reports, government and mission records and published accounts, combined with reconstructing each collector's intellectual and institutional history
  • collectors' diaries and notebooks read for individual transactions (for example Blackwood's diary of the head-binding strip), with purchases recorded by item and price
  • systematic analysis of collections into a database to allow comparison across collectors and periods

Gaps it names

  • the field observations of the four collectors, which they published almost nothing of, so that a major record of thought is missing
  • what happened to the objects once they reached the USA, Europe or Australia, including their display and representation, which the authors say they focused on less
  • comparative studies of colonialism in Africa and worldwide, which the authors say collection research can help
  • the research potential held in museums for understanding colonial histories

Contents and chapter overviews

Greenhalgh, Paul. Ephemeral Vistas: The Expositions Universelles, Great Exhibitions and World’s Fairs, 1851–1939. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1988.9 concepts

Greenhalgh treats international exhibitions from 1851 to 1939 (mainly Britain, France and the United States) as a cultural product of industry and empire: spectacles that presented national identity, imperial economics and racial hierarchy, and that also drew on the arts, design and popular entertainment. Her overall argument is that the exhibitions embodied "neither good nor evil in any simple sense but were a complex mixture of both", and that their negative ideology still shapes the urban environment. It is a cultural and design history with strong imperial, social and gender strands, organised thematically rather than chronologically.

Argues against

  • the view that imperialism was the underlying motive behind every human display: it would be incorrect to assume imperialism was always an underlying motive behind human exhibits; two of the four types were not necessarily imperial or immoral p. 82
  • the 'anti-imperial' phase of British imperial history (the phasal model after Seeley): the major function of such a view, it has been suggested, was to humanise and underplay the real nature of British imperial ambition p. 57
  • art-historical accounts that give the fine arts a central place at exhibitions: fine art brought status, not pleasure, to the site; the fine art palace of 1855 had 906,530 visitors against 3,626,934 for the machine hall p. 198

Sources and ways of working

  • the press, for example the Pall Mall Gazette, read for how events were described and reviewed p. 66
  • attendance figures compared between halls or palaces on the same site p. 198
  • thematic rather than chronological or national organisation, comparing exhibiting policies across events p. 2
  • sorting human displays into types (imperial, educational, commercial, ambassadorial) and noting where they overlap p. 82

Gaps it names

  • the whole tradition of hundreds of exhibitions outside Britain, France and the USA, for example in Africa, Asia, Australasia and South America, which the text says it cannot examine p. 2
  • empirical completeness even for the three main nations: about thirty events are treated in detail and around forty more briefly p. 2
  • the 'banal urban environment' and the lasting ideology of exhibitions in later city design, which the Postscript suggests but does not trace p. 226

Contents and chapter overviews

Hale, Dana S. Races on Display: French Representations of Colonized Peoples, 1886–1940. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 2008.8 concepts

Hale reads the colonial expositions, the commercial trademarks and the official ethnographic notices of the Third Republic as representations in which “race” and kinship place France at the top of a hierarchy and cast colonized peoples as subordinate children. The argument is that the French self-image as an imperial and civilising power was built through these displays, and that the rhetoric moved from a parental to a fraternal register after the First World War without changing the hierarchy beneath it. It is a cultural and political history of empire and national identity, built on world's fair displays and trademark images, and it draws on comparative exposition studies, cultural anthropology and French colonial history (Introduction, lines 210-213).

Argues against

  • an account of the 1848 abolition of slavery as a sign of changed French public attitudes towards Africans and blacks: the abolition was the result of the initiative of a few inspired republicans rather than a reflection of a change in public attitudes towards Africans and blacks in the Caribbean p. 23
  • the official colonial rhetoric of fraternal brotherhood after the First World War: the real attitude in France toward colonial peoples was hierarchical p. 178

Sources and ways of working

  • the trademark registers of Paris and Marseilles, 1886 to 1940, read as a survey of the images merchants chose to identify their products p. 21
  • ethnographic descriptions and official notices prepared for the colonial exposition, read against the claims of colonial administrators to expertise p. 45
  • exposition sources compared with the popular press and its illustrations, following William H. Schneider’s study of the press p. 3

Gaps it names

  • how consumers interpreted the trademark images, which the author says cannot be fully assessed p. 162

Contents and chapter overviews

Harvey, Penelope. Hybrids of Modernity: Anthropology, the Nation State and the Universal Exhibition. London: Routledge, 1996.9 concepts

Harvey takes the universal exhibition as a modernist institution that makes the world appear as representation, after Timothy Mitchell's 'world as exhibition', and uses Expo'92 in Seville as a self-conscious case for asking what happens when institutions treat culture as representation. Her overall argument is that the nation state, the universal exhibition and social anthropology are linked 'hybrid' modernist institutions that objectify culture while deconstructing it, and that representational knowledge and knowledge as embodied practice cannot simply be added together. It is a cultural and social anthropology of a mass event, written reflexively by an author who was there as a journalist, drawing on cultural theory (Baudrillard, Lyotard, de Certeau) to interpret visitors' experience.

Argues against

  • anthropologists who see culture as practice and treat representational knowledge as misrepresenting how people live: The text says there can be no complementarity from this view, but Harvey argues that representational knowledge should be studied through its effects on embodied practice and holds that the construct metaphor implies a more basic reality that is itself a symbolic project. p. 171
  • Baudrillard's account of consumption, in which visitors are simply consumers: The ethnographic material shows visitors to the Expo were more than consumers: they enjoyed simulated sensation yet still attended to political realities. p. 27
  • Latour's claim that the West has never been modern: Harvey offers the alternative that we have never simply been modern even within the modernist frame, which keeps the modern and the postmodern together at the Expo. p. 180

Sources and ways of working

  • interviews with visitors, asking what they remembered, what they enjoyed and what they thought the event was about p. 141
  • journalistic presence on site, with press access, combined with participant observation at a fleeting event p. 11
  • the press and a post-exhibition display ('Memories of the Expo') as records of how visitors discussed and resignified exhibits p. 140
  • auto-anthropology: analysis of an institution close to home, examining the anthropologist's own practice in the same social game p. 24

Gaps it names

  • whether anthropologists should stop interpreting or simply add more perspectives once culture and context are seen as constructs p. 48
  • the attention to embodied specificity is lost when process becomes form and social facts are generated p. 173
  • what anthropology can learn from mass popular events such as Expo'92, where the ethnographic focus on difference is not available, is of a different order from daily practice in a place such as Mount Hagen p. 13

Contents and chapter overviews

Henry, Todd A. Assimilating Seoul: Japanese Rule and the Politics of Public Space in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2014.7 concepts

Henry treats the public spaces of colonial Keijo (Namsan's shrines, the expositions on the Kyŏngbok Palace grounds, arterial roads and neighborhood sanitation campaigns) as contact zones where Japanese assimilation projects were enacted and contested. Her argument is that colonial rule was sovereign, coercive and unevenly reached: it reshaped the city's arteries and spectacles but faltered at the capillaries of everyday life, and Koreans and settlers bent its meanings to their own ends. It is a cultural and urban history of colonial Seoul (1910–45) written with an ethnographic method, ending with the postcolonial remaking of the same sites.

Argues against

  • top-down studies of assimilation that rely on elite debates or state policy as the main criterion of rule: Henry starts from grounded histories of how individuals and groups operated in public places, then works upward to the forms of power in those spaces. p. 7
  • Korean-language scholarship that assumes the Government-General's omnipotence, framed as ilche: The text argues that the colonial state's authority has to be denaturalised and examined in its contested relations with state and nonstate actors. p. 6
  • nationalist history writing that treats the Korean case as an aberrant or warped version of a unitary Western modernity: The text treats the contradictions of colonial rule (excess and neglect) as structural and contested features of Japanese rule. p. 8
  • studies that understand assimilation narrowly as things distinctly Japanese, limited to the spiritual: The text widens assimilation to material and civic practices such as expositions and neighborhood hygiene. p. 4

Sources and ways of working

  • reading Japanese-language and Korean-language newspapers along and against the archival grain, including the official Keijo nippo and the vernacular press p. 13
  • police records, visitor accounts and newspapers on the 1915 and 1929 expositions, read for what crowds did as well as what designers intended p. 13
  • ethnographic history of the archive, which the author says cannot produce its own data as fieldwork does and is limited by the archive's forms and norms p. 13
  • the colonial archive read as both a record of power relations and a technology of rule, following Ann Stoler p. 13

Gaps it names

  • Korean voices, silenced by censorship in the 1910s and the early 1940s, which the author says leaves the subjugated knowledges of poor Koreans only partly recoverable p. 13
  • the subjugated knowledges of nonelite residents, which Henry says her sources cannot fully reach and which remain a limitation of the book p. 14
  • the postcolonial monuments on Namsan and the restored Kyŏngbok Palace, which she says silence the colonial past and invite a dialogue about it p. 216

Contents and chapter overviews

Hoffenberg, Peter H. An Empire on Display: English, Indian, and Australian Exhibitions from the Crystal Palace to the Great War. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001.9 concepts

Hoffenberg treats the popular exhibitions of England, Australia and India from 1851 to 1914 as social texts, authored by commissioners through guidebooks, classifications and the layout of space, and read and partly remade by visitors, so that national and imperial identities were produced through participation rather than imposed. The book is a cultural and political history of empire, with economic, social and architectural strands, and its commissioners-as-experts framing is set against Said- and Cohn-style accounts of a hegemonic imperial knowledge.

Argues against

  • Edward Said and Bernard S. Cohn, and their students, whose work on imperial knowledge is read as suggesting a hegemonic and unilateral model: Commissioners in Australia and India made the construction of imperial knowledge a more participatory, multilateral and mediated process, which could challenge British authority. p. 57
  • the Saidesque conclusion that totalizing knowledge resulted in total control: The representation and performance of science could bring colonial rule into question, and the development of art schools could provoke nationalist reactions. p. 58
  • students of popular culture and politics who perceive an imposition of a coherent elite ideology at the exhibitions: Nationalism and imperialism succeeded through a more subtle and participatory process of permeation and acceptance, not by imposition. p. 27

Sources and ways of working

  • Reader-response approach: exhibitions treated as texts whose meaning is produced by visitors as well as by organisers
  • Private and public papers of commissioners and exhibitors, contemporary periodicals and newspapers, and the memoirs, correspondence and diaries of visitors
  • Nineteenth-century photographic albums, read for the architectural space, physical dimensions and layout of the exhibitions
  • Comparison across colonial and imperial shows, approached in a comparative and interdisciplinary way

Gaps it names

  • The active nature of the exhibition experience: historians have generally ignored the point that visitors took an active part, while scholars highlight passive observation and enjoyment p. 247

Contents and chapter overviews

Hollengreen, Laura, Celia Pearce, Rebecca Rouse and Bobby Schweizer, eds. Meet Me at the Fair: A World’s Fair Reader. Pittsburgh: ETC Press, 2014.12 concepts

Hollengreen and Rouse, in the introduction, call the fair polyvalent: a shrine to new science and technology, a commercial marketplace and a site of nation-building, and they liken its hybrid mix of wonder, art and science to the early modern curiosity cabinet. Rydell's preface frames fairs as a capacity for make-believe that persuades others to occupy a reality. The volume is a multidisciplinary cultural history (anthropology, museums, theatre, film, architecture, urban planning) whose overall argument is that fairs were spectacles of progress and empire that visitors, critics and minorities read and contested in different ways.

Argues against

  • criticism that treats Hagenbeck as a convenient punching bag: the Tierpark was indeed influential, as was his earlier career of 'authentic' displays of life p. 45
  • the standard historical narrative, which treats 'lowbrow' entertainment as only reluctantly incorporated into 'highbrow' expositions: a broad range of performances was always part of exposition culture p. 336
  • the rigorous official discourse separating the entertaining and the educational at the fairs: in practice fairgoers flocked to the more theatrical exhibits p. 343

Sources and ways of working

  • advertisements, playbills, guidebooks and reviews of local theatres, read as a record of exposition-season entertainment (Davis) p. 336
  • fairgoers' diaries and letters, used to show that visitors saw the exposition on stage and the stage in the exposition (Davis) p. 336
  • caricatures, drawings and descriptions of fair visitors and their meals, read as evidence of popular response (Tran) p. 438

Gaps it names

  • the bulk of world's fair literature pays little attention to picnics and outdoor meals (Tran) p. 435
  • what little attention has been paid to Hagenbeck's influence on World's Fairs exhibits, which has tended to be apologetic (Santesso) p. 45

Contents and chapter overviews

Hopson, Nathan. “‘A Bad Peace?’: The 1937 Nagoya Pan-Pacific Peace Exhibition.” Journal article.6 concepts

Hopson reads the 1937 Nagoya Pan-Pacific Peace Exhibition as a city-branding mega-event whose peace theme survived Imperial Japanese Army concessions. He argues that even on the eve of all-out war, Nagoya's business and government elites still held a 1920s vision of peace through trade rather than autarky, and that this shows the continued political diversity of 1930s Japan. It is a regional and political history of urban promotion, with a comparison to Paris 1937.

Argues against

  • Tokyo-centred national histories of 1930s Japan that map 'the ascendancy of authoritarian rule' and the 'road to war' (Smith): Because they focus on Tokyo government, business and military elites, they are limited, or 'less reliable' for understanding other parts of Japan and non-elite Japanese. p. 139
  • the expo as a cynical misappropriation of the concept of 'capitalist peace': Looking past Nagoya's accommodations to the army shows that local business and government elites still clung to a 1920s-style vision of peace through trade rather than autarky. p. 137
  • seeing the mid-1930s as the cusp of the 'dark valley' and judging the peace vision from that end: The mid-1930s should be seen on their own terms as a moment of contestation between multiple programmes and visions for the future, not as a cynical or empty prelude. p. 148

Sources and ways of working

  • the three-volume official expo record (Nagoya Hantaiheiyō Heiwa Hakurankai, Hakurankai kaishi), the main source for the expo's data p. 140
  • a radio tour broadcast of the exhibition (April 1937), read closely for its narration of the army's vision of peace p. 144
  • the expo's bylaws, official publicity and a full-page advertisement in Japan Today and Tomorrow, read for what they promised p. 148
  • comparison across fairs: Nagoya 1937 with Paris 1937, on content, context and planning stages p. 147

Gaps it names

  • scholarship on the NPPPE is thin; Ha Bae-Song's study is described as one of the few scholarly examinations of it p. 148
  • the evidence on the navy's attitude to the expo is admittedly scant; the navy may have been more supportive than the army p. 137
  • how visitors actually experienced the expo is not settled by the record: the military hall and live-fire drills may have left a more lasting impression than peace p. 149

Contents and chapter overviews

Hotta-Lister, Ayako. The Japan-British Exhibition of 1910: Gateway to the Island Empire of the East. Richmond: Japan Library, 1999.7 concepts

Hotta-Lister treats the 1910 Japan-British Exhibition at the White City as a national undertaking of the Meiji government, run with the London entrepreneur Imre Kiralfy, and meant to educate British opinion about Japan and to serve political, diplomatic and economic aims. The author reads international exhibitions as a genre of imperial display in which Japan now took part as an equal. The history is diplomatic and cultural, with economic and racial strands, built from official reports, British and Japanese archives and newspapers in English and Japanese, and it weighs the Exhibition's effects as mixed and limited rather than a failure. No social theory is named in the body of the text.

Argues against

  • the view of Japanese opinion that the 1910 Exhibition was a failure, or was no more than a mere trade fair: The text argues that it was not 'a failure' and not 'a mere trade fair', and that its educational content and specific political and economic aims were central to it. p. 7

Sources and ways of working

  • British and Japanese official reports on the Exhibition, and British and Japanese government archives (Foreign Office papers, Kensei Shiryokan, Gaiko Shiryokan)
  • newspaper and journal articles in English and Japanese, read for public opinion, anecdotes and attitudes
  • letters, speeches and diplomatic correspondence of dignitaries, quoted at length as evidence of how the Exhibition was framed p. 2
  • the accounts of two Japanese visitors with contrasting views of the Exhibition p. 7
  • comparison of the 1910 Exhibition with Japan's earlier exhibitions, as set out in Appendix A p. 8
  • reading the Official Guide's own wording as evidence of racial framing p. 178

Gaps it names

  • Why Kiralfy was so interested in proposing Japan as a partner in a joint exhibition is left unexplained: 'It seems a mystery' p. 46
  • Assessing the success of the Exhibition is open to debate: evidence is strong for attendance, media coverage and sales of Japanese exhibits, but not for diplomatic gains p. 192

Contents and chapter overviews

Hur, Hyungju. “Staging Modern Statehood: World Exhibitions and the Rhetoric of Publishing in Late Qing China, 1851–1910.” Doctoral dissertation.7 concepts

Hur treats world exhibitions as a diplomatic arena in which the late Qing government tried to present China as a modern state, and argues that this aim was repeatedly contested by the Imperial Maritime Customs, by Japan and by reformist and revolutionary Chinese publications. The overall argument is that the same objective was received differently as the historical context changed, and that the Nanyang Industrial Exposition of 1910 briefly reconciled the government with its critics. It is a political and cultural history of late Qing diplomacy and transnational Chinese print, written as a dissertation and using the vocabulary of display and imperial rhetoric.

Argues against

  • The cultural hegemony school (cited to Rydell, Findling and Pelle), which reads world exhibitions through their organisers' objectives: Hur says this school and its counter-hegemony opposite both rest on a binary of hegemonic producers against 'uncivilized' colonial subjects, which does not fit China's ambiguous position; the existing theories should be replaced by audience-oriented approaches. p. 167
  • The counter-hegemony argument (cited to Rydell) that exploited display subjects could use exhibitions to their own advantage: China asserted no counter-hegemonic influence, because the Qing government and Chinese intellectuals largely accepted the premise that exhibitions rewarded demonstrated superiority, and Chinese rhetoric developed internally. p. 167
  • Habermas's public sphere treated as a universal model of civil society: Habermas's public sphere is a particular practice from Western Europe, not a universal one, so late Qing print publics should be studied on their own terms, as Lean and Judge do. p. 171

Sources and ways of working

  • Chinese-language newspapers and journals, domestic and overseas, read for how their reading publics received the exhibits and the Qing government's performance p. 6
  • Japanese newspapers and press interviews, such as the Asahi shimbun, because Chinese mass media lacked their own overseas news sources p. 71
  • Diaries and travelogues by foreign and Chinese officials, such as Robert Hart's diaries and early Chinese travelogues, read alongside the press p. 17
  • Archival documents from Chinese institutions, such as the Archive of Suzhou Chamber of Commerce, for the Nanyang exposition p. 126

Gaps it names

  • Transnationality of Chinese print media, which the author says scholars have not paid enough attention to p. 172
  • The public sphere configured beyond the national boundary, which the text calls a phenomenon requiring further research p. 172
  • China and Japan at the early world exhibitions, which the author says deserve more attention in Euro-centred studies p. 168
  • The Nanyang exposition in the context of sixty years of Chinese experience at world exhibitions, which no scholarly work had examined p. 125

Contents and chapter overviews

Kaiser, Wolfram. “The Great Derby Race: Strategies of Cultural Representation at Nineteenth-Century World Exhibitions.” Article.7 concepts

Kaiser treats the world exhibitions as a global public space that states, the main organisers and exhibitors, filled with cultural representations in order to win a favourable national image, form alliances and set agendas through culture transfer. He argues that governments were the most cohesive actors in this contest, while qualifying how far they controlled what visitors and social groups took from it. The piece is a political and diplomatic history of culture, using exhibitions as evidence for the international relations of France, the United States and Japan.

Argues against

  • the traditional imperialist interpretation of the human representations: does not take account of the cultural exchange at the world exhibitions, which was not one-sided p. 54
  • the assumption that states controlled the public spaces they created at the exhibitions: states were largely responsible for organising the exhibitions, but social groups occupied parts of the space and visitors read displays differently, so state control had two important limits p. 54

Sources and ways of working

  • newspaper articles describing the daily experiences of ordinary visitors in the exhibition grounds p. 54
  • official catalogues, bulletins and exhibition guides, read for the messages states wanted to convey p. 50
  • diplomatic correspondence, such as ambassadors' reports on how governments reacted to the 1889 invitation p. 53
  • the spatial layout of the grounds and buildings, read as a message about universality or difference p. 51

Gaps it names

  • whether and to what extent the governmental strategies of representation were actually successful, which the chapter sets outside its remit and raises only as doubt p. 54
  • culture transfer, which has so far only been applied to bilateral cultural relations, has not been applied to a multilateral event such as a world exhibition p. 56

Contents and chapter overviews

Kargon, Robert H., Karen Fiss, Morris Low and Arthur P. Molella. World’s Fairs on the Eve of War: Science, Technology, and Modernity, 1937–1942. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2015.8 concepts

The book treats the expositions of 1937 to 1942 as contests over what modernity should mean, in which each regime and nation presented its own national version of modern science, technology and design as the route to the future. It argues that these fairs were a propaganda war that ran alongside the armed one, and that the ideological messages of fascist, communist, liberal and militarist regimes can be compared across national boundaries. It is a cultural and political history of science and technology (its subtitle is Science, Technology, and Modernity, 1937-1942).

Argues against

  • Gerald Holton and other historians, who detected romanticized or irrational anti-science currents among conservative scientists in Nazi Germany: The Italian E42 science proposals display none of those currents, and Fascist faith in a modernity based on science and technology 'remained essentially intact'. p. 134
  • The postwar films (Antonioni, Fellini, Pasolini) that made EUR a symbol of alienation and a dystopia: The text calls that memory 'arguably one-dimensional'; to Mussolini and his architects, EUR 'was the dawning rationalist utopia'. p. 136

Sources and ways of working

  • comparison across national boundaries, tracing the same cultural trends in several national archives and printed sources
  • the exposition's own official magazine and reports, read for what they said about the national pavilions p. 26
  • blueprints and plans of unbuilt fairs preserved in state archives p. 108
  • reading an unbuilt monument and other planned artifacts together as an ensemble p. 111

Gaps it names

  • whether a return to the past could ever be a viable route to the future, which the author leaves open for E42 p. 136
  • how Japanese scientists kept doing research under a romantic ideology of imperial descent, which the author calls a fascinating question p. 85

Contents and chapter overviews

Karp, Ivan, and Steven D. Lavine, eds. Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991.14 concepts

Karp and Lavine's volume treats exhibitions as contested, constructed representations, and its chapters ask how objects, labels, installations and festival formats make meanings for makers, exhibitors and viewers. Its overall argument is that display is never neutral: it carries the assumptions of its makers, and cross-cultural or minority displays need to admit this and share authority. The history is cultural and anthropological-museological, with some art-historical and institutional-political strands.

Argues against

  • the view that exhibitors can represent a culture: Exhibitors cannot represent cultures. Exhibitors can be tactful and stimulating impresarios
  • accounts of the modern museum's usurpation of the artist and his or her art: From Bruegel's time to that of Cezanne and Picasso, museums have been a school for craftsmen and artists.
  • the recent attempt to turn museums from temples of wonder into temples of resonance: what has been sacrificed on the altar of cultural resonance is visual wonder centered on the aesthetic masterpiece

Sources and ways of working

  • reports and textual accounts of marvels, such as Durer's account of Mexican objects sent to Charles V
  • reading a museum's architecture, programmed displays and installation practices as a ritual route
  • ethnographic study of festival participants, with daily informal contact and interviews
  • examining the holdings of historical organizations and talking with participants in the event, to build an information base

Gaps it names

  • more experiments involving indigenous experts and the sharing of authority with cultural groups
  • how a non-Indian audience understood the Goswamy exhibitions, which the author says he is not sure of

Contents and chapter overviews

Kwon, Hyeokhui. “An Analysis of Korean Intellectual Responses to the Exhibition of Koreans at Japanese Expositions: Nationalism and the Discourse on Northeast Asian Solidarity at the Turn of the Century.” Journal article.6 concepts

Kwon reads the 1903 Anthropological Pavilion and the 1907 Crystal Pavilion as expositions that combined social Darwinist classification of peoples with commercial entertainment. The Korean reactions to them are read as a shift in Korean intellectuals' thinking from hope in Northeast Asian solidarity with Japan to nationalism, and the argument is that the 'common race and common culture' rationale ended up serving Japanese imperialism. It is a cultural and political history of intellectual responses, built from Korean and Japanese newspapers, magazines and diplomatic records.

Argues against

  • earlier research on the 1903 Anthropological Pavilion (Matsuda 2003; Itō 2005): it has focused on the intentions of the Japanese organisers and on their discriminatory and imperialistic perspective, not on the Korean responses p. 20
  • earlier research on the 1907 Crystal Pavilion's Korean display: it does not pay adequate attention to that display, or to the connections with the international circumstances of Northeast Asia among the people represented p. 20
  • the Japanese Yomiuri shimbun account of the 1907 display, which framed it as women's liberation: the controversy was not related to discrimination against Koreans or to humanitarian principles, but to the freedom of a woman working at the fair p. 31

Sources and ways of working

  • newspaper and magazine records from Korea and Japan, compared across accounts of the same display to reconstruct the names, origins and consent of the people shown p. 24
  • diplomatic documents of the Japanese government, used to explain why the 1903 display was withdrawn p. 27
  • commemorative postcards and souvenir images, read as evidence of how the Koreans were presented p. 22
  • tables that set out how one newspaper described each displayed person, and the Korean newspaper responses sorted by source p. 26

Contents and chapter overviews

Lawn, Martin, ed. Modelling the Future: Exhibitions and the Materiality of Education. Oxford: Symposium Books, 2009.12 concepts

Lawn's editorial introduction frames world exhibitions from London 1851 onward as sites that produced the standards, classifications and comparisons through which modern education was organised, and it calls for a 'materiality of education' approach that studies objects, captions, displays and technologies rather than treating fairs as temporary spectacles. The chapters, by different authors, mostly read fairs and the school museums, materials and images they produced as history of education in a material and visual sense, so the volume is a cultural and material history of schooling with comparative and political strands. Argentina, Spain and Japan are read as nation-building through display, and Glasgow and Wembley as ideological or educational events.

Argues against

  • a view of world exhibitions as temporary displays or explosive spectacles: fairs should be studied within a materiality of education approach that refocuses research on the practices and production modes of school culture p. 11

Sources and ways of working

  • the museum's guidebook, visitor figures and departmental reports, read with the objects displayed beside them p. 80
  • photographs and the press at fairs, used as evidence of how exhibits were presented p. 93
  • reading objects, images and their captions as signs and text, in the manner of a semiotic reading of school material culture p. 31
  • an interview with the principal architect of the 1988 event, with contemporary press reports and guide-catalogues p. 192

Gaps it names

  • historians of education have never intensively studied exhibitions as educational sites p. 7
  • historical outlines of individual school museums are in short supply p. 67

Contents and chapter overviews

Maloney, Cathy Jean. World’s Fair Gardens: Shaping American Landscapes. Charlottesville: University of Virginia Press, 2012.9 concepts

Maloney treats the gardens and grounds of nine US world's fairs (1876-1940) as horticultural and landscape history: fairs were proving grounds for plants, tree transplanting, cold storage and landscape styles, and they left permanent urban parks. Her argument is that fair gardens were ephemeral but their techniques and styles spread to public parks and backyards, so their original design intent deserves understanding and preservation. The book is a design-and-horticulture history with a preservation orientation; it names almost no theoretical framework.

Argues against

  • the view that American fair horticulture should follow European garden trends: The text says world's fairs gave Americans the chance to rethink their dependence on European trends, since plants and styles that worked abroad might prove unsuitable for American soils and climates. p. 4
  • the view that the Jamestown Exposition is a footnote in world's fair literature: The text argues that it nonetheless offers a fine example of urban planning by Warren Manning, and that its small-town character and native plantings shaped later exposition planning. p. 118
  • the view that the buildings and exhibits are the main legacy of a fair: The text says that, overshadowed by the fanfare around buildings and exhibits, an exposition's landscapes and grounds often were its only vestiges within the host city. p. 2

Sources and ways of working

  • periodical and trade reports, such as Garden and Forest, used as contemporary evidence of fair gardens p. 77
  • letters of the designers (Olmsted to Codman, Olmsted to Ulrich) read for their stated intentions p. 63
  • comparison of the lists of designers across fairs, from the single designer of 1876 to the roster of 1939 p. 174
  • seed and flower catalogues read as evidence of how fair displays reached home gardens p. 200

Gaps it names

  • detailed horticultural images from the Columbian Fair are rare, so the record is largely word pictures p. 77
  • physical remnants of the primary structures are scarce p. 77
  • whether Expo 2020 or another future world's fair will revitalize the United States landscape remains to be seen p. 205

Contents and chapter overviews

Mandell, Richard D. Paris 1900: The Great World’s Fair. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1967.9 concepts

Mandell reads the Paris Exposition of 1900 as a political and cultural event: a comprehensive though distorted summary of its civilisation, a weathervane of fin de siecle thought, and a state project whose political calming effect is central. His overall argument is that the fair closed an era of faith in progress and cosmopolitan co-operation and reshaped France's image of itself, though he calls the last effect debatable. It is a political and cultural history (with diplomatic, intellectual and art-historical strands), built on a narrative, chronological and spatial survey of the fair, its finances, attendance and press.

Argues against

  • Writers who treat Art Nouveau as the apotheosis of the 1900 fair, as the outpouring of books on the style frequently suggests.: Mandell says that 'no recent writer has investigated what kind of Art Nouveau was actually at the fair', and that by 1900 the movement was 'already in its period of lost optimism and decay'.
  • Historians who have avoided world's fairs because they are difficult to classify.: The fairs deserve study as sources for political, intellectual and artistic history; Mandell wants historians to take them up.
  • Historiography that has been dazzled by the Crystal Palace of 1851 and the Eiffel Tower's Paris 1889.: Mandell argues that the fairs of 1876, 1893 and 1904 remain largely unstudied, and that the literature is unbalanced by the two large fairs. p. 122
  • Treating the Dreyfus Affair as the main lens on the Paris fair of 1900.: Mandell says that to Frenchmen the fair was 'a more serious and compelling matter than the Affair', and that the fair has been almost forgotten.

Sources and ways of working

  • Size measured by attendance, number of exhibitors, geographical representation, cost and area, compared across fairs
  • A survey of the whole exposition 'spatially, by nations, and chronologically', as a walking tour of the grounds
  • A published inquiry in which journalists and politicians answered on how to restore calm after the Affair (the press and public figures' responses) p. 98
  • Comparing alternative accountings of the same finances (gross deficit, with permanent gifts to Paris counted, with subsidies counted as receipts) p. 107

Gaps it names

  • Very little reliable secondary literature on the great expositions exists, although there are vast amounts of extant materials that could support useful histories.
  • American historians have not studied the fairs of 1876 (Philadelphia), 1893 (Chicago) or 1904 (St. Louis), each of which has scope for several monographs. p. 122
  • Whether the 1900 exposition was itself a factor for change in France is, by Mandell's own admission, debatable. p. 120
  • No recent writer has investigated what kind of Art Nouveau was actually at the fair.

Contents and chapter overviews

Mathur, Saloni. India by Design: Colonial History and Cultural Display. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2007.9 concepts

Mathur reads the display of India in Britain (exhibitions, department stores, museums, oil portraits and picture postcards) as an archive that was anxiously constructed, internally incoherent and contested by Indian nationalists, and treats these forms as suspicious signs and symptoms of imperial crisis. Her overall argument is that the image of a timeless, craft-based traditional India was produced by colonial display and is still reworked rather than resolved in postcolonial staging. It is a cultural history of visual and material display, written across art history, anthropology and museum studies, with case studies from London 1851 to 1886, Chicago 1893 and the postcolonial dispute over Buddhist relics.

Argues against

  • the 'merely cultural' approach, which treats art and aesthetics as relatively autonomous or superstructural to the economic, social and political spheres: The cultural terrain in which colonizer and colonized contested each other cannot be ignored or dismissed; Western cultural forms should be read in the imperial contest in which they were produced. p. 7
  • Malek Alloula's reading of French postcards of Algerian women as a story of visual violation: European women were also collectors and producers of colonial postcards, and the cards show differing, hierarchical constructions of womanhood; Mathur rejects Alloula's nationalist account. p. 25
  • the joint statement of the major museums defending the 'universal museum' and the retention of objects acquired under earlier conditions: The value of the relics was produced through social exchanges between museum officials and their constituencies, and return to a pure point of origin is impossible.
  • art history's notion of 'stylistic influence', which assumed coherent, preexisting homogeneous traditions and a politically neutral field of exchange: Global and comparative thinking should challenge the hierarchy and presumed purity of previous art historical styles. p. 9

Sources and ways of working

  • official police, court, prison, hospital and workhouse records, read to trace the movements of the people on display p. 23
  • reading the dominant archive of exhibition propaganda against the subjects' own petitions and records p. 23
  • comparing a painted archive with a photographic one: Swoboda's portraits set against The People of India, an eight-volume catalogue of photographs p. 23
  • biographical methodology that traces how the value of objects is produced through exchanges between museum officials and their constituencies

Gaps it names

  • Swoboda's paintings have been curiously neglected by anthropologists, art historians, curators and artists p. 82
  • how the museological paradigms of the Holocaust memorial may enhance or hinder the memory of Sikh history and the violent experiences of partition in Punjab

Contents and chapter overviews

Mitchell, Timothy. “The World as Exhibition.” Comparative Studies in Society and History 31, no. 2 (1989): 217–236.7 concepts

Mitchell treats the nineteenth-century exhibition, and above all the world's fair, as a mechanism of order and truth in which the world is set up as a series of models that each claim to show a reality beyond them. The argument is that this system depends on a claimed gap between representation and an external reality, which in practice is never reached, and that Orientalism is part of the same method rather than only a case of cultural portrayal or colonial domination. The history is cultural and intellectual, built from Arabic travel writing, Orientalist scholarship, travellers' accounts and the Paris exhibitions, and it draws on Said and on post-structuralist and anthropological theory.

Argues against

  • The critique of commodity fetishism, which Mitchell says uncovers misrepresentation while leaving representation itself unquestioned.: Mitchell says the commercial parallel with the exhibition is not a commodity-fetishism argument, because the exhibition creates the effect of an external reality as itself a mechanism of power. p. 225
  • The argument of alienation, in which the exhibition or modern commerce separates people from the real world.: The exhibition does not alienate us from the real world; it creates an effect called the real world, in terms of which alienation can be experienced. p. 225
  • The view that Western representations distort a real Orient that exists apart from them.: The East itself is not a place; what appears to be the real is a further series of representations, and the notion of a real beyond representation is what keeps convincing. p. 236
  • Orientalism as one more case of a culture portraying another, or as colonial domination alone.: Orientalism is part of a method of order and truth essential to the peculiar nature of the modern world. p. 236

Sources and ways of working

  • Arabic travel accounts of Europe, and an 1882 Arabic novel, read as evidence of how non-European visitors experienced the exhibition and the street p. 221
  • Official exhibition plans and descriptions, such as the 1889 layout that placed a display of human labour before the exhibition p. 220
  • Guidebooks for travellers, such as Murray's Handbook for Travellers in Lower and Upper Egypt, read for the viewpoint they advise p. 230
  • Travellers' drawings, the camera lucida and photographs, read as a search for a pictorial certainty about the East p. 229

Gaps it names

  • The detailed working of colonial rule in Egypt, which Mitchell says he has examined in Colonising Egypt rather than in this essay p. 226

Contents and chapter overviews

Molella, Arthur P., and Scott Gabriel Knowles, eds. World’s Fairs in the Cold War: Science, Technology, and the Culture of Progress. Pittsburgh: University of Pittsburgh Press, 2019.12 concepts

The editors (Molella and Knowles) frame the Cold War fairs of 1958 to 1970 as proxy fronts and arenas of soft power in which science, technology and national ideals were staged for mass audiences, so that the fairs both mirrored and shaped Cold War culture. Chapters argue that the fairs were sites of US-Soviet rivalry, urban renewal, religious and gender politics, consumerism and media change, and that their optimism about technology was shaped by anxieties of the period. It is an interdisciplinary cultural and political history of science and technology, with architectural, urban and media history alongside it; the author-level reading was limited to the parts listed in the note.

Argues against

  • Studies of the Carousel that treat it mainly as a nostalgic account of technological progress: Demeter argues that what has been neglected is the attraction's embodiment of technological superiority and creative consumerism, both crucial Cold War narrative themes p. 87
  • Science fiction narratives with pessimistic and dystopic readings of technology: Disney's Audio-Animatronics assured audiences that progress should be embraced, offering a counter-narrative to those warnings p. 92

Sources and ways of working

  • Visitor surveys by the USIA at Expo '58, weighed against Belgian press reviews p. 43
  • Exit surveys of Japanese visitors at the American and Soviet pavilions in Osaka p. 53
