  • Archival records, planning documents and press material for an unrealised pavilion p. 110
  • Comparison of a women's pavilion with the Woman's Building at Chicago in 1893 p. 146
  • Press reports, BIE assessments and the fairs' own films, read for the Plovdiv and later expositions p. 197

Gaps it names

  • The connection between world's fairs and the Cold War has not received the systematic attention it deserves p. 4

Contents and chapter overviews

Park, Young-Sin. “Making ‘Modern’ Korean Subjects: The Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition of 1915.” Journal article.7 concepts

Park reads the 1915 Chosŏn Industrial Exhibition in Seoul as a cultural machinery that addressed Korean visitors as modern subjects, using Foucault's disciplinary apparatus and the Panopticon alongside spectacle and consumption. The overall argument is that the exhibition produced a conflicted Korean subject (disciplined citizen, consumer and colonised subject) and that it cannot be explained by colonial propaganda alone. It is a cultural and visual history of representation and visitor experience, with social-historical material on Korean reception and on the early colonial expositions that followed.

Argues against

  • The literature on Korean expositions, which focuses almost exclusively on the colonial political context of the 1915 exhibition and its function as political propaganda: The exhibition is explored as a cultural machinery whose meaning and effects are not reducible to its manifest political purpose, with attention to the modern Korean subjects it constructed p. 2

Sources and ways of working

  • Visitors' responses drawn from the Maeil shinbo's reports, read with the awareness that the contemporary print media managed or censored much of the coverage p. 15
  • Missionary accounts of Korean visitors, by Edwin Wade Koons and William Arthur Noble p. 15
  • A survey of visitors' favourite sites, recorded in the 1915 exhibition review survey conducted in Hyesan City p. 18
  • Architecture and layout read as text: architectural coding, display strategies and the numbered visitor route p. 21

Gaps it names

  • Visitors' responses are poorly documented: material relevant to visitors' experiences is limited and scattered p. 15
  • The 'dark period' of early colonial rule is an understudied era in Korean cultural history p. 22

Contents and chapter overviews

Peterson, William. Asian Self-Representation at World’s Fairs. Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2020.9 concepts

Peterson treats Asian national pavilions at world's fairs from 1915 to 2015 as sites where states, not Western powers, controlled how a nation was represented, and argues that the exposition moved from an 'exhibitionary order' of colonial display to a 'performative order' of live, embodied encounters. The work is a case-study cultural and political history built on fair archives, press and public-relations material, and, for Milan 2015, the author's own repeat visits and affect-focused description of the pavilions. Its overall argument is that as state-run expositions decline, national representation becomes a commercial, affective 'nationalising of the sell'.

Argues against

  • Studies (Benedict; Parezo and Fowler; Greenhalgh; Hinsley; Delmendo) that show the display of colonized peoples as an integral part of the imperial project: This book seeks to turn the lens around by focusing on the agency evidenced in Asian self-representation p. 16
  • Views of the New York fair of 1964-65 as a largely commercial enterprise and a vulgar celebration of American consumer culture: For the Philippines and Indonesia, seeing and being seen in New York ... mattered greatly p. 34

Sources and ways of working

  • Official fair corporation and national-commission archives (press releases, speeches, photos, films, clippings), mostly in English, used to see how each state sought to self-represent p. 28
  • Publicity-office clippings of the 1964-65 fair, tracking how press tropes about Asian women were generated and disseminated p. 31
  • Fieldwork at Milan 2015: repeat visits, personal observation of pavilions and interviews with guides, with the 'sensuous geographies' of the route described for the reader p. 30
  • Scrapbooks and ephemera left by fair enthusiasts, used as evidence of audience response to San Francisco 1915 and Brisbane 1988 p. 31

Gaps it names

  • Archives in the participating nations: the study relies on English-language sources and cannot reach the intentions of Asian officials in their own languages p. 29
  • How the Asian labour at fairs was recruited, trained and housed, and what the lives and careers of performers and guides were after they returned home p. 30
  • The Brisbane 1988 exposition: 'There has been little scholarship on this exposition' p. 34
  • How selected Western nations self-represent at expositions in the Middle East or Asia, since the book looks only at Asian self-representation p. 19

Contents and chapter overviews

Qureshi, Sadiah. Peoples on Parade: Exhibitions, Empire, and Anthropology in Nineteenth-Century Britain. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2011.8 concepts

Qureshi treats London's shows of living foreign peoples as a large commercial entertainment whose links to racism, empire and ethnic difference must be shown historically rather than assumed (lines 262-264). She argues that the shows were arenas where both intercultural and natural knowledge were produced, and that their meanings varied among showmen, performers, patrons and anthropologists. It is a social and cultural history of entertainment and science in nineteenth-century Britain, drawing on the history of anthropology and on fairs.

Argues against

  • Accounts that treat displayed peoples as freaks, in which ethnic difference is equated with freakishness: Comparison with other human displays is most productive where differences between patrons and performers, and between acts, are traced; the 'savage freak show' category flattens them. p. 8
  • Historians who model the shows on white selves observing black others and sort audiences by complexion: Consumers and performers were classified by biologically based definitions of human variety; in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, criteria were wider, including clothing, religion and language. p. 275
  • Discussions of the shows' receptions that rely on colour-based or biological definitions of race: Such definitions are too narrow for the period and fail to account for older ways of framing human variety. p. 274
  • Views that homogenise the shows into racist spectatorship relying on voyeuristic gazing: Spectators exercised observational judgment and did not simply repeat advertising, journalists or moral philosophers. p. 168

Sources and ways of working

  • Press reviews and newspaper reports, the main eyewitness sources, since few spectators left records p. 9
  • Court cases, contracts, anecdotal accounts and newspaper reviews, read for how the archives were formed p. 9
  • Biographies of performers, to recover their agency and their lives as entertainers p. 9
  • Close reading of images for their political charge, including the reproduced prints of the shows p. 10

Gaps it names

  • Showmen, spectators and performers left few or no records of their encounters with one another p. 9
  • Sources that would reconstruct performers' motivations and perceptions are rare p. 9
  • The intercultural encounters of foreign communities resident in London have had less research integrated into discussions of the city's cosmopolitan crowd p. 45
  • The incorporation of the Völkerschauen (people shows) into German anthropology, as an exception to the wider neglect of human displays in anthropology's history p. 186

Contents and chapter overviews

Raizman, David, and Ethan Robey, eds. Expanding Nationalisms at World’s Fairs: Identity, Diversity, and Exchange, 1851–1915. London: Routledge, 2018.9 concepts

The editors (Raizman and Robey) treat world's fairs of 1851 to 1915 as networks of exchange in which goods and displays expressed national identity, and they frame national identity as constructed, contested and hybrid rather than given. Their argument is that material culture, not only print, helped make nations, and that fair displays were political acts within imperial and commercial rivalry. The book is a cultural and global design history, with chapters that also draw on postcolonial, Orientalist and cultural-diplomacy critique and on close study of individual designers, commissioners and objects.

Argues against

  • Pevsner's modernist narrative, in which the fairs serve largely as a foil to the rise of functionalist design: The editors say the fairs deserve study on their own terms, not only as a contrast to modern design. p. 2
  • A Eurocentric viewpoint in design history: The essays give voice to alternative nationalisms and to networks of international exchange. p. 2
  • Nationalism scholarship (Anderson and others) that acknowledged print culture but neglected material culture: The editors argue that the goods at fairs were essential to national and colonial aspirations and need political reading. p. 6
  • Recent Orientalist scholarship on Islamic architecture at fairs, which Hedrick says has obscured Diebitsch's work: Hedrick argues that the modernity and internationalism of Diebitsch's Islamic architecture were obscured in that scholarship. p. 45

Sources and ways of working

  • Study of the artifacts themselves (the pavilions, displays and objects) as the source of the fairs' interpretive richness p. 8
  • Reading the architecture of the halls and the arrangement of packaged goods as political statements, as Guldberg does for the Copenhagen Nordic Exhibition p. 8
  • Following a designer's career across fairs and commissions, as Hedrick does for Carl von Diebitsch p. 10
  • Comparing a national display with the products of rival countries shown at the same fair p. 9

Gaps it names

  • The histories of overlooked fairs, such as Brussels 1880, Antwerp 1885, Copenhagen 1888 and the 1910 centenaries in South America, which the volume argues are under-studied p. 8
  • The world's fairs and the displayed goods that carried national and colonial aspirations, which nationalism scholarship has largely ignored p. 6

Contents and chapter overviews

Roche, Maurice. Mega-Events and Modernity: Olympics and Expos in the Growth of Global Culture. London: Routledge, 2000.9 concepts

Roche defines mega-events as large cultural, commercial and sporting occasions with dramatic character, mass appeal and international significance, and studies the world's fairs (expos) and the Olympic Games as elements of modern public culture, cultural citizenship and cultural inclusion/exclusion. The argument is that these events are simultaneously drama, a political-economic project for elites and nations, and a long-run element of modernity, so they need a multi-perspectival political sociology with critical political sociology as the priority. The text is a sociology of modernity with strong political, economic and cultural-history content; it is not a history of single exhibitions.

Argues against

  • Functionalist accounts (economic, critical and cultural functionalism) that see mega-events as reproducing social systems: Intermediate-level analysis that stops at reproduction loses touch with the long-run structural change; mega-events are also sites where popular and resistant responses can develop. p. 20
  • Bennett's account of the exhibitionary complex: It underplays the dramatological or performance aspects of producing and consuming exhibitions, and it misses the link between expos and the sport and Olympic movements. p. 34
  • Foucault's surveillance and disciplinary account, if over-generalised to museums and exhibitions: Museums and exhibitions worked in almost the reverse way, by attracting the public to participate and by entertainment rather than confinement. p. 37
  • Castells's network-society analysis, which Roche draws on for hubs and switches: Castells makes no substantial reference to World's Fairs, Olympic Games or other cultural and sporting mega-events; Roche extends his analysis to them. p. 233

Sources and ways of working

  • A multi-perspectival combination of the dramatological, the contextual (critical political sociology) and the long-run historical perspectives, applied to each event p. 11
  • Re-presenting and analysing event producers' and participants' voice and agency from their documents, speech and attitudes p. 15
  • A long-range historical perspective, to bring the origins and changes of mega-events into view together with their contexts p. 20
  • Cross-national reception analysis of how audiences in different countries received a mega-event on television, which Roche recommends for future Olympic media research p. 188

Gaps it names

  • Mega-events have attracted relatively little research attention, and they fall between several disciplines p. 5
  • The popular culture of sport, which was at least as important as exhibitions in forming collective identities in 1870-1914, is missing from accounts centred on exhibitions p. 38
  • Cross-cultural reception analysis of the audience for Olympic television, which the Barcelona 1992 research team said had not been done well enough p. 188
  • The book is a preliminary contribution to a research agenda on mega-events, agency, structure and continuity in modernity p. 235

Contents and chapter overviews

Rydell, Robert W. All the World’s a Fair: Visions of Empire at American International Expositions, 1876–1916. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1984.8 concepts

Rydell frames the American world’s fairs of 1876 to 1916 as “symbolic universes” that gave visitors a ritual confirmation of progress, understood as economic growth and racial hierarchy, and so legitimated the authority of corporate, political and scientific leaders. His overall argument is that the expositions were hegemonic, upper-class productions that used evolutionary ideas about race to blur class divisions among whites and to justify racial exploitation at home and empire abroad. It is a cultural and political history of ideology, in which the Smithsonian, anthropology and the midway are the main instruments.

Argues against

  • historians who question the legitimating function of Darwinian ideas: World’s fairs provide a partial but crucial explanation for the interpenetration and popularization of evolutionary ideas about race and progress.
  • historians who debate the symbolic significance of only one fair: The significance lies in the series of fairs held between 1876 and 1916, and in the way midway entertainments gained legitimacy by 1904.
  • the view that the midways were just for fun: Their development into integral components of the expositions reflected upper-class efforts to influence popular culture.

Sources and ways of working

  • reading the spatial layout of the grounds, the White City set against the Midway, and the colour scheme of the Buffalo fair
  • the classification schemes and exhibit plans of the fair directors and Smithsonian scientists, such as Goode’s classification for Chicago
  • visitors’ own accounts of the fairs, such as Rao Telang’s description of the Midway
  • comparison across the fairs: the analysis asks how each fair contributed to the ideological process

Gaps it names

  • how scientific ideas about evolution, race and culture reached popular consumption from academic circles, which the author says is less well understood
  • American fairs, which the author says remain largely unstudied
  • the degree of lower-class acquiescence to upper-class visions of progress, which the author says may have been far less than total

Contents and chapter overviews

Rydell, Robert W. World of Fairs: The Century-of-Progress Expositions. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993.9 concepts

Rydell reads the century-of-progress fairs of the 1930s as ideological constructs that were designed to restore faith in government, business, science and intellectual leaders during the Depression, and whose promise of abundance rested on a racially exclusive social order. He stresses continuity with the Victorian fairs, and he treats the expositions as theaters of power and as an arena of contest, most clearly in the African American chapter. The book is cultural and political history, with strong institutional and economic content (fair finance, corporate exhibitors, scientists' advisory committees), and it reads exhibits, publicity and planning documents as the carriers of that ideology.

Argues against

  • Accounts that treat the Victorian fairs chiefly as the rise of a consumer culture, built on Benjamin's reading of world exhibitions: The fairs certainly promised material abundance, but they did so in contexts that elaborated visions of empire as well. p. 18
  • The view that the 1925 Paris decorative arts fair alone shaped modernistic sensibilities between the wars: Colonial expositions, especially the 1931 Paris exposition, played an equally decisive role. p. 61
  • Studies of the New York fair in isolation from its predecessors and from San Francisco: Such studies imbalance the historical record by overvaluing the New York fair and underestimating the cumulative strength of the century-of-progress movement. p. 9
  • Critics who said that the era of great world's fairs had gone the way of dinosaurs after the 1926 Philadelphia fair: What those critics failed to appreciate was the depth and breadth of exhibition culture in the 1920s. p. 6

Sources and ways of working

  • Corporate exhibitors' promotional materials and the advertising they produced, read as evidence of the fairs' messages p. 217
  • Surveys of fairgoers by a market research firm, used cautiously as evidence of audience response (assessing audience responses) p. 154
  • Oral histories of fairgoers and the press, read together, as sources on what visitors took from a fair p. 19
  • Fairgoers' photo albums and souvenir books, read as windows on how people chose to remember the fair p. 217

Gaps it names

  • The author says no scholar had yet published a book-length study of the 1933-34 Chicago Century of Progress Exposition p. 9
  • There is no modern history of the Belgian and Spanish fairs of the interwar period p. 8
  • British and French fairs of the period are only beginning to receive their due p. 8
  • Only the 1936 Texas Centennial Exposition has been the subject of a monograph by a historian p. 8

Contents and chapter overviews

Rydell, Robert W., John E. Findling and Kimberly D. Pelle. Fair America: World’s Fairs in the United States. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press, 2000.9 concepts

Rydell, Findling and Pelle argue that American world's fairs carried the political reconstruction of the nation after the Civil War into culture, promoting overseas expansion and racial hierarchy as remedies for class conflict, and that fairs served as a medium for winning popular consent for ruling-class and imperial policies. They treat fairs as contested arenas, where midway performers and displayed peoples could subvert sponsors' intentions, and their closing argument ties the medium to transnational corporate capitalism. It is a cultural and political history of the American political economy, with strong social and racial history and a critical view of technological and ideological progress.

Argues against

  • Fairs as cultural ephemera, money-losing sideshows, or leisure with no long-term significance: The authors concede that such objections are not unimportant, but argue that fairs were initiated by those in positions of power and influence, and that their designers, managers and visitors make them a window onto American history.
  • The view that fairs are cultural dinosaurs, displaced by theme parks, Olympic spectacles and electronic media: The authors say fairs keep supplying ideological and cultural armor, so the real question is whether that armor will let the species survive for as long as dinosaurs lived.
  • The claim that Expo 2000's sustainability ideology breaks from the ideology of progress of earlier fairs: They doubt it: if the sustainability theme makes its ideal depend on the globalization of transnational corporate capitalism, the culturally produced armor will only get heavier and give a false sense of security.

Sources and ways of working

  • Printed matter as a way fairs reached people who never visited: press accounts and picture postcards
  • Official histories of fairs, read against what they leave out (for example, an event never mentioned in the fair's official history)
  • Official catalogues and congressional reports, quoted for what they said an exhibit proved (the Colt revolver case)
  • Reading the spatial layout of a fair, such as whether a nation's exhibits sat in central or peripheral locations, as a statement of racial ranking

Gaps it names

  • Whether recent fairs, now tied to transnational corporations, will address the nuclear and ecological crises of the present or leave us whistling in the dark
  • Whether Expo 2000 at Hannover will escape the technological utopianism of earlier fairs; the authors say it is too early to tell

Contents and chapter overviews

Samuel, Lawrence R. The End of the Innocence: The 1964–1965 New York World’s Fair. Syracuse: Syracuse University Press, 2007.8 concepts

Samuel frames the 1964–65 New York World's Fair as a popular experience set against a failed official enterprise: visitors remembered a joyous, reassuring and conservative Fair, while its management, finances and critics judged it a failure. The work is a cultural and institutional history of one fair, built from press, audit and exhibitor records and from period photographs. Its overall argument is that the Fair was a success in popular memory and marked the last moment of American postwar innocence.

Argues against

  • histories that dismiss the Fair as a failure, such as Arthur Gelb and Sam Robert of the New York Times: the Fair was not a failure at all, but a major success, offering millions of people a wonderful, unforgettable experience
  • Robert W. Rydell, John E. Findling and Kimberly D. Pelle, Fair America: they sum up the Fair as a large, rambling, unfocused exposition, and do not mention that it was the nation's most attended or how visitors felt
  • critics who read the Fair's conservatism as a liability: the conservative tone was a key asset that contributed heavily to the Fair's popularity
  • top-down, producer-oriented, operation-focused tellings of the Fair's history: history should put people ahead of institutions and tell the Fair's popular memory

Sources and ways of working

  • period sources: the press of the time, and the WFC's and exhibitors' own records held in libraries, archives and the world's fair subculture; Samuel treats later oral recollections with caution
  • photographs taken by an average visitor (Bill Cotter), used in place of staged archive photographs, to show the real Fair experience
  • a chronological Part I combined with a thematic Part II, to pair a linear narrative with a more subjective account of the Fair's main ideas
  • reading the Fair's sponsors' displays (e.g. Futurama, the Hall of Science) as texts that promote a future, and checking them against the costs and criticism of the time

Gaps it names

  • the individual experiences of visitors, which the Fair's story has largely left out
  • the popular music, jazz, folk and rhythm and blues, and the youth culture and African American expression that the Fair did not include
  • the attendance of 52 million: far less attention has been paid to the people who came than to the eighteen million who did not

Contents and chapter overviews

Shepherdson-Scott, Kari. “Conflicting Politics and Contesting Borders: Exhibiting (Japanese) Manchuria at the Chicago World’s Fair, 1933–34.” Journal article.7 concepts

Shepherdson-Scott reads the 1933 Manchuria pavilion at Chicago as a piece of diplomatic and corporate public relations: the Japanese government, army, Manchukuo government and Mantetsu used a small building and its displays to present Manchuria as a Japanese-developed economic project rather than a political one. Her argument is that the exhibits could not fix a single idea of Manchuria, because the American-sponsored Golden Temple of Jehol and the fair's own catalogues contested the borders the pavilion drew. It is a political and cultural history of exhibitions, built from display design, official catalogues, pamphlets and the press, and it is written by an art historian.

Argues against

  • Japanese claims to the international community that the new state of Manchukuo would not be placed under Japanese governmental control: The text calls the claim a ruse that was not successful, and says the army's account of its actions and the new state's supposed sovereignty were all suspect from the beginning. p. 542
  • Duara's argument that Manchukuo's sovereignty was not solely the product of Japanese intervention, which the text cites while discussing whether Manchukuo was a puppet state: The text qualifies the argument: it remains important to remember the coercive forces at work in Manchukuo, such as colonial displacement, mass killings and forced labor. p. 542

Sources and ways of working

  • Official fair catalogues and guidebooks, read for the space and illustrations each gives to a display, including what they omit (the Golden Temple against the Manchuria pavilion) p. 560
  • Photographs of the fair and of the pavilion in the official album and view book, read for what they show and what they erase p. 560
  • Close reading of the wording of Mantetsu's pamphlets, including their policy statements and passive phrasing p. 552
  • Comparison of Japanese domestic magazines with the methods used in the Chicago exhibit p. 553

Gaps it names

  • Audience reception of the Manchuria pavilion, which the text says is difficult to quantify p. 557
  • Who rejected the Survey of Manchoukuo film for American screening, which the source does not identify p. 544
  • When the location of the China pavilion was chosen, which the fair literature does not record p. 557

Contents and chapter overviews

Thomas, Nicholas. Entangled Objects: Exchange, Material Culture, and Colonialism in the Pacific. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1991.9 concepts

Thomas does not treat exhibitions as a main topic: the book is about exchange and material culture in the Pacific, and fairs appear only in chapter 4 (Sydney 1879, Melbourne 1880). Its argument is that gift and commodity should be studied through the particular colonial histories of each place, that objects are what they have become through contact rather than what they were made to be, and that both indigenous appropriation of European goods and European collecting of indigenous things reworked the meanings of those things. It is a historical and cultural anthropology of material culture, with a colonial political history of Fiji.

Argues against

  • Malinowski's account of the kula as strictly ceremonial and cut off from barter and from the history of his own society: Kula items were used in many ways, including as payment for food, canoes and assassinations, and the barter sphere was not separate from kula gifts; Malinowski 'misled his readers' on this point. p. 12
  • Strathern's claim that work or objects cannot be alienated in Melanesian systems: Thomas says it is a reformulation of the Maussian model, derived from the proposition that a gift regime cannot permit such transformations, and it ignores the variants that developed historically. p. 57
  • the view that Melanesian, Polynesian or other tribal societies are communal or 'gift' economies: The text rejects this view; in some systems alienation and virtually commodity transactions occur. p. 4
  • Western liberal writing and some indigenous histories that European goods drew Pacific peoples into dependence through barter: Objects are culturally mutable: an axe or musket gained its value from local practice and ideas about the foreign visitors who brought it. p. 83

Sources and ways of working

  • comparative reading across regions, extracting items selectively from ethnographies of New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, New Zealand and Micronesia, with Fiji and eastern Polynesia as the main base p. 6
  • travellers' and officials' writings as sources: Keate's account, Von Hugel's collecting, and the letters and diaries of Governor Gordon's household p. 164
  • exhibition catalogues and fair displays read for how native material culture was selected and framed (Sydney 1879, Melbourne 1880) p. 176
  • reading a myth (Tabua, who obtains a wife with whale teeth) as evidence for the meaning of valuables p. 70

Gaps it names

  • the lack of a synthetic intermediate level of theory: the discipline has treatises on ritual, myth, ethnicity and gender and a mass of ethnographies, but little regional or thematic synthesis p. 6
  • an account of Pacific exchange within the colonial and 'postcolonial' periods that stands on its own; the text says the facts of colonial history do not themselves provide a sufficient context for interpretation p. 205

Contents and chapter overviews

Weimann, Jeanne Madeline. The Fair Women: The Story of the Woman’s Building, World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893. Chicago: Academy Chicago, 1981.8 concepts

Weimann's book is a narrative history of the Woman's Building at the 1893 Chicago fair, reconstructed from the Board of Lady Managers' papers at the Chicago Historical Society, with newspapers, Congressional records and exhibit descriptions. It presents the Building as a contested space: the Board's real achievements are shown against constraints from the fair's male commissioners, from the press, and from splits inside the women's movement between suffragists and clubwomen. Miller's introduction calls it an attempt to 'recreate' the Building and to judge what women achieved, concluding that the Building had little effect on the vote but some on education. Its kind of history is social and institutional history of women's organising, with cultural history of the exhibits.

Argues against

  • Architectural critics, Henry Adams and Mumford, who dismissed the Fair's classical White City as stage decoration and who ignored the Woman's Building: Miller notes that Adams does not mention the Woman's Building, and argues that its exhibits were not 'vague' and 'ill-defined', since they raised questions as real as those the machines raised
  • Some modern feminists, who denigrate many of the philanthropies as maternalistic and condescending and object to the volunteerism of the women's clubs: Miller says the educational displays of the Woman's and Children's Buildings 'were not minor matters', and leaves the value of women's accomplishments to the reader

Sources and ways of working

  • The Board of Lady Managers' official papers, held at the Chicago Historical Society, as the main archive
  • Newspaper reports from both sides and the press debates over the Board, read by date, such as the Chicago News for April 4, 1891 p. 86
  • The Fair's official History and press reports, used to reconstruct events such as the opening of May 1, 1893 p. 241
  • Reconstructing the Building from its circulars, correspondence and exhibits, which Miller describes as an attempt 'to recreate the Woman’s Building'

Gaps it names

  • What women achieved for themselves through the Building, beyond its displays; Miller asks 'what she achieved for herself is a question' and notes that the Building did not bring the vote closer
  • Bertha Palmer's own credit for the Building, which Miller says is usually given to Susan B. Anthony, who served the Board in no capacity

Contents and chapter overviews

Çelik, Zeynep. Displaying the Orient: Architecture of Islam at Nineteenth-Century World’s Fairs. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992.8 concepts

Celik reads the Islamic pavilions and quarters of the nineteenth-century fairs as a double-sided representation: the fairs claimed scientific accuracy while indulging fantasy, so the buildings show both how Europeans constructed the Orient and how Muslim states tried to define a modern cultural identity. The argument is that the fairs' architecture was ahistorical and stylistic, and that in the colonies France appropriated Islamic forms for its own repertoire, a pattern the epilogue finds still at work. It is architectural history that reads building styles and urban layouts alongside the political history of the Ottoman, Egyptian and North African states and of colonial rule.

Argues against

  • The view that architectural histories of the fairs treat the buildings in isolation from the exposition as a whole: Celik takes the fairs as a whole, because architectural historians have discussed the buildings in isolation or looked at them only in their immediate environments p. 5–6
  • The dichotomy between a non-Western (Eastern, Orientalist) and a Western (Occidental) world, and the terms 'Islamic civilization' or 'Western civilization': Cross-cultural dialogue disrupts this polar system and questions the validity of fixing cultural boundaries p. 5–6
  • The European tendency to consider Islamic civilization a single entity: Insistence on national identities in the pavilions was a reaction against that tendency and against Ottoman suzerainty p. 137–138
  • The notion that architecture can be manipulated to summarise cultures and nations visually: Architectural representation is never pure and is always colored by power relations p. 195–196

Sources and ways of working

  • Reading the site plans of the expositions as diagrams of the prevailing power relations and the grouping of the Islamic pavilions p. 15–16
  • A contrapuntal reading of specific cases, set side by side to show overlapping and interconnected histories p. 11–12
  • Comparison across fairs and decades, tracing how layouts and styles changed between 1867 and 1900 p. 57–58
  • Travel accounts, newspaper and magazine articles, and visitors' reports read alongside the official publications of the exposition commissions p. 17–18

Gaps it names

  • Cross-cultural studies of architecture and its exchanges are just beginning p. 179–180
  • The cross-cultural influence of the fairs on Western architecture has remained in the background of exposition studies p. 153–154
  • The colonial discourse of the occupied territories, with its arguments embedded in the culture of the mother country, was not included in this study p. 11–12

Contents and chapter overviews

Gaps the authors name

Things the authors themselves say are neglected, unknown or worth further research: a list of openings for new work.

  • why the degradation of American life happened after the 1960s, which the author says no current explanation has answered (Gelernter 1995p. 368)
  • the causal link between the 'little oughts' of daily life and the social character of the late 1930s, which the author admits is unprovable (Gelernter 1995p. 218)
  • the other side of the 1930s story about Jewish prominence and anti-Semitism, which the author says we tend to know only one side of (Gelernter 1995p. 291)
  • how scientific ideas about evolution, race and culture reached popular consumption from academic circles, which the author says is less well understood (Rydell 1984)
  • American fairs, which the author says remain largely unstudied (Rydell 1984)
  • the degree of lower-class acquiescence to upper-class visions of progress, which the author says may have been far less than total (Rydell 1984)
  • Archives in the participating nations: the study relies on English-language sources and cannot reach the intentions of Asian officials in their own languages (Peterson 2020p. 29)
  • How the Asian labour at fairs was recruited, trained and housed, and what the lives and careers of performers and guides were after they returned home (Peterson 2020p. 30)
  • The Brisbane 1988 exposition: 'There has been little scholarship on this exposition' (Peterson 2020p. 34)
  • How selected Western nations self-represent at expositions in the Middle East or Asia, since the book looks only at Asian self-representation (Peterson 2020p. 19)
  • Audience reception of the Manchuria pavilion, which the text says is difficult to quantify (Shepherdson-Scottp. 557)
  • Who rejected the Survey of Manchoukuo film for American screening, which the source does not identify (Shepherdson-Scottp. 544)
  • When the location of the China pavilion was chosen, which the fair literature does not record (Shepherdson-Scottp. 557)
  • The volume does not offer an exhaustive list of 'marginal' exhibitions in the period, and it aims to initiate further research on aspects left aside. (Filipová 2015p. 15)
  • Colonial exhibitions in remote locations (Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India, Brazil) have only recently attracted attention as sites of the adoption of the exhibition medium. (Filipová 2015p. 14)
  • the whole tradition of hundreds of exhibitions outside Britain, France and the USA, for example in Africa, Asia, Australasia and South America, which the text says it cannot examine (Greenhalgh 1988p. 2)
  • empirical completeness even for the three main nations: about thirty events are treated in detail and around forty more briefly (Greenhalgh 1988p. 2)
  • the 'banal urban environment' and the lasting ideology of exhibitions in later city design, which the Postscript suggests but does not trace (Greenhalgh 1988p. 226)
  • modern history museums have received little attention in the scholarship, which has focused more on fine arts museums such as the Palace Museum (Denton 2014p. 10)
  • how negotiation among historians, curators, cadres and officials shapes PRC exhibitions is not made public, so it is hard to study (Denton 2014p. 14)
  • alternative memories (independent films, unofficial memorial sites, online blogs) are present but small and hidden, and have yet to enter the mainstream the way they have in Taiwan (Denton 2014p. 4)
  • The histories of overlooked fairs, such as Brussels 1880, Antwerp 1885, Copenhagen 1888 and the 1910 centenaries in South America, which the volume argues are under-studied (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 8)
  • The world's fairs and the displayed goods that carried national and colonial aspirations, which nationalism scholarship has largely ignored (Raizman & Robey 2018p. 6)
  • whether the propaganda altered history in less obvious ways, for example by delaying American actions to counter Japanese aggression (Brown)
  • the degree to which Theodore Roosevelt's support for Japan in the Russo-Japanese War was influenced by the Japanese displays at the 1904 fair (Brown)
  • Brussels, with its exhibitions of 1897, 1910 and 1935, is named as a dramatically under-researched exhibition hub (Geppert 2010p. 13)
  • other European and American fairs (Barcelona 1888, Milan 1906, Turin, the American world's fairs) are left out of the sample and need study (Geppert 2010p. 14)
  • the Berliner Gewerbeausstellung of 1896 is described as an under-researched counter-case (Geppert 2010p. 14)
  • Visitors' responses are poorly documented: material relevant to visitors' experiences is limited and scattered (Parkp. 15)
  • The 'dark period' of early colonial rule is an understudied era in Korean cultural history (Parkp. 22)
  • the bulk of world's fair literature pays little attention to picnics and outdoor meals (Tran) (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 435)
  • what little attention has been paid to Hagenbeck's influence on World's Fairs exhibits, which has tended to be apologetic (Santesso) (Hollengreen et al. 2014p. 45)
  • historians of education have never intensively studied exhibitions as educational sites (Lawn 2009p. 7)
  • historical outlines of individual school museums are in short supply (Lawn 2009p. 67)
  • a Francophone or German global knowledge in the nineteenth century, which Withers raises as unexplored, and whether having an empire was necessary for global knowledge (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 253)
  • a 'global Livingstone', which Henderson calls a worthwhile question though one that could underplay local reception (Finnegan & Wright 2015p. 243)
  • Transnationality of Chinese print media, which the author says scholars have not paid enough attention to (Hurp. 172)
  • The public sphere configured beyond the national boundary, which the text calls a phenomenon requiring further research (Hurp. 172)
  • China and Japan at the early world exhibitions, which the author says deserve more attention in Euro-centred studies (Hurp. 168)
  • The Nanyang exposition in the context of sixty years of Chinese experience at world exhibitions, which no scholarly work had examined (Hurp. 125)
  • The share of native visitors who were the better off and educated, and how many came from Semarang as against other north-coast cities; the author says this remains unclear. (Cotép. 33)
  • How the native spectator would have regarded the display of ‘native tradition’ and its evolutionary message, which the author raises as the more important question in hindsight. (Cotép. 26)
  • the images the audience is allowed or encouraged to form about exhibited people and the attitudes these produce among those exhibited, which Benedict says is beyond the scope of his study (Benedict 1983p. 43)
  • Whether the ethnic exhibits along the Midway actually encouraged viewers to see non-white peoples as barbaric; Badger raises the question and leaves it open (Badger 1979p. 106)
  • whether and to what extent the governmental strategies of representation were actually successful, which the chapter sets outside its remit and raises only as doubt (Kaiserp. 54)
  • culture transfer, which has so far only been applied to bilateral cultural relations, has not been applied to a multilateral event such as a world exhibition (Kaiserp. 56)
  • Why Kiralfy was so interested in proposing Japan as a partner in a joint exhibition is left unexplained: 'It seems a mystery' (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 46)
  • Assessing the success of the Exhibition is open to debate: evidence is strong for attendance, media coverage and sales of Japanese exhibits, but not for diplomatic gains (Hotta-Lister 1999p. 192)
  • The detailed working of colonial rule in Egypt, which Mitchell says he has examined in Colonising Egypt rather than in this essay (Mitchell 1989p. 226)
  • The author says no scholar had yet published a book-length study of the 1933-34 Chicago Century of Progress Exposition (Rydell 1993p. 9)
  • There is no modern history of the Belgian and Spanish fairs of the interwar period (Rydell 1993p. 8)
  • British and French fairs of the period are only beginning to receive their due (Rydell 1993p. 8)
  • Only the 1936 Texas Centennial Exposition has been the subject of a monograph by a historian (Rydell 1993p. 8)
  • detailed horticultural images from the Columbian Fair are rare, so the record is largely word pictures (Maloney 2012p. 77)
  • physical remnants of the primary structures are scarce (Maloney 2012p. 77)
  • whether Expo 2020 or another future world's fair will revitalize the United States landscape remains to be seen (Maloney 2012p. 205)
  • the letters on Indian topics that Borgese left out of his edition, which the author says the edition forces readers to overlook (Della Coletta 2006p. 179)
  • Abruzzese's notion of the metropolitan landscape is left abstract and interchangeable; the author says he does not carry his analysis further (Della Coletta 2006p. 83)
  • an equally important, if contradictory, facet of Salgari that Magris neglects (Della Coletta 2006p. 139)
  • The connection between world's fairs and the Cold War has not received the systematic attention it deserves (Molella & Knowles 2019p. 4)
  • whether a return to the past could ever be a viable route to the future, which the author leaves open for E42 (Kargon et al. 2015p. 136)
  • how Japanese scientists kept doing research under a romantic ideology of imperial descent, which the author calls a fascinating question (Kargon et al. 2015p. 85)
  • scholarship on the NPPPE is thin; Ha Bae-Song's study is described as one of the few scholarly examinations of it (Hopsonp. 148)
  • the evidence on the navy's attitude to the expo is admittedly scant; the navy may have been more supportive than the army (Hopsonp. 137)
  • how visitors actually experienced the expo is not settled by the record: the military hall and live-fire drills may have left a more lasting impression than peace (Hopsonp. 149)
  • Spain's nineteenth-century artistic production is largely unknown to English-speaking scholars, unlike its seventeenth-century golden age (Boone 2019p. 3)
  • the role of Spanish women in the period, for which the text says readers will find few sources, all of them in Spanish (Boone 2019p. 4)
  • the recovery and wider dissemination of nineteenth-century Spanish art, design and visual culture, and its relationship to the United States, which the text calls a work in progress (Boone 2019p. 4)
  • the schism between Spain and immigrant cultures from postindependence Latin America, which the text says continues to impede development of this history (Boone 2019p. 11)
  • The active nature of the exhibition experience: historians have generally ignored the point that visitors took an active part, while scholars highlight passive observation and enjoyment (Hoffenberg 2001p. 247)
  • Maori uses of and responses to the European images, which Bell leaves to another writer (Bell 1992p. 256)
  • material left unaccounted for in the narrative (Bell 1992p. 8)
  • social and political history, which the book does not attempt (Bell 1992p. 2)
  • Cross-cultural studies of architecture and its exchanges are just beginning (Çelik 1992p. 179–180)
  • The cross-cultural influence of the fairs on Western architecture has remained in the background of exposition studies (Çelik 1992p. 153–154)
  • The colonial discourse of the occupied territories, with its arguments embedded in the culture of the mother country, was not included in this study (Çelik 1992p. 11–12)
  • The Paris 1855 essay's bibliography says very little work has been done on the 1855 exhibition and its significance, despite attention to the London 1851 exhibition. (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 26)
  • The Dublin 1853 entry says there is only one secondary source on the exhibition (Alun C. Davies). (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 17)
  • The Hanoi entry says sources from the Hanoi fair are limited (author of that entry not checked). (Findling & Pelle 2008p. 171)
  • the lack of a synthetic intermediate level of theory: the discipline has treatises on ritual, myth, ethnicity and gender and a mass of ethnographies, but little regional or thematic synthesis (Thomas 1991p. 6)
  • an account of Pacific exchange within the colonial and 'postcolonial' periods that stands on its own; the text says the facts of colonial history do not themselves provide a sufficient context for interpretation (Thomas 1991p. 205)
  • an extended study of the material context that shaped the formation of the field of religion, which the author says does not exist (Burris 2001)
  • the early history of a field of religion in Germany or France, which the author sets aside as a formidable undertaking (Burris 2001)
  • whether the 'primitive' has been adequately brought into consciousness in the field of religion today, which the author calls an open question (Burris 2001p. 177)
  • Whether recent fairs, now tied to transnational corporations, will address the nuclear and ecological crises of the present or leave us whistling in the dark (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000)
  • Whether Expo 2000 at Hannover will escape the technological utopianism of earlier fairs; the authors say it is too early to tell (Rydell, Findling & Pelle 2000)
  • Dublin 1853: modern scholarship is scant (Davies, Allwood only) (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 11)
  • Paris 1855: the fine arts sections are the only facet examined seriously by scholars (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 21)
  • London 1862: secondary sources have largely overlooked the exhibition (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 30)
  • Fair statistics: substantial discrepancies abound in the literature on attendance, dates and accounts (Findling & Pelle 1990p. 375)
  • whether anthropologists should stop interpreting or simply add more perspectives once culture and context are seen as constructs (Harvey 1996p. 48)
  • the attention to embodied specificity is lost when process becomes form and social facts are generated (Harvey 1996p. 173)
  • what anthropology can learn from mass popular events such as Expo'92, where the ethnographic focus on difference is not available, is of a different order from daily practice in a place such as Mount Hagen (Harvey 1996p. 13)
  • Swoboda's paintings have been curiously neglected by anthropologists, art historians, curators and artists (Mathur 2007p. 82)
  • how the museological paradigms of the Holocaust memorial may enhance or hinder the memory of Sikh history and the violent experiences of partition in Punjab (Mathur 2007)
  • Mega-events have attracted relatively little research attention, and they fall between several disciplines (Roche 2000p. 5)
  • The popular culture of sport, which was at least as important as exhibitions in forming collective identities in 1870-1914, is missing from accounts centred on exhibitions (Roche 2000p. 38)
  • Cross-cultural reception analysis of the audience for Olympic television, which the Barcelona 1992 research team said had not been done well enough (Roche 2000p. 188)
  • The book is a preliminary contribution to a research agenda on mega-events, agency, structure and continuity in modernity (Roche 2000p. 235)
  • Very little reliable secondary literature on the great expositions exists, although there are vast amounts of extant materials that could support useful histories. (Mandell 1967)
  • American historians have not studied the fairs of 1876 (Philadelphia), 1893 (Chicago) or 1904 (St. Louis), each of which has scope for several monographs. (Mandell 1967p. 122)
  • Whether the 1900 exposition was itself a factor for change in France is, by Mandell's own admission, debatable. (Mandell 1967p. 120)
  • No recent writer has investigated what kind of Art Nouveau was actually at the fair. (Mandell 1967)
  • a broader picture of museum developments beyond Britain, Australia and the United States, which the author says still needs to be examined (Bennett 2004p. 2)
  • the Postscript does not engage adequately with the relations between museums and government, and maps only directions for future work (Bennett 2004p. 11)
  • Showmen, spectators and performers left few or no records of their encounters with one another (Qureshi 2011p. 9)
  • Sources that would reconstruct performers' motivations and perceptions are rare (Qureshi 2011p. 9)
  • The intercultural encounters of foreign communities resident in London have had less research integrated into discussions of the city's cosmopolitan crowd (Qureshi 2011p. 45)
  • The incorporation of the Völkerschauen (people shows) into German anthropology, as an exception to the wider neglect of human displays in anthropology's history (Qureshi 2011p. 186)
  • Whether the Fair's business elite succeeded in regulating the Midway and its audience: 'Whether they even half succeeded, however, is something that requires much more careful examination' (Gilbert 1991p. 82)
  • The workers' city: the book is 'not a book about work or workers' and does not venture into the city of the men and women who built the Fair's environment (Gilbert 1991p. 2)
  • The Midway as a neglected part of the Fair in earlier historiography, which Gilbert presents as only partly redressed by recent work (Gilbert 1991p. 80)
  • how consumers interpreted the trademark images, which the author says cannot be fully assessed (Hale 2008p. 162)
  • What women achieved for themselves through the Building, beyond its displays; Miller asks 'what she achieved for herself is a question' and notes that the Building did not bring the vote closer (Weimann 1981)
  • Bertha Palmer's own credit for the Building, which Miller says is usually given to Susan B. Anthony, who served the Board in no capacity (Weimann 1981)
  • The economic benefit to participants of exhibiting at a world exposition: the text says there has never been a comprehensive study on it. (Allwood et al. 2001p. 195)
  • The smaller, specialized-type expositions: the text says there is no consensus of any sort on them. (Allwood et al. 2001p. 201)
  • Analytical research on the medium as a whole, which the bibliographic note says is more difficult to find than books on individual events. (Allwood et al. 2001p. 215)
  • What role the medium should play in international affairs in the future, which the authors call for an international conference to decide. (Allwood et al. 2001p. 201)
  • the field observations of the four collectors, which they published almost nothing of, so that a major record of thought is missing (Gosden & Knowles 2001)
  • what happened to the objects once they reached the USA, Europe or Australia, including their display and representation, which the authors say they focused on less (Gosden & Knowles 2001)
  • comparative studies of colonialism in Africa and worldwide, which the authors say collection research can help (Gosden & Knowles 2001)
  • the research potential held in museums for understanding colonial histories (Gosden & Knowles 2001)
  • How audiences experienced the bazaar, museum and department store, which the text says is difficult to gauge from the sources (Giberti 2002)
  • The non-visual experience of the exhibition (sound, smell, the din of the crowd), which the text says must be recovered to understand its full reality (Giberti 2002)
  • more experiments involving indigenous experts and the sharing of authority with cultural groups (Karp & Lavine 1991)
  • how a non-Indian audience understood the Goswamy exhibitions, which the author says he is not sure of (Karp & Lavine 1991)
  • a collective history of women as a population group, not only of individual women, in the history of the fair and of exhibitions (Ganz 2008)
  • the fair itself is little recognised compared with government-sponsored Depression-era projects such as the Tennessee Valley Authority, because it was a privately run project (Ganz 2008)
  • the individual experiences of visitors, which the Fair's story has largely left out (Samuel 2007)
  • the popular music, jazz, folk and rhythm and blues, and the youth culture and African American expression that the Fair did not include (Samuel 2007)
  • the attendance of 52 million: far less attention has been paid to the people who came than to the eighteen million who did not (Samuel 2007)
  • Korean voices, silenced by censorship in the 1910s and the early 1940s, which the author says leaves the subjugated knowledges of poor Koreans only partly recoverable (Henry 2014p. 13)
  • the subjugated knowledges of nonelite residents, which Henry says her sources cannot fully reach and which remain a limitation of the book (Henry 2014p. 14)
  • the postcolonial monuments on Namsan and the restored Kyŏngbok Palace, which she says silence the colonial past and invite a dialogue about it (Henry 2014p. 216)
